full_text:
I’m sharing my Jindal Steel placement experience to help juniors understand the process and prepare more effectively. My selection process had two stages: an online assessment (OA) followed by a technical interview. The details below reflect my personal experience, so the exact format and questions may vary for other candidates.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The OA consisted of technical questions from Mechanical Engineering, along with basic aptitude questions. The overall difficulty level was moderate.

How to prepare

Revise core Mechanical Engineering subjects and practise objective-type technical questions.

Prepare basic aptitude topics and solve a few timed practice sets.

Focus on understanding concepts rather than memorising answers.

2. Technical Interview

The interview started with my introduction. After that, the interviewer moved straight into a rapid-fire round of technical questions. I was asked around 30–35 questions covering almost every subject I had studied during my Mechanical Engineering academics.

Most of the questions were basic and focused on fundamental concepts rather than deep, detailed theory. The interview itself was quite short, and the interviewer moved quickly from one question to the next.

My recommendations for this round

Prepare the fundamentals of as many core Mechanical Engineering subjects as possible. You do not necessarily need to study every topic in extreme depth, but you should be able to explain the basic concepts clearly.

Give extra attention to Material Science and Strength of Materials (SOM), as these are especially important areas to revise.

Practise answering short technical questions aloud. The rapid-fire format means you should be comfortable giving clear, direct answers without getting stuck on one topic.

Revise key definitions, laws, formulas, material properties, and basic applications across your core subjects.

Do not prepare only a few favourite subjects. Questions can come from almost anywhere in your Mechanical Engineering coursework.

Final Advice for Juniors

My main advice is to revise the fundamentals across your Mechanical Engineering subjects instead of going too deep into only a few topics. Pay special attention to Material Science and Strength of Materials (SOM), and make sure you can explain basic concepts, formulas, and applications in simple words. Since the interview may move quickly between subjects, practise giving concise answers and keep revising the core concepts.

full_text:
This year, I got the opportunity to participate in the campus recruitment drive of Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) for the post of Engineer Officer (Instrumentation).

The selection process consisted of three stages:

1. CGPA-Based Screening: Students were shortlisted based on their CGPA for the next round.

2. Group Task (GT): Shortlisted candidates were given a one-page case study with 3–4 problem statements to discuss and solve as a team. From our Instrumentation department, 48 students were shortlisted for the GT, 28 proceeded to the interview, and 12 were finally selected.

My advice for the GT is to focus on solving the given problems rather than discussing only the general pros and cons of the case study. Write down your expectations and solutions in points, listen to others, and contribute constructively. Try to speak at least twice during the discussion, and be confident and respectful towards your teammates.

3. Personal Interview: The interview lasted around 10–12 minutes and included HR and technical questions. For preparation, I would recommend revising core Instrumentation subjects, particularly Industrial Instrumentation (flow, level and pressure measurement), PLC, DCS, SCADA, and industrial safety with practical examples.

Prepare your internship, projects, and every skill mentioned on your resume thoroughly. Be ready to explain your contributions, what you learned, and the working principles of the instruments you encountered. Also, prepare for HR questions about your family background, hobbies, career goals, and interest in higher studies or entrepreneurship. If you mention any skill or hobby, be prepared to answer follow-up questions about it.

My interview focused mainly on HR questions, and I was also asked about MATLAB and LaTeX. Technical questions were asked to other candidates, so preparation across all areas is important. The questions and discussion topics varied from candidate to candidate.

Finally, I would like to thank my college and Instrumentation department for providing relevant coursework and building a strong technical foundation, and our Training and Placement Office (TPO) for providing this opportunity and ensuring a smooth placement process. I am equally grateful to my family and friends for their constant support and encouragement throughout this journey.

I hope my experience helps juniors preparing for their placement season. All the best to everyone!

Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn if anyone have any questions about the HPCL placement process or preparation. I would be happy to help.

Reliance Industries – Internship PPO Experience

I received my PPO opportunity at Reliance Industries Limited, Hazira, through a three-stage selection process.

1. Online Assessment (OA)
The first round was an online assessment conducted in the CC Lab. It was the initial screening stage of the process.

2. Company Shortlisting
Following the assessment, the company shortlisted candidates for the next round. The shortlisting was done by the company, and the criteria were not explicitly communicated to us.

3. Personal Interview (PI)
The final stage was a personal interview, which covered three major areas:

Resume-based questions: Questions about the projects, internships, technical skills, and experiences mentioned in my resume.

Manufacturing-related questions: Questions assessing my understanding of manufacturing processes and core mechanical engineering concepts.

Company-related questions: Questions about Reliance Industries, its business operations, and the company's work.

The interview was a mix of questions about my past experiences, technical knowledge, and understanding of the company.

Preparation tips for juniors:

Be thorough with every project and experience mentioned on your resume.

Revise core mechanical engineering and manufacturing concepts.

Research Reliance Industries, its major business segments, and the operations of the Hazira manufacturing complex.

Practise explaining your answers clearly and confidently.

Overall, having a strong understanding of your resume, engineering fundamentals, and the company can help you prepare well for the selection process.

full_text:
The recruitment process at San Pharma consisted of an Online Assessment (OA), followed by HR and Technical Interview rounds. The entire interview process was completed in a single day.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an online assessment based on the candidate’s engineering domain. For example, students from Production Engineering were asked questions related to production and manufacturing concepts. Therefore, revising the core subjects of your respective branch is important.

2. Interview Process

Candidates who cleared the OA proceeded to the interview rounds. Both the HR and Technical interviews were conducted on the same day.

HR Round:

The HR round focused on basic personal and professional questions, including:

- Tell me about yourself.

- Describe your family background.

- Are you comfortable with relocation?

- Why do you want to join San Pharma?

Technical Round:

The technical interview focused primarily on the candidate’s resume, knowledge of the company, and understanding of pharmaceutical manufacturing. Questions included:

- Detailed questions about the projects, internships, and skills mentioned in your resume.

- What do you know about San Pharma?

- What is the production process in a pharmaceutical company?

- What types of products are manufactured in the pharmaceutical industry?

- What are the different stages involved in pharmaceutical production?

3. Preparation Tips

Based on my experience, I would recommend the following preparation strategy:

- Prepare your resume thoroughly: Be ready to explain every project, internship, technical skill, and achievement mentioned in it.

- Revise your core subjects: Focus on concepts related to your engineering branch, particularly production and manufacturing.

- Review the company presentation: Go through the PPT shared during the pre-placement presentation to understand the company, its operations, and its products.

- Prepare for basic HR questions: Practise questions such as “Tell me about yourself,” “Why do you want to join San Pharma?” and “Are you comfortable with relocation?”

- Understand pharmaceutical manufacturing: Familiarise yourself with the basic production processes and different types of pharmaceutical products.

Overall Experience

The recruitment process was straightforward and focused on domain knowledge, resume-based questions, company awareness, and basic HR assessment. Thorough preparation of your resume, core subjects, and the company presentation can help you approach the process with greater confidence.

The HPCL placement process began with the shortlisting of students based on their CGPA and category. This was followed by document verification, during which our category certificates and all semester DMCs were verified.

The next day, we had a Group Task (GT) based on a case study. A problem related to the given case study was presented, and our group had to discuss it and propose a suitable solution. A panel of eight members observed the entire discussion. They paid attention to students who actively participated, contributed relevant points, listened to others, and helped the group reach a logical solution. One important thing I learned was to focus on the discussion rather than looking at the panel while presenting my points. It is essential to maintain a natural discussion with fellow group members, support your arguments with logical reasoning, and ensure meaningful participation throughout the task.

After the GT, students were shortlisted for the interview round. My interview lasted approximately 15 minutes and included both HR and technical questions. I began by introducing myself, after which the panel asked two to three questions related to my internship and project work. They also asked questions about my family background, followed by a technical question about communication protocols used in industries.

Overall, my experience taught me the importance of having a clear understanding of my projects and internship, preparing both technical and HR questions, and developing effective communication and teamwork skills. For future aspirants, I would suggest staying confident, being honest in your answers, participating actively in the GT, and revising the fundamentals of your core subjects, especially industrial instrumentation, automation, PLC, DCS, SCADA, and industrial communication protocols.

full_text:
1. There was a category wise shortlisting based upon cgpa. In our case, total 48 students got shortlisted for the Group Task.

2. Again the GT was conducted category wise, with each group of around 7-8 candidates. Each group was given 10 minutes of reading time for a case study followed by 15 mins for the actual group task to be performed. So, a GT is very different from a GD, here you are supposed to work as a team. Try speaking for atleast 4-5 times with quality points and never disagree with the points put by your teammates. Remember that a good leader is a good listener. If someone tries to cut your point then simply stop speaking, let the other person speak and note down his point instead (you would be provided with a notepad as well to jot down important things , and better to maintain that nicely because that is evaluated at the end by the panel). There is no fixed rule to how many candidates from a group would make it to the interview. From most of the groups, 4 were selected for PIs and from my group, 7 out of 8 went ahead.

3. For all the categories the PIs were mostly resume based so only mention what you actually know, they will only check whether you are actually who you are trying to claim. For the UR category, the level of interviews shot up, situation based questions were asked.

4. My PI experience: so I was mostly asked situation based questions which were actually thought-provoking with multiple follow up questions. Very good technical questions from the refinery operations were also asked. What I could feel was that they were trying to build a lot of pressure on me and check how well I could perform under pressure. You may never know what they are trying to look into you, so just stay honest with who you actually are as a person.

Keep working hard, you may never know which moment could change the trajectory of your life.

title: Medtronic Internship and Full-Time Conversion Experience

key_questions: Interview Experience

full_text:
1. Online Assessment

OA of Medtronic was too long.

Date of Test: 12th November 2025

The online assessment was conducted in three parts, one after another:

Generic Test

Technical Test

Psychometric Test

The test login window was from 7:00 PM to 7:30 PM, so we had to log in within that time.

Once you complete the Generic Test, a message appears on the screen saying, "Another test is lined up for you." You need to click on "Take me to the next test" to proceed to the Technical Test. The same process is followed after completing the Technical Test to start the Psychometric Test.

2. Interview Experience

I got shortlisted for the interview, which was initially scheduled for 18th November 2025 at 3:30 PM. However, the timing was later postponed to 8:00 PM.

One thing I would like to mention is that if your interview doesn't happen at the scheduled time, don't worry. You can mail the HR team about it, and they will help you with the next steps.

The interview was scheduled for 30 minutes, but mine went on for around an hour.

The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself. He then went through my resume and asked me about the projects I had mentioned. I was asked to explain what I had done in those projects and give a brief overview of my work.

After that, he asked me questions related to Operating Systems, Databases, and other core Computer Science subjects. I don't remember all the exact questions now, but the interview was mostly theoretical. He also asked me two basic coding questions.

Towards the end, he asked me about some of the technologies the company was currently using and whether I had worked with them before. I was familiar with two of the technologies, but I hadn't worked with one of them. I honestly told him that I wasn't familiar with it but would definitely learn it if required.

My advice would be to be clear with your fundamentals, prepare the projects mentioned in your resume properly, and be honest if you don't know something. You don't need to know everything, but you should be willing to learn.

3. Internship Experience and Full-Time Conversion

After the interview, I got selected for the internship with a PPO opportunity. The internship duration was eight months.

During the internship, I worked on an assigned project for the entire eight-month period. Generally, interns may not get access to all the company's internal data and systems, so the project I worked on was more of a standalone project that I could work on independently.

At the end of the internship, we had to give a presentation about our work during those eight months. We had to explain what we had worked on, the things we had learned, and our overall experience during the internship. From my experience, the focus was mostly on what we had learned throughout the internship period.

After completing this process, I got my full-time offer at Medtronic!

Overall, it was a really good experience, and I learned a lot during my internship. It was a great opportunity to understand how things work in a corporate environment and to improve both my technical and professional skills.

My advice to future candidates would be to focus on your fundamentals, know your projects well, and make the most of your internship. Be open to learning new technologies, ask questions whenever you need help, and try to learn as much as possible during your internship.

All the best to everyone preparing for the upcoming placement season!

full_text:
My placement journey at NIT Jalandhar has been a truly memorable and rewarding experience. Initially, I was quite worried about my career prospects, especially because I come from the Department of Textile Technology. Like many students, I had concerns about finding the right opportunity and building a successful career after graduation.

However, as the placement process progressed, my perspective changed. Serving as a Placement Representative (PR) for my department gave me a unique opportunity to understand the placement process from a different perspective. I witnessed the tremendous effort, coordination, and dedication required from the Training and Placement Office (TPO) to create opportunities for students. This experience helped me understand the hard work that goes on behind the scenes and made me appreciate the entire TPO team even more.

One of the biggest milestones in my journey was receiving an international opportunity. I joined Jay Jay Mills Lanka as a Management Trainee for a six-month internship and subsequently transitioned to Jay Jay Textile Lanka. Working in Sri Lanka has been an incredible experience, allowing me to gain practical industry exposure, understand real-world challenges, and grow both professionally and personally. Looking back, I never imagined that my placement journey would lead me to an international career opportunity, and I am genuinely grateful for how things have turned out.

Throughout this journey, the support and guidance of the TPO team have been invaluable. Having experienced the placement process both as a student and as a Placement Representative, I understand that arranging opportunities for students requires immense effort, patience, and coordination. I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to the entire TPO team, my department, and NIT Jalandhar for their continuous support.

My Message to My Juniors

My biggest advice to my juniors is simple: Be confident, be honest, and be ready to work hard.

During interviews and group discussions, companies look beyond academic knowledge. Your communication skills, confidence, problem-solving ability, teamwork, attitude, and willingness to learn all matter. You do not need to know everything, but you should be willing to learn anything. Express your thoughts clearly, listen to others, respect different opinions, and be honest about what you know.

For group discussions, focus on contributing meaningful points rather than simply speaking more than everyone else. For interviews, prepare well, understand your strengths, work on your weaknesses, and never hesitate to acknowledge something you do not know. Confidence comes with preparation and practice, so keep working on your speaking ability and overall personality.

Do not lose confidence when you see others performing better than you. Everyone has a different starting point, and everyone improves at their own pace. Instead of comparing yourself with others, learn from them. Practise together, share knowledge, and help one another improve. Build a strong group where everyone encourages others to grow rather than treating every opportunity as a competition. When you grow together, everyone benefits.

Also, do not limit yourself because of your branch or your initial placement expectations. Your first opportunity may not always be the one you imagined, but staying open to different possibilities can take you in unexpected directions. Focus on developing your capabilities, remain consistent, and trust the process.

Finally, have faith in yourself and keep working hard, even when things do not go as planned. There will be moments of uncertainty, but do not let them define your potential. Be patient, stay disciplined, support your peers, and never stop improving yourself. With consistent effort, you will eventually become a better version of yourself and be ready to make the most of the opportunities that come your way.

I will always be thankful to NIT Jalandhar for the opportunities, experiences, and lessons that have shaped my professional journey. Moving from a worried student to working in an international environment has taught me the importance of perseverance, adaptability, and continuous learning.

Thank you, NIT Jalandhar and the entire TPO team, for being an important part of my journey.

full_text:
1. Overall Experience

My experience with the campus placement drive was a mix of learning and challenges. While I appreciate the opportunity provided by the company and the efforts made by the placement team to facilitate the recruitment process, there were certain aspects that made the overall experience difficult for students.

2. Clarity Regarding the Job Offer

Initially, our primary expectation was to secure a full-time employment (FTE) opportunity. However, after the interview process, it became clear that the offer was primarily structured around an internship, with the internship being a compulsory part of the process. This was something we had not fully anticipated beforehand.

Having clear information about the nature of the offer, the mandatory internship requirements, and the available employment options before the recruitment process would have helped students understand the opportunity better and make decisions with greater clarity.

3. Stipend and Financial Considerations

Another major concern was the internship stipend of ₹25,000 per month, particularly considering the cost of living in metropolitan cities such as Bangalore and Hyderabad. Expenses related to accommodation, food, transportation, and other necessities can consume a significant portion of the stipend, making it difficult for students to manage their finances comfortably.

A more competitive stipend or some flexibility in the compensation structure would have made the opportunity more practical and financially sustainable for students relocating to these cities.

4. Flexibility and Consideration of Student Concerns

During the process, we tried to express our concerns and explore whether there was any possibility of flexibility in the offer terms. However, there appeared to be limited scope for discussion or adjustment from the company's side.

The situation also created pressure from both the placement process and the company's requirements, leaving students with limited alternatives once the interview process was completed and the offer was presented. Greater flexibility and an open discussion of student concerns could have helped create a more comfortable and balanced decision-making process.

5. Suggestions for Future Placement Drives

Based on this experience, I believe a few improvements could make future placement drives more effective:

Clear communication: Specify whether the opportunity is for an internship, full-time employment, or a mandatory internship-to-employment pathway before the recruitment process begins.

Transparent compensation: Communicate the stipend, employment terms, and other relevant conditions in advance.

Student-centric approach: Consider students' financial constraints, relocation expenses, and genuine concerns when structuring offers.

Scope for discussion: Provide reasonable flexibility to address concerns and clarify expectations before students make their final decisions.

6. Final Thoughts

Despite these challenges, I value the opportunity to participate in the placement drive and the experience gained through the recruitment process. My feedback is intended to highlight areas where communication, transparency, and flexibility could be improved, rather than to disregard the opportunity itself.

I believe that campus placements work best when the expectations of both the company and the students are aligned. A more transparent and student-centric approach would help students make confident decisions, reduce uncertainty, and create a more positive placement experience for future batches.

full_text:
Selection Process

The selection process consisted of 3-4 rounds, covering DSA, core computer science fundamentals, system design, and HR.

Round 1: Written Test (Pen and Paper)

The first round was a written test conducted using pen and paper. It covered topics such as Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA), SQL, and other technical fundamentals.

Preparation tip: Practise solving problems on paper, revise SQL queries, and focus on understanding the logic behind your solutions.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The second round was a technical interview in which DSA questions were given to solve on a laptop. After the coding questions, the interviewer asked questions about core computer science fundamentals and concepts/teckstacks mentioned in resume.

Topics included:

Data Structures and Algorithms

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)

Computer Networks (CN)

Operating Systems (OS)

Java fundamentals

Spring and Spring Boot basics

Preparation tip: Practise coding problems in your preferred programming language and revise core CS subjects alongside DSA and projects in resume. Be prepared to explain your approach, complexity, and edge cases.

Round 3: Technical Interview

This round focused entirely on technical fundamentals and system design. No DSA questions were asked.

The discussion covered core computer science concepts and some basic system design questions and resume projects. A clear understanding of fundamental concepts and the ability to explain technologies used in projects are important for this round.

Preparation tip: Revise OOP, OS, CN, Java, database concepts, and basic system design. Understand how these concepts apply to real-world software applications.

Round 4: HR Interview

The final round was relatively straightforward. The interviewer asked a few questions about my preferences and other general HR-related topics. At the end of the round, I was informed that I had been selected.

Final Preparation Advice

My recommendation to future candidates is to prepare for both coding and conceptual rounds. Do not focus exclusively on DSA; core CS fundamentals, Java, Spring basics, SQL, and system design can also play an important role in the selection process.

Practise coding regularly, revise the fundamentals, and prepare to explain your projects and technical decisions clearly. Stay confident and approach each round systematically.

Overall, the key is to maintain a balance between problem-solving skills and a strong understanding of computer science fundamentals.

I am Muskan Kaur from Instrumentation and Control Engineering

Round 1: Technical Interview

The interviewer asked me to briefly introduce myself including my family background academic background internship and projects.

They then went through my resume and asked questions about my project and its aim. Based on my project they asked about accuracy precision range and span. They also asked whether I had studied set and subset concepts and which of range and span is a subset of the other.

Next they asked basic questions about PLCs and asked me to draw a ladder logic diagram. They also asked how to configure a PLC using TIA Portal.

They gave me a tank level control problem and asked me to identify the inputs and outputs. They also asked about the working principle of a level sensor and the type of signal produced by a float level sensor.

The interviewer then asked about the experiments I had performed in my microprocessor lab and the difference between a microprocessor and a PLC.

They also asked whether I had studied analog and digital electronics. From this topic they asked about flip-flops and how to implement them using PLC ladder logic.

Round 2: Technical and HR Interview

The second technical round and HR round were combined.

I started with my introduction and then faced a series of questions related to my major project. They asked how I implemented the project and achieved its aim. They also asked why I chose a stepper motor and how I implemented PID control in the project. I was also asked why I had selected this project.

The interviewer then shifted to control systems and asked about predictive control and the Kalman filter.

During the HR discussion I was asked who had contributed the most work in my project team and how I would handle a situation where one of my teammates was not contributing.

They also asked about family restrictions and whether I was comfortable with relocation travelling and meeting clients.

Preparation Tips

I would suggest focusing on your resume first because the interviewers asked several questions based on the projects and technical skills mentioned in it.

Prepare your projects thoroughly and be ready to explain their aim working principle implementation and challenges.

For core subjects I would recommend giving special attention to Industrial Instrumentation and Measurement and Control Systems. Make sure your fundamentals are clear and practise explaining concepts in simple words.

All the best everyone! Mehnat karte raho aur khud par bharosa rakho. You never know which opportunity can change your journey.

Online Assessment

The Online Assessment consisted of aptitude questions (both verbal and quantitative), image-based pattern completion questions, and core subject questions. The core section mainly covered Control Systems, including Bode plot, Nyquist plot , gain and phase margin, PID controllers, compensators, etc., along with some questions from Sensors.

Accuracy vs. precision

full_text:
I am Abhishek Yadav, from Instrumentation and Control Engineering.

Talking about the whole process. It was a one-day process with 5 panelists in total — 4 technical panelists and 1 HR.

The process started with a PPT session of around 30 minutes followed by Technical Interview 1 → HR Round → Technical Interview 2.

PPT Session

The process started with the company PPT. One thing I would suggest is that you should not just prepare basic information like revenue or number of employees. Try to know what makes the company different. Read about their major projects, recent innovations and press releases.

During the PPT there was some interaction with the panel. My interaction went quite well and the panelists actually clapped for me which gave me a good confidence boost for the interviews.

Technical Interview 1

I was the first candidate to be interviewed.

It started with a brief introduction and then they asked me about my favourite subject. From there they mainly focused on the technical skills and subjects that I mentioned.

They started with IMS and then moved towards PLC and some Control Systems.

They did not go very deep into my projects. Instead they focused more on the technical topics I had mentioned during my introduction.

My suggestion would be that jo bhi apne resume ya introduction mein bol rahe ho usko properly prepare karke jaana. They can pick any topic from there.

HR Round

My HR round was actually very good.

She asked me to introduce myself in a way that would help her understand what kind of person I actually am. It was not just the usual "tell me about yourself".

She asked about my personality, managerial skills, strengths, qualities and how I work in a team.

The conversation was quite comfortable and realistic. At that point I honestly felt that I had a very good chance of getting selected.

Technical Interview 2

The final technical round was with the remaining panelists.

They asked about my IOCL internship and the instruments I had worked with or observed there. They asked about instrument calibration and some basic instrumentation terminology.

They also asked about higher studies and why I would or would not consider them. Apart from technical questions they also asked about my PORs and soft skills.

Overall both technical interviews were roughly 80-20 for me. Around 80% of the questions I was able to answer properly. For the remaining 20% I either didn't know the answer or my answer had some deviation from the actual concept.

Some things I would personally suggest

1. Know the company properly.
Read about the company as much as you can. Go through their press releases, major projects, innovations and what makes them different from their competitors.

2. Focus strongly on Control Systems, PLC and IMS.
These were quite important in my interviews.

3. Remember the important formulas and principles.
Don't just memorize them. Understand the principle behind them and where they are used. If possible remember the derivations too.

4. Stick to your answer.
Don't unnecessarily drift away from what you have said. The panel can pick up something you mentioned earlier and ask a follow-up question.

5. Don't worry too much about English.
You don't need to speak fancy English. Just try to speak clearly and correctly. But yes I would prefer answering in English during the interview.

6. In HR be realistic.
Don't try to give a textbook answer just because you think that is what HR wants to hear. Be honest and realistic about your personality, strengths, weaknesses and future plans.

At the end I would say the interviews were not about knowing everything. They were more about how clearly you understand what you claim to know and how you handle the questions you don't know and how honest you are with company as well as with your resume

At last, all the best to everyone preparing for Siemens Energy. Believe in you, believe in God – and you will succees 100%.....

full_text:
I am sharing my Toshiba recruitment experience to give juniors an idea about the selection process, questions asked, and how to prepare, especially for CSE/IT students interested in low-level and embedded development.

Coming from an IT background, I initially wasn't sure how much embedded and low-level knowledge would be expected during the interviews. The overall process turned out to be a great test of C programming, embedded fundamentals, operating systems, computer fundamentals, bit manipulation, problem-solving, and project knowledge.

Recruitment Process

The selection process consisted of:

Online Assessment

Technical Interview – Round 1

Technical Interview – Round 2

HR and Managerial Rounds

1. Online Assessment

The Online Assessment consisted of 40 questions in total. There was 1 coding question in C, 14 C-based MCQs, and the remaining questions focused on mental ability and analytical reasoning.

The coding question was a very basic DSA/problem-solving question and was quite straightforward. It was primarily meant to test whether the candidate was comfortable with basic logic and C programming rather than advanced DSA. I was able to solve it quickly.

For the MCQs, a good understanding of C fundamentals and output-based questions is important. The mental ability and analytical sections were also manageable, but time management and accuracy were important because of the overall time constraint.

Overall, I found the OA to be relatively easy, especially if your C fundamentals and basic problem-solving skills are clear.

2. Technical Interview – Round 1

The first technical interview started with a brief self-introduction, after which the interviewer quickly moved into technical questions. The discussion initially focused on embedded systems and low-level concepts, which was especially relevant to the role.

Some of the questions I was asked included:

What is an interrupt?

Difference between polling and interrupt-driven I/O

Difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor

What does the volatile keyword mean in Embedded C?

What is an RTOS?

The interview then shifted towards Operating Systems, where I was asked about concepts such as:

Deadlocks

Mutex

Semaphores

After the conceptual discussion, the interview moved to coding. I was asked a few bit-manipulation problems, followed by 2–3 follow-up questions based on my approach. Bit manipulation was an important part of the coding discussion, so I would strongly recommend preparing it well.

The interviewer then asked me LeetCode 2 – Add Two Numbers, a linked-list problem involving the addition of two numbers represented using linked lists. This tested basic linked-list implementation and problem-solving skills.

Overall, the interview was a very positive experience. The interviewer was really chill and approachable, which made the discussion feel more like a technical conversation than a stressful interrogation. Even during the follow-up questions, I was given enough space to explain my approach and reasoning.

3. Technical Interview – Round 2

The second technical interview started with a brief introduction, after which the interviewer went through my resume and focused on my projects.

For a project, I was asked to explain it end-to-end, including:

The problem statement and motivation behind the project

The overall architecture and workflow

The technologies and components used

The challenges I faced during development

How I approached and solved those challenges

The key learnings from the project

The interviewer then moved to a coding question based on bit manipulation. I was asked to implement the functionality of __builtin_popcount, i.e., count the number of set bits (1s) in a number.

The interview also included a brief feedback discussion towards the end.

Compared to the first technical round, this interview was considerably shorter and was more focused on my projects, implementation details, and basic problem-solving rather than a wide range of core technical concepts.

4. HR & Managerial Rounds

The final rounds were comparatively relaxed and mostly focused on getting to know me beyond the technical aspects of the interview.

I was asked about my family background, my overall interview experience, and whether I had appeared for any previous interviews. There was also a general discussion about my background and career interests.

One question that I think is particularly important for CSE/IT students applying for this role is:

"Why embedded development, especially when you are from CSE/IT?"

I would recommend preparing a genuine and convincing answer for this. Since the role involves working with low-level systems, C/C++ and embedded technologies, the interviewer may want to understand why you are interested in this domain and whether you are genuinely willing to work in it.

Overall, the HR/managerial discussions were quite comfortable and felt more like a conversation than a formal interview.

Tips for Juniors

Based on my experience, I would recommend the following to anyone preparing for the Toshiba recruitment process:

C is extremely important throughout the process. Be comfortable with pointers, arrays, functions, structures, operators, memory, strings, and output-based questions. Also practice writing small programs in C without relying too much on IDE assistance.

For an IT student, I would recommend revising Operating Systems, Computer Organization and Architecture, memory concepts, OOP and basic embedded systems concepts.

For embedded-related topics, focus on understanding the fundamentals rather than trying to memorize advanced microcontroller details.

If you're from CSE/IT, prepare for the "Why Embedded?" question

This is something I would definitely prepare beforehand. Be ready to explain why you are interested in embedded/low-level development despite coming from CSE/IT, and make sure the answer is genuine.

Know your resume inside out and explain your thought process.
Stay calm.

All the best for your placements!

full_text:
The Process

My journey with Reliance started with an Online Assessment conducted through Unstop. After the OA, the list of shortlisted students was released, followed by a virtual interview.

My interview lasted around 25 minutes and was mostly about my projects and core subjects. When I was asked about my favourite subject, I said IMS, and the interviewer followed it up with questions on topics like thermocouples, cold junction compensation. Other candidates were asked questions like i/p convertor, feedback system, control valves.

He also asked me:

Why Reliance?
Why Instrumentation & Control Engineering?
Why NIT Jalandhar?
What was the inspiration behind my project?

After the interview, I was selected for the summer internship at Reliance.

Important topics you must know : IMS (flow measurement, pressure measurement, temp measurement, level measurement), control valves, PDC, KNOW EVERYTHING WRITTEN IN YOUR RESUME.

The Internship

After joining, I was assigned a project and spent the internship working on it and learning from the people around me.There were two assessments during the internship to track our progress. Towards the end, we were asked about our internship experience and whether we were interested in a PPO.

And eventually, I got the PPO from Reliance.

What I Learned from the Interview

One thing I realised is that an interview is not about knowing the answer to every question. It is also about knowing how to handle the questions you don't know.

The very first question of my interview was something I couldn't answer. Instead of panicking or trying to make up an answer, I simply told the interviewer that I didn't know. We moved on to the next question.

So, a few things I would suggest:

1. Don't panic when you don't know something.
It's okay not to know an answer. Be honest and move on. Don't bluff.

2. Work on your communication.
Getting nervous is completely normal, but don't let it affect how you communicate what you know. Practice ques from chatgpt. Give mock interview at least 2 days before your main interview, despite the level of preparation.

3. Don't compare yourself with other candidates.
It's easy to think about how others are performing. I feel it's better to focus on your own preparation and your own progress.

4. Believe in yourself.
You may not know everything, and you may make mistakes, but don't let that make you doubt yourself. Prepare well, give your best, and keep improving. Stay away from people who let you down or say "tera to ho hi jayega".

5. Practice more.
According to me interview is not about how much knowledge you have its about how well you deliver whatever you know, so practice communication. Be honest.

ALL THE BEST. YOU ARE THE BEST. YOU CAN DO IT!!!

full_text:
PPT

This may come out as a surprise to most of you, but this Toshiba is pretty strict with the PPT attendance. The ones who didnt attend the PPT were debarred. I arrived 15 minutes late, and I was debarred too. But I talked with the HR and explained my situation that I was returning from my hometown and could not make it in time. They were kind enough to make that exception and Im glad that they did.

OA

Round 1 2 4 were MCQ, Round 3 was DSA in C

Round 1 and 2 were aptitude, pretty standard questions.

Round 3 was DSA in C. Q-> You are given an array of integers with some integers set as 0. U have to populate the 0s with the neighbour with largest magnitude. In case of continuous 0s, u have to take the neighbour as the first int that comes after the 0s. I was unable to arrive to the correct solution in time and I thought I had lost my chances of selection. But I got selected without having correctly solved the question, but some students who had gotten easier questions and did solve the question did not get selected. So remember, luck plays an important role.

Round 4 was C syntax/codes MCQ

Among Round 1 2 4, I skipped maybe 5 questions out of the ~30. I focussed on accuracy, so that is something you should keep in your mind.

Interview

Interview was the next day. Round 1 and 2 - technical. Round 3 - HR

I arrived at CTP at 9am. CSE/IT Round 1 was being conducted online, meanwhile Round 1 for ECE was being conducted in-person. There were different job descriptions, so Ive heard. By 3:00pm. Most of the candidates who got their interview in the beginning were done with their Round 3, while I was still waiting for Round 1. At this point I had lost all hopes of getting a fair chance so I was really demotivated. But by 3:30pm I got my Round 1.

Round 1 - The interview openned with My introduction and project/internship experience. I had pretty decent background in microcontrollers so I might have an edge above other candidates. I was followed with some questions regarding my internship. Then I was given some C code problem statements revolving around bit operations. 1. C code to convert Little Endiyan to Big Endiyan. 2. Swap 15th and 30th bit of a number. 3. Given an array with all but 1 numbers in pairs (1, 2,2, 3,3), You have to find the unique number. I was able to solve this quickly as it was a leetcode easy. Then I was followed with a modified question - How to find 2 numbers when there are 2 unique numbers and others are in pairs. I was unable to solve this question and the interviewer acknowledged that it was a rather tough question. 4. Next question was to explain static and public keyword. It was followed by question "What does static keyword do if it is used to define a variable in the global scope of a C file" I was unable to answer this question too. 5. I was given a puzzle as the final Question. "There are 100 numbered doors. Each person to come across a door will toggle it. There are 100 numbered people. Person 1 was toggle all doors, Person 2 can toggle 2,4,6,..100 and so on. You have to find the number of doors open after every person has taken their turn. I thought of using bruteforce but that wouldve been too long. So I checked which numbers from 1 to 25 have odd number of factors. And using this logic, I was able to observe the pattern required to come to the solution - 10.

Round 2 - I waited ~30 mins for my round 2 which lasted 10~15 minutes. I was asked about my internship experience and I was able to answer all the following questions. Then I was asked what is the range of signed and unsigned char. Interview was shorter than I had anticipated, which made me think either I was selected in round 1 only and other rounds were just a formality.

HR Round - As soon as I left the interview room for Round 2, I was told to go for the HR Round, they asked me about my family background and informed me that they were looking for someone that would work their long term. My Round 1 interviewer for example had been working there for 28 years. It was a very pleasant experience.

My advice for everyone is to be patient, because good things take time, and something will surely come your way. You need to remain calm despite all the chaos that brews in your final year.

In case of any doubts, you guys are free to reach out to me and I will be more than happy to be of help.

full_text:
Round 1: Technical & HR Mix

This round was a blend of core computer science fundamentals and behavioral questions. The interviewer focused on evaluating technical breadth and how I approach situational problem-solving.

○ Core Fundamentals Tested: The technical portion covered a wide spectrum of subjects, specifically OOPs, Computer Networks (CN), DSA and DBMS.

○ Question Style: Expect a lot of comparison-based questions and scenario-based questions where you have to apply theoretical knowledge to a given situation.

○ HR Integration: Along with the technical questions, there were general HR questions. These focused on standard behavioral scenarios.

Round 2: Pure Technical Deep-Dive

After receiving the callback, the second round was entirely focused on technical depth.

○ Resume & Project Grilling: The interviewer went through my resume meticulously. I was asked to explain the technical concepts, frameworks, and architecture behind every project I had listed. You must be prepared to defend your development choices.

○ Advanced Core Tech: The round included in-depth questions on SQL query writing, advanced DBMS concepts, and DSA problem-solving.

○ Specialized Topics: They also touched upon modern concepts, specifically asking about AI, ML and DL.

Key Takeaways & Tips:

○ Own Your Resume: Do not include any technology or project on your resume that you cannot explain in intricate detail. The second round will expose any gaps in your practical knowledge.

○ Master the Basics: Your foundation in OOPs, DBMS, and CN needs to be strong enough to answer abstract, comparison-based questions rather than just standard definitions.

○ Practice Scenario Mapping: When studying core subjects, think about how they apply to real-world systems, as the interviewers favored scenario-based evaluation over textbook answers.

author: NITIN KUMAR
title: Reliance interview experience
full_text:
My Reliance interview was mostly a mix of resume-based questions and core Instrumentation concepts. I’ll share what I was asked so that you can get an idea of what to prepare.

Introduction: I was first asked to introduce myself. I talked about my projects, hobbies, and the positions I held in different clubs.

Resume/Projects: After my introduction, the interviewer picked things directly from what I had mentioned. He asked questions about my projects, what exactly I had worked on, and what my responsibilities were in the clubs. So, whatever you mention in your introduction or resume, make sure you actually know it properly.

Instrumentation & Measurement: A major part of my interview was from core IMS (Industrial Measurement System). I was asked about pressure, flow, temperature, level, and force measurement — mainly which instruments are used, their working principles, applications, and basic differences.

Comparisons: Questions like Orifice vs Venturi were asked, so don't just study individual instruments. Know why one is preferred over another, their advantages, disadvantages, and applications.

Control Systems: I was asked about basic control concepts and controllers like PI and PID. There were also some questions related to cascade and ratio control, although these were not the major focus of my interview.

Valves: Valves were quite important. Prepare the different types of valves, their working, characteristics, applications, and where each type of valve is used. You should be able to answer questions like “Why would you use this valve instead of that one?”

Overall, I would say don't prepare only definitions. Try to understand the working principle + application + advantages/disadvantages + selection criteria of every important instrument and valve. And most importantly, whatever you put on your resume, be prepared for the interviewer to go deep into it.

title: Toshiba Placement Experience

full_text:
I am Prajjwal Jain, a B.Tech student from the Electronics and Communication Engineering (ECE) branch, currently holding a CGPA of 8.57. I am sharing my placement experience with Toshiba to provide an overview of the recruitment process, the types of questions asked, and the preparation strategies that helped me.

Recruitment Process

The Toshiba recruitment process consisted of the following stages:

Online Assessment

Technical Interview – Round 1

Technical Interview – Round 2

HR Interview

I have described each stage in detail below.

1. Online Assessment

The online assessment consisted of four sections and had to be completed within 75 minutes. There was no separate time limit for individual sections, and candidates could freely switch between sections and questions during the assessment.

Section 1: Mental Ability Assessment

The first section was a mental ability assessment based primarily on pattern recognition.

A series of images was provided along with multiple options, and we had to identify the missing image by observing and understanding the pattern formed by the given images.

Section 2: Numerical Assessment

The second section consisted of numerical aptitude questions. The major topics included:

Work, time, and efficiency

Bar chart analysis

Pie chart analysis

Interest calculations

The questions were primarily based on basic mathematical concepts and data interpretation.

Section 3: Coding

The third section was a coding round, and the coding language used was C.

In my case, the coding question was relatively straightforward. I was able to solve it using a simple for loop and basic logic, and my solution successfully passed all the test cases.

For preparation, I would recommend being comfortable with the basic syntax and concepts of C, along with practicing simple programming problems involving loops, conditions, arrays, and functions.

Section 4: C Language MCQs

The fourth section consisted of multiple-choice questions based on C programming.

There were several output-prediction questions where we had to determine the output of a given code snippet. There were also questions where we had to identify which code from the given options would correctly accomplish a particular task.

For this section, I would recommend revising:

Pointers

Structures (struct)

Functions

Loops

Operators

Output prediction

Basic memory concepts

Preparation for the Online Assessment

For the online assessment, I would recommend revising the fundamentals and syntax of C thoroughly. In particular, candidates should have a good understanding of pointers, structures, functions, and loops.

For the aptitude sections, practicing numerical aptitude and data interpretation questions can be helpful. It is also important to practice solving questions under time constraints because all four sections have to be completed within the overall 75-minute duration.

2. Technical Interview – Round 1

The first technical interview lasted approximately 45–50 minutes.

The interviewer initially went through my resume thoroughly and then asked me to introduce myself.

After my introduction, I was asked to explain the Computer Networks project mentioned on my resume. I explained the project and the work I had done in it. The interviewer then asked several questions related to Computer Networks.

I was able to answer some of the questions, while I was unable to answer a few others. The interview then moved to bit manipulation.

Bit Manipulation

The interviewer asked several questions related to manipulating specific bits of a number, such as:

How would you find the 8th bit?

How would you toggle the 8th bit?

How would you toggle the 15th bit?

How would you combine multiple bit operations into a single instruction?

How would you swap the 8th and 15th bits?

I was able to solve most of these questions. For the bit-swapping question, I was unable to provide the complete solution, but I explained the approach I would take to solve it.

The interviewer then focused on my understanding of XOR operations and asked me to draw the gate-level diagram of an XOR gate.

After that, I was asked to design an AND gate using universal gates (NAND/NOR). I was able to solve this and draw the required gate-level representation.

C Programming and Puzzles

The interviewer then asked me a basic C programming question and asked me to write the code on paper.

I wrote an optimized solution and explained the logic behind it.

Towards the end of the interview, I was also asked two puzzle-based questions, which I was able to answer.

The interview concluded after approximately 45–50 minutes.

Interview Mode

The interview was conducted offline for ECE students, whereas the interviews for Computer Science and Information Technology students were conducted online.

Preparation for Technical Interview – Round 1

Based on my experience, I would recommend:

Revise C programming thoroughly – Be comfortable with syntax, pointers, functions, loops, operators, and writing code on paper.

Know your resume well – Be prepared to explain every project, technology, and skill mentioned on your resume.

Strengthen Computer Networks fundamentals – Revise important concepts and be prepared for both theoretical and practical questions.

Practice bit manipulation – Focus on setting, clearing, toggling, checking, and swapping bits.

Practice puzzles – Resources such as GeeksforGeeks can be useful for practicing logical puzzles.

Explain your approach – Even if you do not know the complete answer, try to explain your thought process logically.

3. Technical Interview – Round 2

The second technical interview was conducted online and lasted approximately 15–20 minutes.

I started by introducing myself, after which the interviewer asked me several questions covering C programming, operating systems, computer fundamentals, and problem-solving.

Questions Asked

The interviewer first asked me:

How would you represent 64 in binary?

This was followed by a question about memory:

What is stored in the stack section of memory?

The interviewer then asked about:

Difference between a process and a thread

Real-life examples of a process and a thread

How C source code is converted into an executable file

The different steps involved internally during compilation

The meaning of char a = 255;

I was able to answer all of these questions.

The interviewer then asked:

What is the meaning of char a = -1;?

Initially, I said that I was not sure about the answer. However, the interviewer encouraged me to think about it and explain whatever came to my mind.

I then explained my understanding based on the representation of negative numbers using two's complement. Since a char is typically 8 bits, I explained how -1 is represented using two's complement and how its bit pattern relates to the representation of 255 in an 8-bit unsigned interpretation.

Coding Question

The interviewer then asked me to open an online C compiler and share my screen.

I was asked to write a program to determine whether a given number is a power of 2.

I solved the problem using bit manipulation. My approach was to count the number of set bits in the given number. If the number contained exactly one set bit, I concluded that it was a power of 2; otherwise, it was not.

Core Project Discussion

Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer asked me about core projects.

Although I had not mentioned a core project on my resume, I explained that I had worked on a hardware-based minor project during my third year.

I explained the project, described how I had worked on it, and provided details about its implementation.

After discussing the project, the interviewer informed me that the interview was complete.

4. HR Interview

After the technical interviews, there was an HR round.

The HR interview was relatively short and mainly consisted of basic and formal questions. The interviewer asked questions such as:

My name

My father's occupation

My mother's occupation

Whether I was planning to pursue higher studies

There was also some general conversation before the interviewer asked me to wait outside.

I waited outside, and later that evening, the results were announced. I was selected for the position at Toshiba.

Overall Preparation Strategy

Based on my complete experience, I would recommend focusing on the following areas if you are preparing for the Toshiba recruitment process:

1. C Programming

Have a strong understanding of C fundamentals, including:

Pointers

Functions

Structures

Loops

Operators

Memory

Character and integer representation

Output prediction

Basic coding problems

2. Bit Manipulation

This was an important topic in my technical interviews. Practice operations such as:

Checking a bit

Setting a bit

Clearing a bit

Toggling a bit

Counting set bits

Swapping bits

Using XOR for different operations

Checking whether a number is a power of 2

3. Computer Networks

If you have a Computer Networks project on your resume, make sure you understand the project thoroughly and revise the important CN concepts because the interviewer may ask questions directly from your project as well as from the subject.

4. Operating Systems and Computer Fundamentals

Revise fundamental topics such as:

Processes and threads

Stack and heap

Memory management

Compilation process

Source code to executable conversion

5. Projects

Be prepared to explain every project mentioned on your resume in detail.

Additionally, since I was specifically asked about core projects, I would recommend ECE students to consider mentioning at least one relevant core/hardware project on their resume if they have worked on one.

6. Puzzles and Logical Reasoning

Practice basic logical puzzles and problem-solving questions. GeeksforGeeks can be a useful resource for this.

Final Advice

My biggest takeaway from the entire process is that it is important to have a strong command of your fundamentals rather than preparing only advanced topics.

For ECE students particularly, I would recommend having a good combination of C programming, bit manipulation, Computer Networks, operating-system fundamentals, and core/hardware project knowledge.

Also, know your resume thoroughly. Anything written on your resume can become a discussion point during the interview.

That was my experience with the Toshiba placement process. I hope it helps other students preparing for similar recruitment processes. All the best for your placements!

author: ROSHAN KUMAR VERMA
title: Interview Experience

rounds.summary: Round 1: Online Coding Assessment (OA) Format: 3 coding problems in 60 minutes.

key_questions: Data Structures & Algorithms
full_text:
JUSPAY - 27 CTC

I recently went through a multi-round technical recruitment process. The process consisted of an Online Assessment, MCQ round, two hackathon rounds, an in-person technical interview, and an HR/Technical round.

Round 1: Online Coding Assessment (OA)

Format: 3 coding problems in 60 minutes.

One important aspect of the OA was strict chronological navigation. Once you submitted/moved forward from a question, you could not return to modify it. So, time management and confidence while submitting each solution were important.

Question 1 – Tree + DP / LCA

We were given an N-ary tree with Q queries. There were two types of operations:

Update the edge weight/value between two nodes.

Find the distance between two given nodes.

The problem required concepts related to trees, LCA, and dynamic updates.

Question 2 – Binary Search on Answer

There were multiple water taps, each having a specific capacity and cooldown period. Given the total amount of water that needed to be filled, we had to determine the minimum number of days required.

The key idea was to identify the monotonic condition and apply Binary Search on Answer.

Question 3 – Tree Traversal

An N-ary tree was given where each node was either normal or infected/defected.

We had to find the number of leaf nodes for which the path from the root to the leaf contained no more than M consecutive infected nodes.

This mainly involved DFS/tree traversal while maintaining the count of consecutive infected nodes.

Round 2: MCQ Round

Format: 16 Multiple-Choice Questions.

The questions covered a combination of:

Core Computer Science fundamentals

Applied Mathematics

Physics

Basic programming and problem-solving concepts

A good understanding of fundamental CS subjects was helpful for this round.

Round 3: Hackathon – Part A

This round was based on the Tree of Space problem.

The objective was to implement the underlying tree data structure and support operations such as:

Locking a node

Unlocking a node

Checking the required conditions before performing these operations

This round mainly tested data structures, tree concepts, and implementation skills.

Round 4: Hackathon – Part B / Virtual Technical Interview

This was a 1:1 virtual technical interview based on the solution developed in Part A.

The interviewer started by asking me to explain the time and space complexity of my implementation. I was then asked how the solution could be optimized further.

I had to perform live coding to implement the proposed optimizations.

The discussion then moved towards thread safety and concurrency. I was asked to modify the Tree of Space implementation so that it could safely handle simultaneous operations.

Topics discussed included:

Multi-threading

Concurrency

Race conditions

Locks and synchronization

Thread-safe data structures

Concurrent access to shared resources

This was one of the more technically intensive rounds, as it required not only solving the problem but also understanding how the implementation behaves in a concurrent environment.

Round 5: In-Person Technical Interview – Bengaluru

This round was officially designated as a System Design round, although the actual discussion can vary depending on the interviewer.

In my case, instead of focusing heavily on conventional system design, the interviewer spent significant time discussing my projects and cryptography concepts.

The discussion involved:

Detailed explanation of projects mentioned on my resume

Design decisions and implementation details

Technical challenges faced during projects

Cryptography fundamentals

Questions related to the technologies used in my projects

I would recommend being prepared to explain every project and technology mentioned on your resume in depth.

Round 6: HR + Technical

This is generally a 1:1 round combining HR and technical questions.

Typical areas may include:

Introduction

Projects and resume

Behavioral/HR questions

Basic technical concepts

Communication and situational questions

I personally did not have this round, but it can be part of the process for candidates.

Preparation Takeaways

Based on my experience, I would recommend preparing the following areas thoroughly:

1. Data Structures & Algorithms

Trees and N-ary Trees

LCA

DFS/BFS

Dynamic Programming

Binary Search on Answer

Complexity Analysis

2. Operating Systems

Processes vs Threads

Multi-threading

Concurrency

Race Conditions

Mutexes and Locks

Semaphores

Synchronization

Deadlocks

Thread Scheduling

3. Computer Networks

TCP/IP

TCP vs UDP

HTTP/HTTPS

TLS/SSL Handshake

Sockets

Packet Flow

Basic networking concepts

4. LLD / OOP

OOP principles

Class design

Encapsulation and abstraction

Modular code structure

State management

Thread-safe data structures

5. Projects & Resume

Be prepared to explain every project on your resume in depth, including:

Why you built it

Architecture

Technology choices

APIs and database design

Challenges faced

Optimizations

Security considerations

Possible improvements

Overall Experience

The process was quite problem-solving and fundamentals oriented. The later rounds focused less on simply writing code and more on understanding why the code works, how it can be optimized, and how it behaves under concurrent execution.

For preparation, I would particularly recommend practicing tree problems, Binary Search on Answer, concurrency/thread-safety concepts, OS/CN fundamentals, LLD, and deep project-based interview questions.

All the best to everyone preparing!

full_text:
The OA consisted of 40 questions in total out of which 1 was a normal coding question (to be done in C language), 14 C based MCQ questions, and the rest were mental ability and analytical checking questions. Take care of the time constraint and the accuracy simulataneously.

Coding question asked: Given an array of chocolate jar where amount[i] represents the amount of chocolates at ith jar, there are 3 students, A, B and C eating chocolates simultaneously, one by one with A starting first. You need to output the number of chocolates that A will eat finally. For example jar[] = {3,2,4} then from the first jar, A eats one chocolate, B eats one chocolate C eats one chocolate; from the second jar, A eats one chocolate, B eats one chocolate and then from the final jar, A eats one chocolate, B eats one chocolate, C eats one chocolate then A again eats one chocolate. So pretty easy question tbh should take you not more than ~2-3 minutes.

The interview was conducted the next day after the shortlisting (out of 140 candidates who appeared in the OA, only 18 were shortlisted for the interview). The interview round consisted of 4 rounds => 2 technical, 1 managerial and 1 HR (or maybe 2 HR). The first two technical rounds are the most important, the last 2 were a formality. In the first round, the interviewer focused on core C concepts, Computer organization and architecture, Microprocessors and microcontrollers, some basic OOP concepts and one normal coding question (not dsa just to check your familarity with C programming). The second technical round the interviewer again focused on these concepts plus asked me to implement singly linked list, a bit manipulation question (check if a number is power of 2), revolving around that and how memory is stored, types of memory, cache, cache coherence, concurrency etc. The last 2 HR rounds were just formality they asked me about my family members, interview experience, any past interview experience, etc. Also if you are from CSE/IT, make sure you have a valid answer to the question "why the field of embedded development; why did you go for CSE and not ECE". Overall pretty easy

TLDR: Material to study:
Bit manipulation (vvv important) (mostly striver); Computer Organization and Architecture, OOP, OS, C programming, Memory Management, Microprocessors and Microcontrollers (not 8086 and 8085 or any instructions etc)

full_text:
As a Mechanical Engineering student at NIT Jalandhar, my preparation focused heavily on revising fundamental core subjects and understanding the practical reasoning behind engineering principles. The recruitment process was divided into three main stages: an Online Assessment (OA), an HR Interview, and an intensive Technical Interview.

​The selection process began with an Online Assessment consisting of 40 questions. Among these, 10 questions evaluated general quantitative and logical aptitude, while the remaining 30 questions tested core Mechanical Engineering concepts, specifically covering Strength of Materials (SOM), Fluid Mechanics, and Material Science.

​The HR Interview was interactive and friendly, designed to assess communication skills, personal background, and overall behavioral fit. The conversation touched upon family background, personal hobbies, and interests, alongside questions highlighting leadership experiences, project work, and teamwork dynamics.

​The Technical Interview was rigorous and evaluated the depth of fundamental concepts. Rather than focusing solely on basic definitions, the interviewers prioritized the underlying reasoning behind every concept—asking why specific engineering phenomena occur and how core principles apply in practice. The questions spanned across almost all key mechanical domains, including SOM, Material Science (Iron-Carbon phase diagram, TTT diagram), Fluid Mechanics (Bernoulli’s equation), Thermal Engineering (IC engines, RAC), and Theory of Machines (governors, flywheels, gyroscopes).

The HSBC Technology India selection process started with an online assessment on 16th September. The OA consisted of three questions: one easy DSA question similar to LeetCode, one bug-solving question of around medium LeetCode difficulty, and one AI-assisted repository-based question where I had to understand the existing codebase and implement a feature. The shortlist was released on 19th September.

The technical interviews were conducted on 29th September. My technical interview was quite different from what had been asked from our seniors. I was asked two DSA questions along with two HR/behavioral questions. After the technical round, 8 out of 13 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round.

The HR interview included my introduction, discussion about my projects, strengths, handling pressure, how I would process and prioritize a large amount of information during a meeting, plans for higher studies, preferred location, how I could contribute to HSBC, and how I would be comfortable adapting to a corporate environment despite not having prior internship experience. full_text:
more nuances at: https://rishiahuja.github.io/blurb/cisco-interview

OA

The OA had around 20 MCQs, 2 coding problems, and some subjective questions. Two interview lots were held, on 8 and 11 September, with 75 and 87 people shortlisted respectively. I was in the 8 September lot. There were 3 interviews: Technical, Managerial, and HR/ETR.

Changes this year
AI-assisted assignment: We were emailed 2 problem statements and asked to pick one. The task was to build it using AI tools and agents, and document our prompts and decisions. The brief said they might ask for edits on the spot using AI. This did not happen in my interview.
Inclusive resume: We were given a template and asked to remove name, college, CGPA, languages spoken, and any other personal identifier. After submitting it, we were added to a Webex space.

Resume I submitted: https://artifacts.rishia.in/blurbs/cisco-interview/CC7141.pdf

Technical round (50 min)

The interviewer had 6-7 years of experience at Cisco.

Introduction and project (15-20 min): He skipped my publications etc., and asked about the one project I had listed, with detailed scenarios and design decision questions and nuances.
Academics: Whether AI was part of my curriculum, which courses I found most interesting, and how I was in CN.
DSA: Standard Cisco PYQs. Approach for Longest Common Subsequence (2D DP) and code to reverse a linked list.
OS: Page faults, virtual memory, MMU, segmentation, paging etc.
Assignment (end): I opened the assignment and he asked about the architecture and a few small design choices.

After this round, 10-15 people were removed from the space as rejected.

Second round (45 min)

The interviewer had 20+ years of experience at Cisco. It began with how the previous interview went. The questions were resume-based and mostly open-ended, with some technical content and a little to almost nothing managerial. The focus was on why I made certain decisions and whether the projects were collaborative, cost optimization in projects, securing GPUs and much more.

HR round (10 min)

After another round of rejections, 38 of the original 75 reached the HR call. It was short. They confirmed my college, asked if I was willing to relocate, asked about my experience with the interviews and the OA, and a few basic questions.

Result

Results came out on 25 September.

From what I heard, the 11 September lot went from 87 to about 50 people. Not sure about the selection %age from 38 and 50 people.

I recently appeared for an interview for the Assistant Professor position at Parul University. My overall interview experience was positive and comfortable. The interview was mainly focused on my academic background, teaching ability, subject fundamentals, and interest in pursuing a career in academics.

The interview started with a brief introduction. I was asked to explain my educational background, academic qualifications, areas of interest, technical skills, and previous academic or project experience. I introduced myself and explained my background in Computer Science and Data Science, along with my interest in teaching and research.

The interviewers were polite and created a comfortable environment during the discussion. The questions were mostly based on fundamental concepts rather than highly advanced or research-level topics. They wanted to check whether I had a clear understanding of the subjects and whether I could explain technical concepts properly. The discussion covered basic concepts related to computer science, programming, databases, data structures, and machine learning.

The interviewers also wanted to understand my flexibility as a faculty member. There was discussion about the subjects I could teach and my willingness to handle different courses according to the requirements of the department. This made it clear that an Assistant Professor is expected to have a broad understanding of Computer Science rather than expertise in only one narrow area.

The interview was conversational rather than extremely formal. Whenever I answered something, the interviewers sometimes continued the discussion based on my response. Therefore, it was important to remain calm and answer honestly instead of trying to give unnecessarily complicated answers.

Overall, my experience at Parul University was good. The interview was manageable and the environment was comfortable. The interview mainly tested my fundamental technical knowledge, academic background, communication skills, teaching ability, and interest in research and academics. I did not feel that the interview was focused on extremely difficult or advanced technical problems.

For anyone preparing for a similar Assistant Professor interview, I would suggest revising the fundamentals of your core subjects thoroughly and being completely familiar with your CV, academic projects, and areas of specialization. It is also important to practice explaining technical concepts in simple language because teaching ability is an important part of the selection process.

Overall, the interview was a useful academic experience. It helped me understand that for an Assistant Professor position, having strong fundamentals, good communication skills, confidence, and the ability to explain concepts clearly can be just as important as knowing advanced technical topics.
