full_text:
My placement experience at Nit Jalandhar was a great learning experience. I appeared for interviews for several companies, and throughout the placement season, I learned that getting placed is not only about technical knowledge. Communication skills, confidence, preparation, and the ability to handle pressure are equally important.

The Placement Process

For most of the companies I appeared for, the selection process started with an Online Assessment (OA). Depending on the company, the assessment included areas such as aptitude, logical reasoning, coding, and technical fundamentals.

After clearing the online assessment, candidates were shortlisted for the interview rounds. The interview process generally focused on technical knowledge, projects, skills mentioned on the resume, and communication.

Preparing for the Interview

One of the most important things I focused on was preparing a strong introduction. Your introduction is usually the first interaction with the interviewer, so it should be clear, concise, and relevant. I made sure to include my educational background, technical skills, projects, and areas of interest.

I also learned that you should be completely comfortable with everything mentioned on your resume. If you mention a particular technology, programming language, or project, you should be prepared to answer questions about it.

Projects

Projects play an important role in an interview because they give the interviewer an idea about how you apply your technical knowledge.

I believe projects should not just be added to a resume for the sake of having them. They should actually demonstrate your skills and problem-solving ability.

You should be able to explain your project in a simple way:

What problem does it solve?
What technologies did you use?
What was your role?
What challenges did you face?
How did you solve them?

Initially, give a short overview so that the interviewer understands the project. If the interviewer asks you to elaborate, you can then explain the technical details in greater depth.

Communication During the Interview

One of the biggest lessons I learned from my interviews was the importance of communication skills.

It is not enough to know the answer; you should also be able to explain it clearly. Try to define your thoughts precisely and avoid unnecessary explanations.

I also learned not to rush while answering. Take a moment to understand the question, think about your response, and then answer. If you don't know something, it is better to be honest rather than trying to give an incorrect answer.

An interview is a conversation, so you should allow it to proceed naturally. While discussing your skills and projects, you can highlight the areas where you have genuine experience and knowledge. This can often lead to follow-up questions where you get an opportunity to demonstrate your strengths.

Technical and Domain Knowledge

Along with your projects and skills, you should have a good understanding of the core subjects related to your degree.

For a Computer Science student, subjects such as Data Structures and Algorithms, DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and Object-Oriented Programming can be important depending on the company and role.

You should also revise the fundamentals of the technologies mentioned on your resume instead of focusing only on advanced topics.

Research About the Company

Before appearing for an interview, I recommend spending some time researching the company.

Try to understand what the company does, its major products or services, the role you are applying for, and the skills that are relevant to that role.

This preparation can be particularly useful when the interviewer asks questions such as “Why do you want to join our company?” or “What do you know about our company?”

Being able to connect your interests and skills with the company's work can also demonstrate that you are genuinely interested in the opportunity.

Handling Nervousness

Nervousness was another challenge during the placement process. Even after preparing well, it is natural to feel nervous when sitting in front of an interviewer.

The important thing is to make sure that nervousness does not affect your ability to communicate.

Mock interviews can help a lot in this regard. Practicing your introduction, project explanations, and common technical questions in an interview-like environment makes the actual interview feel more familiar.

I also found it important to slow down during an interview. Listen carefully to the question, take a moment to think, and then respond instead of trying to answer immediately.

Challenges During the Placement Season

The placement season can be mentally challenging, especially when you see other students receiving offers while you are still waiting for your opportunity.

It is easy to compare yourself with others and feel discouraged. However, I learned that everyone's placement journey is different. Someone else's selection does not mean that your opportunity is over.

Instead of getting upset after a rejection, try to understand what you could improve. Every interview can provide useful experience for the next one.

The most important thing is to continue preparing even when things are not going your way. I like to think of every day during placement season as a preparation day.

Learning From College Activities

During college, we sometimes think that activities such as PPT presentations, viva examinations, seminars, and group discussions are not very useful because they may not appear directly related to our careers.

However, these activities actually help develop confidence and communication skills.

Presenting a topic or answering questions in front of others teaches you how to organize your thoughts, understand questions, explain concepts clearly, and respond to unexpected situations. These skills become extremely useful during interviews.

I would also encourage students to be socially active in college. Interacting with people, participating in activities, working in teams, and speaking in front of others can gradually improve your confidence.

Managing Placement Pressure

Placement preparation can become stressful, particularly when you are continuously attending assessments and interviews.

It is important to have activities outside academics and placement preparation that help you relax. For me, activities such as sports, physical exercise, music, or spending time doing something you enjoy can help in managing stress.

Taking some time to refresh yourself does not mean that you are losing preparation time. Maintaining a balanced mindset can help you stay consistent throughout the placement season.

Final Thoughts

My placement journey taught me that preparation for placements goes beyond coding and technical subjects. Technical knowledge, communication, confidence, projects, and the ability to handle pressure all contribute to your interview performance.

There will be interviews where you don't get selected, and there may be times when you feel that others are moving ahead of you. The important thing is to keep learning from each experience and continue preparing.

Every day is a preparation day.

Stay consistent, work on your weaknesses, practice communicating your ideas, and don't let temporary setbacks discourage you. With continuous preparation and the right mindset, every interview becomes an opportunity to learn and improve.

The biggest takeaway from my experience was that they focus heavily on fundamentals, depth of understanding, and problem-solving approach. The exact questions can vary significantly depending on the i

key_questions: What is the requirement → how would you approach it → what architecture would you choose → how would you implement it in RTL → what hardware will it generate → what corner cases can occur → how would you verify it?
full_text:
I recently appeared for the Silicon Labs campus placement process for RTL Design / Verification / Digital IP roles, and I wanted to share my experience in detail. The overall process consisted of an Online Assessment, two technical interviews, and an HR round.

The biggest takeaway from my experience was that they focus heavily on fundamentals, depth of understanding, and problem-solving approach. The exact questions can vary significantly depending on the interviewer, so I would recommend preparing concepts rather than trying to predict a fixed set of questions.

Online Assessment

The OA had around 30 questions to be completed in 1 hour 30 minutes. The questions covered a broad range of core electronics and digital/VLSI fundamentals.

There were questions from Digital Electronics, Verilog/RTL, FSMs, DFT, STA and basic CMOS/VLSI. In Verilog, there were questions involving code debugging, output prediction, latch inference and basic RTL concepts. FSM questions included concepts such as Moore and Mealy machines and selecting the appropriate FSM.

There were also basic DFT and ATPG questions, including the purpose of DFT, why testability is required, basic fault concepts and what DFT helps improve. I would definitely recommend preparing basic DFT even if you are primarily targeting RTL/Verification roles.

The STA questions included setup time, hold time, setup slack and hold slack, along with basic timing concepts. There were also basic CMOS/VLSI questions.

Around 80–90 students appeared for the process, out of which approximately 27 were shortlisted for interviews.

Technical Interview — Round 1

The first technical round was around one hour. There were different interview panels, so different candidates experienced somewhat different styles of interviews. From discussing with other candidates, I found that the common theme was testing fundamentals and the ability to reason through a problem.

Some interviewers focused heavily on the candidate's resume. They would pick projects from the resume, ask you to explain them in detail and then ask you to write Verilog code related to those projects. So if you mention a project on your resume, you should be prepared to explain not only what you did but also the architecture, implementation and design decisions behind it.

Another interviewer had his own set of Verilog and digital-design questions. He started from very basic concepts and gradually went deeper. Instead of simply asking for a final answer, he would ask things like how you would start solving the problem, why you were choosing a particular approach and what hardware your solution would actually generate. Questions included concepts around D flip-flops, FSMs and other basic RTL design problems.

My First-Round Experience

My interviewer happened to have an analog-oriented profile, which was unexpected because the role itself was primarily related to digital RTL, verification and digital IP. Most of us had prepared mainly for digital topics.

He started by asking me about my favourite subjects. I mentioned Digital Electronics, VLSI Design, CMOS and then Analog Electronics/EDC. Since I mentioned analog electronics, he started exploring that area in considerable depth.

He started with ADC design. He asked me to draw the block diagram and then went through the individual blocks, asking why each block was required, what would happen if a particular block was removed, and what I would change if I wanted to achieve a particular specification. He then went deeper into components such as the sampler and asked about their internal operation.

After that, he asked about BJT and MOSFET, including their structures, differences, applications and why particular devices are preferred for particular applications.

He then gave me an LC oscillator circuit and asked me to explain its working. From there, the discussion moved into transfer functions and control-system concepts such as root locus, stability and ROC.

Since I had mentioned a current-starved ring oscillator designed in Cadence on my resume, he also went quite deep into that project. He asked about the current-starving mechanism, the current mirror used in the design, why it was required, transistor-level operation and the post-layout aspect of the design.

My OFDM-related internship/project experience was also discussed, so he asked some questions about OFDM and basic communication concepts.

Overall, this round tested fundamentals from multiple areas rather than being restricted to only the role-specific topics.

Technical Interview — Round 2

The second technical round started with my resume and focused heavily on my biggest project, which was my RISC-V-based secure SoC for IoT applications.

The interviewer went very deep into almost everything I had mentioned on my resume. Since Silicon Labs has a strong focus on low-power applications, a significant part of the discussion was around low-power VLSI concepts.

We discussed clock gating and power gating in detail, including why they are used, how they are implemented, where they would be used in an SoC, how they are represented in RTL, how glitch-free clock gating works, and what happens at the transistor level.

He also asked questions related to threshold voltage and power, such as what happens when the threshold voltage of a MOSFET is increased and how it affects leakage, drive current and delay.

After the project discussion, he moved to his own set of digital-design questions. One of the questions was to design a sequence generator, after which he changed the conditions by asking what would happen if repetition was allowed or not allowed. This led to a discussion about Moore vs Mealy FSMs, their differences and design considerations.

He also asked about synchronizers and metastability, including the reasoning behind synchronization techniques.

Another question was to design a D flip-flop using NAND gates. He specifically wanted a flip-flop and not just a latch, so understanding how the latch-based structures combine to form an edge-triggered flip-flop was important.

There was also a relatively large STA problem where I had to analyze the timing path and calculate the maximum clock frequency. So I would strongly recommend being comfortable with setup/hold constraints, skew, uncertainty, slack and timing diagrams.

He also asked a 6-variable Karnaugh map problem.

At the end of the technical round, he asked some behavioral questions such as my strengths, weaknesses, and why he should choose me over other candidates.

HR Round

The HR round was relatively short, around 5 minutes, and was mostly conversational.

The questions included whether I was comfortable relocating, whether I would be comfortable with Hyderabad as a location, whether I was considering higher studies, whether I genuinely enjoyed the kind of work associated with the role, and some questions about my family background.

There were no particularly difficult technical questions in this round.

My Overall Takeaways

The biggest lesson I took from the process is that you should not prepare only according to the job description. Prepare the fundamentals behind everything you have studied and everything you have written on your resume.

Also, different interviewers can have very different approaches. One interviewer may go deeply into your resume and projects, another may have a fixed set of Verilog/digital-design questions, while another may take you into a completely different subject based on what you say are your interests.

So if you mention something as your favourite subject, be prepared for questions from that subject in considerable depth.

For RTL/Verification preparation, I would particularly focus on Digital Design, Verilog/RTL, FSMs, Computer Architecture, RISC-V, functional verification, STA, CDC/metastability, low-power design and basic DFT/ATPG. At the same time, don't completely ignore your other core subjects because the interview can move across domains.

Most importantly, don't just memorize the final answer to a design question. Be prepared to explain:

What is the requirement → how would you approach it → what architecture would you choose → how would you implement it in RTL → what hardware will it generate → what corner cases can occur → how would you verify it?

That problem-solving approach was one of the most important things I felt the interviewers were evaluating.

full_text:
I recently appeared for the Jio-bp Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) recruitment process, and overall, my experience was quite smooth and positive. The process had multiple rounds, including an online assessment, GD, technical interview, and HR interview.

Online Assessment

The first round was an online assessment consisting of aptitude and technical questions. The questions were manageable if your basic concepts are clear. I would suggest revising aptitude along with your core engineering subjects before the test.

Group Discussion

After the OA, shortlisted candidates were called for the GD. The discussion was not very difficult, but communication and the way you present your points matter a lot. It is better to listen to others properly, avoid interrupting, and speak whenever you have a relevant point to add. Being too aggressive is not necessary.

Technical Interview

The technical interview was quite comfortable and more like a conversation rather than a very stressful interview. A good amount of discussion was around my internships and the work mentioned on my resume, so make sure you know your resume really well.

Questions were also asked from core engineering subjects. In my experience, they were more interested in practical understanding and applications rather than just asking theoretical definitions. So, while preparing, try to understand how the concepts are used in real-life situations.

HR Interview

The HR round was also quite relaxed. Questions were mainly related to my background, interests, career plans, and why I would be suitable for the role.

One thing I found important was the HR form that candidates had to fill before the interviews. Some questions from that form were discussed again during the HR round, so make sure the information and answers you provide in the form are consistent with what you say during the interview.

My Overall Take

Overall, I found the Jio-bp GET recruitment process well structured. The process tests a combination of technical knowledge, aptitude, communication, practical understanding, and personality.

For anyone preparing for this role, I would mainly suggest:

Keep your aptitude basics clear.

Revise your core engineering subjects.

Be very thorough with your resume and internships.

Focus on practical applications instead of only memorising theory.

Participate confidently in the GD without interrupting others.

Prepare common HR questions and keep your answers genuine and consistent.

Overall, good fundamentals, confidence, and clear communication can make a big difference throughout the process.

Selection Process

The selection process started with the Online Assessment (OA) which consists of General Aptitude Questions and Chemical Engineering questions based on fundamental concepts.

After being shortlisted, I appeared for the interview, where I was asked questions related to my Chemical Engineering fundamentals, projects, internship interests, and behavioral situations.

A few things that helped me during the process:

- Be clear about your fundamentals and resume.

- Know your projects well — understand not just what you did, but why you did it and what you learned.

- For behavioral questions, use real examples from your college, projects, or extracurricular activities.

- Most importantly, stay calm and communicate honestly. You don't need to know everything.

After successfully completing the selection process, I was offered an internship at Honeywell.

The Internship Journey:

I joined Honeywell as a Digital Chemical Engineering Intern and worked with the CCR Platforming technology team.

During my internship, I got exposure to tools such as Seeq and Power BI and worked on tasks involving:

- KPI and operational dashboards

- Data monitoring and quality checks

- Exception-based analysis and alerts

- Data analysis and visualization

- Supporting technology and performance reviews

One of the biggest learning experiences for me was working with real industrial data and understanding how data-driven tools can support decision-making in chemical engineering.

During the internship, I learned the importance of:

- Asking questions when you're unsure

- Communicating your progress clearly

- Being open to feedback

- Learning from people around you

- Managing deadlines and priorities

I also realized that being technically capable is only one part of working in a professional environment. Communication, collaboration and willingness to learn matter just as much.

Towards the end of my internship, I got the opportunity to be considered for a full-time role at Honeywell.

I’m extremely happy to share that I have received a full-time conversion offer from Honeywell.

full_text:
I recently appeared for the interview process at KEC International Ltd. for Engineering Leadership Trainee role. Sharing my experience to help juniors understand what they can expect and how they can prepare.

1. Self Introduction

The interview started with a self-introduction. I was asked to briefly explain:

My educational background

Internship experience

Major/academic project

Technical skills and other relevant experiences

Important: Most of the questions afterward were based on what I mentioned in my introduction, so I would suggest mentioning only those projects, subjects, and skills that you are comfortable explaining in detail.

2. Internship & Major Project

After the introduction, the interviewer asked detailed questions about my:

Internship experience

Major project

My individual contribution

Tools/software used

Technical concepts involved in the project

They mainly wanted to understand whether I actually worked on the things mentioned in my resume.

3. Civil Engineering Technical Questions

I was then asked around 3–4 technical questions from core Civil Engineering subjects.

Some questions included:

What are the different types of subgrade?

What is the difference between determinate and indeterminate structures?

Which is your favourite Civil Engineering subject?

I answered RCC (Reinforced Cement Concrete) as my favourite subject.

Based on that answer, they asked further questions such as:

What are the steps involved in designing a column?

What are the steps involved in designing a beam?

How do you determine whether a slab is one-way or two-way?

Basic RCC design concepts and assumptions.

4. Portal Frame Question

Toward the end of the technical round, the interviewer shared their screen and showed me a portal-frame problem.

I was asked to explain/identify how the Bending Moment (BM) and Shear Force (SF) diagrams would look.

The focus was more on understanding the structural behaviour and explaining the approach rather than simply memorizing formulas.

5. HR & Situational Questions

Finally, they asked some general HR and situational questions, such as:

What are your strengths?

Are you comfortable with relocation?

How do you handle pressure?

What would you do if a deadline is approaching but your task requires more time?

How would you handle a situation where multiple tasks have to be completed simultaneously?

My Overall Experience

The interview was a combination of self-introduction → resume-based questions → internship/project discussion → core Civil Engineering concepts → practical/structural problem → HR & situational questions.

The main takeaway for juniors is that your self-introduction and resume are very important. Anything you mention can become a follow-up question. So, prepare your internship, major project, favourite subjects, and every technical skill mentioned on your resume properly.

Preparation Tips for Juniors

I would recommend preparing:

Core Civil:

RCC

Structural Analysis

Soil Mechanics

Foundation Engineering

Highway Engineering

Construction Materials

Final tip: Don't just memorize answers. Be ready to explain the concepts in your own words. The interviewer may change the question based on your answer, so understanding the basics is more important than memorizing a fixed list of questions.

full_text:
I recently appeared for the Jio-bp Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) recruitment process. The overall process was smooth and focused on assessing aptitude, technical understanding, practical knowledge, and overall personality.

1. Online Assessment (OA)
The first stage was an Online Assessment consisting of:

Aptitude questions

Technical questions

A good understanding of basic aptitude concepts and core engineering subjects is important for clearing this round.

2. Group Discussion (GD)
Candidates who cleared the OA were shortlisted for a Group Discussion. The GD was relatively straightforward. The key factor was maintaining professionalism during the discussion. Avoid interrupting or speaking over other candidates, listen carefully, and contribute meaningful points when appropriate. Effective communication and teamwork appeared to be valued more than being overly aggressive.

3. Technical Interview
The technical interview was conducted in a comfortable and conversational manner. A significant portion of the discussion revolved around my internship experiences, so candidates should be thorough with the projects and work mentioned on their resumes.

The interviewers also asked questions from core engineering subjects. The emphasis was more on practical applications and real-world understanding rather than purely theoretical concepts. Therefore, candidates should focus on understanding how concepts are applied in industry rather than memorizing definitions.

4. HR Interview
The HR round was relaxed and consisted of typical HR questions related to background, interests, career goals, and suitability for the role.

One important point is that candidates were required to fill out a form containing HR-related questions before the interviews. During the HR round, several questions were repeated from this form. The interviewers appeared to cross-check responses, so it is advisable to answer consistently and honestly both in the form and during the interview.

Overall Advice

Prepare aptitude and core technical subjects thoroughly.

Be confident while discussing internships and projects mentioned on your resume.

Focus on practical understanding of engineering concepts.

During GD, communicate clearly and avoid interrupting others.

Be consistent with the information provided in any pre-interview forms and your interview responses.

Overall, the recruitment process was well structured, and candidates with good technical fundamentals, practical understanding, and clear communication skills should be able to perform well.

General Preparation Tips

Before jumping into the rounds, here are a few key things to keep in mind:

Focus on Core Subjects: Having strong knowledge of your core civil engineering subjects is the most important step.

Master Your Resume: Practice explaining the projects mentioned in your resume clearly and confidently. You should know everything you have written inside out.

Research the Company: Have good knowledge about Reliance UBP. Whenever possible, try to integrate the company’s models, goals, or values into your answers to show your genuine interest.

Stay Confident: Just keep working on your skills and maintain your confidence throughout the process.

The Selection Process

The hiring process consisted of four main rounds:

1. Online Written Evaluation (OWE) / Technical Assessment

This was the first screening round. The test primarily focused on core civil engineering questions to check your foundational knowledge. There were also a few mental ability and aptitude questions included.

2. Group Discussion (GD) Round

The topics given for the GD were very general. The main thing they look for here is not how loud you are, but the quality of your thoughts. Prepare how to start a discussion smoothly and focus on putting forward logical, high-quality points.

3. Technical Interview

This round lasted for about 10 to 15 minutes. The interviewers directly asked questions related to core engineering concepts. As long as you have studied your core subjects well, you will be able to handle this round comfortably.

4. HR Interview

The final round was a short conversation of about 10 to 12 minutes. This was mainly to understand me as a person. They asked questions about my background, my working style, how I handle past failures, and how passionate and dedicated I am to joining the job. Just be honest and show your enthusiasm.

Keep working hard on your basics, stay confident in your answers, and trust your preparation. All the best for your placements!

full_text:
Getting a PPO at Mondelez International has been one of the most meaningful experiences of my college journey. What started with getting my internship opportunity in October last year eventually turned into a two-month summer internship from June to August this year, and finally into a Pre-Placement Offer.

Looking back, the biggest learning for me was that the journey was not just about getting the opportunity—it was about making the most of it once I got there.

1. The Interview Process: What I Learned

Before joining Mondelez, I went through the selection process, which itself taught me a lot.

Group Discussion

The Group Discussion was one of the first stages, and my biggest takeaway was confidence matters, but so does communication.

A few things that worked for me:

Try to speak early in the discussion if you have a relevant point.
If possible, initiate the discussion. It helps you establish your presence from the beginning.
Be confident and loud enough so that your point is clearly heard.
You don't have to keep speaking continuously. Listen to what others are saying and contribute when you have something meaningful to add.
Whenever there is a pause in the discussion, enter confidently with your point.
Don't be afraid of disagreement. You can disagree with someone's point while still being respectful.
Most importantly, don't speak just for the sake of speaking. Quality and clarity matter.

One thing I personally learned is that confidence does not mean dominating the discussion. It means being comfortable enough to put your thoughts forward.

2. The Interview

The interview taught me another important lesson: your resume is your responsibility.

Anything you write on your resume can become a question.

So, if you have mentioned a project, internship, technical skill, certification, achievement or extracurricular activity, make sure you genuinely understand it.

The interviewer may ask:

Why did you do this project?
What exactly was your contribution?
What challenges did you face?
What did you learn?
Why did you choose this particular approach?
What would you do differently?
How did you arrive at the results you mentioned?

They may also take the conversation in an unexpected direction or put you under pressure to see how you respond.

My biggest learning was:

Never lose your composure.

If you don't know something, it is better to acknowledge it honestly than to try to bluff your way through it.

And throughout the interview, stay confident. Even when you are unsure about an answer, take a moment, think, and then respond.

3. Your Resume Matters More Than You Think

One of the most important things I would recommend to anyone preparing for placements is to make a strong and well-formatted resume.

It doesn't have to be overloaded with information.

Instead:

Keep the formatting clean and professional.
Highlight your important projects and experiences.
Quantify your work wherever possible.
Keep your points concise.
Make sure every statement is something you can explain.
Proofread it multiple times.
Prepare questions based on every major point on your resume.

A good resume doesn't just get you shortlisted—it also becomes the foundation for your interview.

My Internship Journey at Mondelez

I got my internship opportunity in October last year, and I joined the summer internship from June to August this year.

This was my first experience working in a manufacturing plant, and honestly, the initial days were challenging.

There was a completely new environment to understand—the plant, processes, people, machines, terminology and the way work actually happens on the shop floor.

Initially, it can feel overwhelming.

But that's where one of my biggest learnings came in:

Trust the process.

You don't have to understand everything on Day 1.

Take it step by step.

Learn something new every day.

Ask questions, Observe, Make mistakes, Learn from them. And slowly, things start making sense.

One thing I would strongly recommend to anyone joining an internship—especially a manufacturing internship—is:

Don't stay limited to your project.

Go out and explore the plant.

Interact with people.

Talk to operators, engineers, supervisors, managers and everyone around you.

Because everyone has something to teach you.

Some of the most valuable things I learned during my internship came from conversations and observations that weren't necessarily part of my formal project.

Don't hesitate to ask questions just because you think they might sound basic.

A question that seems basic to you might actually help you understand the entire process better.

Understand Your Project Properly

Once you are assigned your project, spend enough time understanding why the project exists in the first place.

Don't immediately jump into finding solutions.

First understand:

What is the problem? → Why does it matter? → What is causing it? → What data do I have? → What can I actually improve?

Ask as many questions as you need.

Take help whenever you feel stuck.

Talk to your mentor.

Talk to your guide.

Talk to people working on the process.

There is absolutely no harm in asking for help.

In fact, I believe that knowing when to ask for help is itself an important professional skill.

Keep Learning Outside Your Project Too

An internship is not only about completing the project assigned to you.

It is also an opportunity to explore.

So while working seriously, make sure you also take some time to:

Explore different areas of the organization.
Learn about processes outside your project.
Interact with new people.
Develop new skills.
Explore things you're genuinely interested in.
Spend time doing things that make you happy.

Maintaining a balance helped me enjoy the experience much more.

My Biggest Learning

If I had to summarize my entire internship experience in one message, it would be:

Have fun.

Take your work seriously, but don't forget to enjoy the journey.

Enjoy the problems you are solving.

Enjoy the people you meet.

Enjoy learning something new.

Enjoy stepping outside your comfort zone.

And enjoy the small wins along the way.

Because when you genuinely enjoy what you're doing, you don't constantly keep checking how much time is left.

And before you realize it, the internship is over, you've grown tremendously, and you've achieved what you were working towards.

For me, the journey from getting the internship opportunity in October, joining the plant in June, navigating the challenges of my first manufacturing experience, learning from the people around me, and eventually receiving a PPO from Mondelez International has been incredibly rewarding.

The PPO is definitely a milestone I'm proud of.

But more than the offer itself, I'm grateful for everything the journey taught me.

full_text:
I recently went through the placement process for SRF Limited for the Senior Executive position. The selection process was quite comprehensive and consisted of five interview rounds—two rounds during the campus placement process and three rounds at Gurugram.

Selection Process

Campus Selection

1. Technical Interview

2. HR Interview

Gurugram Selection

3. HR Interview

4. Technical Interview

5. CEO Interview

---

1. Campus Technical Interview

The first round was a Technical Interview conducted during the campus placement process.

The discussion mainly focused on my Mechanical Engineering fundamentals, projects, internship experience and practical understanding of engineering concepts.

I prepared topics from:

- Thermodynamics

- Heat Transfer

- Fluid Mechanics

- IC Engines

- Manufacturing Processes

- Strength of Materials

- Refrigeration and Air Conditioning

- Basic Mechanical Engineering

The interview was not restricted to direct theoretical questions. Several concepts required me to explain their practical applications and reasoning.

Project Discussion

My projects were also an important part of the discussion, particularly my CFD project.

I prepared to explain the complete project, including:

- Problem statement

- Objective

- Turbulence model

- Reynolds number

- Nusselt number

- Validation

- Results

- Practical application

One of the most important lessons from this round was:

«Whatever you mention on your resume, make sure you can explain it in depth.»

A small point mentioned in a project can lead to multiple follow-up questions.

---

2. Campus HR Interview

The second campus round was the HR Interview.

The focus shifted from purely technical knowledge to my personality, communication skills, career goals and suitability for the organization.

The discussion included questions around:

- Tell me about yourself.

- Why SRF?

- Why do you want to join the company?

- What are your strengths?

- What is your weakness?

- Where do you see yourself in five years?

- Tell me about your internship.

- Tell me about your projects.

- How do you handle pressure?

- How do you handle conflicts?

- How would you respond if your manager rejected your leave application?

- Are you comfortable with relocation?

- What are your expectations from your first job?

The main focus was on giving genuine and structured answers rather than highly rehearsed responses.

After completing the two campus rounds, I was shortlisted for the next stage at Gurugram.

---

3. Gurugram HR Interview

The first round at Gurugram was another HR Interview.

Although I had already faced an HR round on campus, this interaction was more detailed. The discussion focused on my overall personality, motivation, career expectations and ability to adapt to a professional and industrial environment.

Topics included:

- Academic background

- Internship experience

- Projects

- Why SRF?

- Career aspirations

- Strengths and weaknesses

- Teamwork

- Leadership

- Handling pressure

- Conflict management

- Relocation

- Workplace situations

- Expectations from the organization

---

4. Gurugram Technical Interview

The second Gurugram round was the Technical Interview.

This was one of the most detailed rounds of the entire process. The discussion covered core Mechanical Engineering concepts along with my projects and internship experience.

Thermodynamics

Heat Transfer

- Heat exchangers

Fluid Mechanics

- Cavitation

- Causes of cavitation

- Methods to reduce cavitation

IC Engines

I also revised:

- SI and CI engines

- Four-stroke and two-stroke engines

Projects and Internship

The interviewer also went into detail about my projects and internship.

For my internship, I focused on explaining:

- What work I performed

- What I learned

- How the system/process worked

- Problems I encountered

- How I applied engineering concepts

- What practical exposure I gained

The biggest lesson from this round was that conceptual clarity is much more useful than memorizing answers.

---

5. Final CEO Interview

The final round at Gurugram was the CEO Interview.

This was probably the most different round compared with the technical interview.

The discussion was more focused on my personality, values, decision-making, career aspirations, motivation and approach toward professional situations.

The discussion included areas such as:

- Why SRF?

- What do you know about SRF?

- Why should SRF hire you?

- What are your career goals?

- What values are important to you?

- What are your strengths?

- How do you handle failure?

- How do you handle pressure?

- How would you deal with disagreement with a senior?

- What would you do if you were given a difficult or unfamiliar task?

- What do you expect from your organization?

- Questions related to my projects and internship

---

Overall Experience

The complete SRF selection process consisted of:

Campus

→ Technical Interview

→ HR Interview

Gurugram

→ HR Interview

→ Technical Interview

→ CEO Interview

Total: 5 Interview Rounds

Going through all five rounds gave me exposure to different styles of interviews—from technical fundamentals and project discussions to HR conversations and senior-management interaction.

Key Takeaways

1. Know your resume inside out

Every project, skill, internship and technical term mentioned on the resume can become a potential interview question.

2. Focus on fundamentals

For Mechanical Engineering candidates, I found it extremely useful to revise:

Thermodynamics + Heat Transfer + Fluid Mechanics + Manufacturing + IC Engines + Basic Mechanical Engineering

3. Understand your projects

Don't simply memorize the project description.

Be prepared to explain:

Problem → Objective → Methodology → Tools → Results → Challenges → Validation → Application

4. Research the company

Before the interview, understand SRF's businesses, products, manufacturing operations, values and the responsibilities associated with the Senior Executive role.

5. Prepare for situational questions

Questions involving managers, teamwork, pressure, conflicts, responsibility and decision-making can be just as important as technical questions.

full_text:
I recently went through the hiring process at RAIK Solutions, which consisted of 5 rounds — 2 assessment rounds, 2 technical interviews, and 1 HR interview.

All rounds were elimination/shortlisting based, so clearing each round was necessary to move forward.

I’ll explain each round and the type of questions I encountered, which may help others preparing for a similar software development role.

Round 1 — Online Assessment

The first round consisted of 30 questions covering a mixture of:

Logical reasoning

Computer Science fundamentals

Technical MCQs

Programming-related concepts

The CS fundamentals included topics such as:

OOPs

DBMS

Operating Systems

Basic programming concepts

Other core CS concepts

The difficulty was moderate, with a combination of conceptual and logical questions.

Round 2 — Technical + Aptitude Assessment

The second round consisted of 13 questions.

The paper included:

10 technical/puzzle-based questions

3 behavioral/writing questions

The technical section tested problem-solving ability and understanding of programming/CS concepts, while the puzzle questions focused more on logical thinking.

The behavioral section was written on paper, where we had to answer questions about ourselves, our approach, and general workplace situations.

This round was slightly different from a typical coding assessment because it tested both technical thinking and behavioral aspects.

Round 3 — Technical Interview

The third round was primarily focused on my projects and technical fundamentals.

The interviewer asked questions related to the projects mentioned on my resume, including:

What problem does the project solve?

What technologies did you use?

Why did you choose those technologies?

How does the application work?

What challenges did you face?

How did you implement particular features?

Apart from projects, I was also asked about:

Basic DSA

SQL

Programming fundamentals

General development concepts

The interview was largely conversational, but knowing your resume and projects thoroughly was important.

Round 4 — Technical Deep Dive

The fourth round was a deeper technical discussion.

The main focus was on:

Projects

Development approach

Technical decision-making

Basic system design

Core programming concepts

The interviewer went deeper into the projects I had previously discussed and asked questions around why I implemented things in a particular way rather than only asking what technologies I used.

Some questions focused on understanding whether I could think beyond simply writing code — for example:

How would you make a feature scalable?

How would you structure the application?

What happens when the number of users/data increases?

How would you improve an existing implementation?

What design choices would you make and why?

This round helped evaluate practical development understanding and problem-solving rather than just theoretical knowledge.

Round 5 — HR Interview

The final round was an HR interview.

The questions were fairly basic and focused on getting to know me better.

Some common areas discussed were:

Tell me about yourself.

Educational background

Projects/internship

Strengths and weaknesses

Career goals

Why do you want to join the company?

General HR/behavioral questions

The conversation was more about personality, communication, career expectations, and overall fit.

Final Takeaway

The RAIK Solutions process was not limited to one particular skill. Across the five rounds, it tested logical reasoning, CS fundamentals, technical knowledge, projects, DSA, SQL, development thinking, system design basics, communication, and behavioral aspects.

My biggest takeaway was:

Don't prepare only to solve coding questions. Prepare to explain how you build, debug, improve, and scale software.

If you're preparing for a similar software development role, make sure you can confidently discuss everything written on your resume and understand the fundamentals behind the technologies you've used.

full_text:
Role: Aladdin Data

Online Assessment (OA)

The OA consisted of:

2 DSA questions — 1 Easy + 1 Advanced

95 MCQs covering: Design Patterns, Cloud Computing, AI, DBMS, Aptitude

Round 1 — Technical + Behavioral

Duration: ~25–30 minutes

The round started with a brief “Introduce yourself” question.

After that, the interviewer asked:

Is there any project you would like to discuss?

Explain your project in detail.

Follow-up and counter questions based on the project.

I discussed one of my projects and was then asked about another project based on GraphRAG. The interviewer specifically asked me to explain GraphRAG as if he had no prior knowledge of it—what it is, why it is used, and what it actually does.

There were multiple counter questions based on my explanation. He also asked whether the project was an individual or team project.

Since I had applied for the Aladdin Data role, my projects were quite relevant to the role and helped me during the discussion.

The interviewer also asked behavioral questions such as:

Have you worked in a team?

How did you manage your project as a team?

How did you handle conflicts within the team?

The round went quite well for me because I had a strong understanding of my projects and was comfortable explaining the technical decisions behind them.

Round 2 — Technical Deep Dive

Duration: ~15–20 minutes

This round was primarily based on my resume and projects.

The interviewer asked me to explain my project and continuously asked counter questions based on whatever I mentioned.

The discussion went quite deep into the technical aspects, including:

Project architecture

Data flow

Technologies and libraries used

How the different components interact

How changes and incremental updates are handled

Which database I used and why I chose it

Why I didn't use an alternative database

Whether the database supports concurrency and why

What concurrency means

What a deadlock is

Whether I faced any deadlock while working on the project

What an LLM is — “Explain it to a 10-year-old”

What MCP is

What a transaction is in DBMS

Something I was particularly proud of while working on the project

The interviewer kept digging deeper into my answers, so knowing the project beyond just the high-level implementation was very important.

Overall Experience

Both rounds were heavily project-oriented, especially around the projects mentioned on my resume. The interviewers were interested not just in what I had built, but also in why I made certain technical decisions and how the system worked internally.

My biggest takeaway was:

If you mention a project on your resume, be prepared to explain every important technical decision behind it and handle multiple “why?” and “what if?” follow-up questions.

For project-heavy interviews, having a strong understanding of your architecture, data flow, database choices, concurrency, libraries, edge cases, and implementation details can make a big difference.

full_text:
I got selected for Juspay and here’s what the placement process actually looked like. It started with an OA with 3 questions mainly based on Graphs DP and Trees. Then came a pen and paper MCQ round covering CS fundamentals Physics and Maths.

After that was the Hackathon Part A and Part B. Hackathon A was mainly about solving the Tree of Space problem and getting the implementation right. Hackathon B was around 7 hours long. It focused on optimizing the solution and figuring out better approaches along with their time complexities and deriving the complexity of the optimized approaches. There were also questions around OS Networking and other CS fundamentals.

Then came the interviews. They were conducted in person in Bengaluru and the technical round was around 1 to 1.5 hours. It went deep into DSA especially Graphs and DP. They kept pushing on the approach and asked why it works and whether it can be optimized and what the complexity would be along with edge cases. Then came LLD and System Design where I was asked to design something around BookMyShow. There were also basic maths questions followed by a proper resume deep dive. Basically anything you put on your resume was fair game. Skills projects and technologies could be picked up and drilled into. Then came questions around OS and even CPU microarchitecture.

After around 1 to 1.5 hours of technical questioning there was another 30 minute HR round.

Small tip: It’s not just about getting the answer. Make the interviewer understand how you think. Explain your approach step by step. Talk through your assumptions and why you are choosing a particular solution. If you see a better approach then say it. Even when you are stuck keep communicating your thought process. Sometimes how clearly you explain your thinking matters just as much as the final answer. 😄

full_text:
Note: All the 4 rounds(2 Online Assessments and 2 Technical Interviews) are shortlisting based elimination rounds.

The first 2 rounds were pretty easy to clear so I will be focussing on the interview rounds in this article.

OA 1:- Algorithm Coding questions in JavaScript (Very basic questions). MCQs on CS Fundamentals[OOPS, OS, DBMS]. Format of the questions - Video on questions to expect in the first round.

OA 2:- Coding questions on SQL (All from Leetcode). Output based MCQs on JavaScript. CS fundamentals[OOPS, OS, DBMS]. Similar to OA1

with a slight more difficulty level.

Technical Interview 1:- This round was a heavy resume based round and primarily evaluated javascript knowledge via output based questions. Difficulty in this round can vary from person to person [Check My profile here] , for me personally, they asked about the remote internship I worked for 6 months, my role there, the products/features I built (not in depth due to NDA, just how a general product/feature like that is made). Focussed on web development approach and style, react + node.js, RAG and mobile app development (purely due to my resume).

Spent around 10 minutes discussing theoretical Operating Systems and OOPs in Java.

Then finally before ending the meeting asked me to approach designing a database (no right or wrong answers), it was a library management system where a Student can issue a Book, a Book can have multiple Copies and these Copies can be on different LibraryShelfs.

Technical Interview 2:- This round primarily focus on you development skills. Focus was on how you approach a real-world problem while working on a codebase, mainly senario based questions and design based questions.

Here are some of the questions (only the ones I can remember)-

Question1- The dev before you wrote a particular code for an admin dashboard, find the mistake in it and tell us how you'd improve it. The dashboard rendered 50 items at once in a react component. It worked well in development/testing but breaks in production.

Question 2- There 4 small tables for an inventory management system was given. My task was to indentify PK and FKs in them.

Question 3- Hands-on live coding in React. For the given flat list,

comments = [

{

id: '...',

parentId: '...',

heading: '...',

description: '...'

},

...];

render it in a tree like structure,

ParentComment

|-- ChildComment

|-- |-- GrandChildComment

... and so on.

The depth of the tree is not restricted, can be upto any limit.

Question 4- Design database for an inventory management system considering a User can place multiple Orders, there are several Products the user can choose to directly buy or buy through cart. (Only database design and reason for those design choices, how those choices will make it able to make the code scalable and production safe).

Question 5- In a React code, the dashboard page is taking a lot of time to load, this problem only occurs in production not in local development testing. Identify how you would debug this problem, what main issues would you first look for in the code-base, how you aim to improve the quality now. (Give answer from Front-end, Back-end and DB side perspective).

How to prepare -

Learn CS fundamentals well.
Actively make hands-on projects with least AI assistance.
Learn just not to code but also to build and ship an optimised product.

full_text:
Amex Internship: Interview Experience

Role
- Most likely Product Development (not SDE), so little DSA
- Focus is on ML and big data
- If you land in Enterprise Technology, expect DSA

Round 1: Online Assessment (~90 min, fast-paced)
- Random shortlisting, mostly by CGPA
- CAT-style data interpretation problems
- One full section on deep learning

Round 2: Group Discussion (eliminatory)
- Amex and finance topics
- Eg: how Amex makes money, what Buy Now Pay Later is

Round 3: Interview 1 (eliminatory)
- Past internships make a big difference
- SQL queries
- Product management and leadership questions
- Guestimates and puzzles
- Possibly tech depth (eg: stack)

Round 4: Interview 2, fully HR (eliminatory)
- Strengths and weaknesses
- A puzzle
- Situational questions, eg: "If we don't hire you but your friend gets hired, how will you react?"

Prep checklist
1. Practice CAT-level data interpretation under time pressure
2. Revise deep learning basics
3. Understand Amex's business model (card fees, merchant discount, interest, BNPL)
4. Brush up SQL
5. Practice guestimates and puzzles
6. Prepare leadership stories from your internships
7. Prepare HR answers: strengths, weaknesses, why Amex, situational questions
8. If Enterprise Technology, add DSA

All the best, and be lucky 😄

full_text:
Introduction

I got the opportunity to participate in Code with Cisco (CWC), through which I was eventually selected for Cisco's pool hiring process. The entire journey was a multi-stage process involving an Online Assessment followed by Technical, Managerial, and HR interviews.

What made the process interesting was that the selection did not happen through a single centralized shortlist. Candidates were shortlisted in multiple batches over time, so there was a considerable gap between the assessment and the interview for some students.

Initial Registration & Pre-Placement Talk
15 June 2026 — Registration

The process started when our Training & Placement Office (TPO) shared the opportunity on the college TPO portal.

Date: 15 June 2026
Opportunity: Code with Cisco
Hiring approach: Pool hiring

I filled out the registration form through the TPO portal and registered for the process.

24 June 2026 — Pre-Placement Talk

A Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) was conducted online on 24 June 2026.

The session provided information about Cisco, the opportunity, and the overall recruitment process. We were informed about the upcoming Online Assessment and the subsequent selection stages.

Round 1 — Online Assessment
25 June 2026 — Original OA

The first round was an Online Assessment conducted on HackerRank.

However, there was a technical issue with the assessment platform on 25 June, because of which the assessment had to be revised.

27 June 2026 — Revised OA

The revised Online Assessment was conducted on 27 June 2026.

The CWC assessment consisted of three sections:

Section 1 — MCQs

This section tested fundamental Computer Science concepts, particularly:

Computer Science fundamentals
Computer Networks
Basic technical concepts
Section 2 — DSA

This section consisted of:

2 DSA coding questions
Difficulty: Medium to Hard

This section primarily tested problem-solving ability, algorithmic thinking, and implementation skills.

Section 3 — Subjective Questions

The final section consisted of subjective/scenario-based questions.

Shortlisting Process

One interesting aspect of Cisco's process was that the OA shortlist was not released as one single list.

The shortlisting happened in multiple batches, and candidates could receive their shortlist at different points in time.

The process continued with shortlisting happening over an extended period, with batches being released until around September 2026.

My Shortlisting

For our batch, the first shortlist was very small, with only two students being shortlisted initially.

The result was communicated by both the company and our TPO on:

29 July 2026

After receiving the shortlist, my interview was scheduled for:

10 August 2026

So there was a significant waiting period between the OA and the interview.

Round 2 — Technical Interview

The first interview round was the Technical Interview.

Duration

Approximately 50–60 minutes

The interview generally started with Introduction.

I started by introducing myself, my background, skills, and interests.

After the introduction, a major part of the conversation revolved around my projects.

The interview also included DSA.

Depending on the interviewer, this could include:

1–2 DSA coding questions
DSA conceptual/theoretical questions
Discussion around the approach
Complexity analysis

The interviewer could also ask follow-up questions based on the solution.

Note :- Every interview round was eliminatory.

Round 3 — Managerial Interview
Duration:- Approximately 60–70 minutes

This was a detailed round and involved considerable discussion around my resume and projects.

Resume Grilling

The interviewer could pick almost any line from the resume and ask questions about it.This made it very important to be completely comfortable with everything written on the resume.

Project Deep Dive:- There was also a detailed discussion around the projects mentioned on my resume.
Behavioral Questions:- The round also included behavioral and situational questions.

My Biggest Takeaway:- Only put things on your resume that you genuinely understand.

A resume should not contain technologies, metrics, or project details simply because they look impressive.

If something is written on the resume, you should be prepared for the interviewer to ask.

Round 4 — HR Interview
Duration:- Approximately 15 minutes

I briefly introduced myself and my background.

The interviewer then asked some relatively easy and conversational HR questions.

The discussion was more focused on getting to know me beyond the technical aspects.There was also a discussion about preferred work locations.

All interviews are on the same day only.

Result

The final result could be announced relatively quickly. The result is most probably on same day or next day.

Preparation Tips

Based on both my experience and discussions with other shortlisted candidates:

Your resume is extremely important. Every project and claim mentioned on it should be something you can confidently explain in depth.
Be comfortable with DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and OOP, as these topics are asked extensively.
Strong fundamentals in Data Structures and Algorithms are sufficient; highly advanced competitive programming is generally not required.
Complete the Striver SDE Sheet thoroughly and supplement it with additional practice on:
Practice explaining both brute-force and optimized solutions, including time and space complexity.
Expect interviewers to ask why you chose a particular data structure or algorithm instead of alternatives.
During project discussions, be ready to justify architecture decisions, scalability, edge cases, and security considerations.

Overall, I found Cisco's interview process to be fair and knowledge-driven. The interviewers emphasized clear thinking, solid fundamentals, and genuine understanding of projects rather than memorized answers.

full_text:
Getting placed at UKG was a valuable and enriching experience. The selection process consisted of multiple rounds designed to evaluate technical knowledge, problem-solving ability, AI understanding, communication skills, and overall personality.

1. Online Assessment

The first round was an online assessment consisting of two questions:

DSA Problem: A data structures and algorithms-based coding problem was given to assess problem-solving and coding skills.
Debugging Problem: The second question involved a folder containing multiple files of an existing project. We were given the flexibility to choose a preferred technology/tech stack and were required to analyze the project, identify the issues or errors, and debug the code accordingly.
2. Technical Interview

The second stage was a virtual technical interview, which lasted approximately 30–40 minutes.

The interview covered:

Discussion about the projects I had worked on, including my contributions and the technologies used.
Questions related to Computer Science fundamentals, including core concepts.
A medium-level DSA problem, where I was asked to explain my approach and arrive at a solution.
Follow-up questions based on my projects and technical knowledge.
3. AI Assessment Round

The third stage was an in-person AI assessment, lasting approximately 1 hour.

In this round:

I was given a problem statement and asked to develop appropriate prompts to solve the given problem.
I had to explain the reasoning behind my prompts and how I would improve them.
The interviewer asked questions about prompt engineering and AI concepts.
There was also a discussion around my AI-related projects and the approaches I had used.
The round involved considerable questioning, reasoning, and iteration, which tested my ability to think critically and communicate my approach.
4. HR Interview

The final stage was an HR interview, which lasted around 10–15 minutes.

The discussion focused more on my personality and background. Some of the areas covered were:

Introduction and questions about myself and my background.
My inspirations and career goals.
Questions about my family and hobbies.
Questions related to leadership, teamwork, and handling responsibilities.
General questions to understand my personality and interests beyond academics.

full_text:
I was selected for a two-month Software Development Internship at Zscaler through the campus placement process, which was conducted in September 2025. The internship was scheduled from 8 June to 8 August 2026, and based on my performance during the internship, I was subsequently converted to a Full-Time Employment (FTE) offer.

Selection Process

The selection process consisted of an Online Assessment followed by three interview rounds.

1. Online Assessment (OA)
The OA primarily tested basic Computer Science fundamentals through MCQs, along with programming skills. It included:

CS fundamentals and basic technical MCQs

One Data Structures coding question in a language of the candidate's choice

One Python-based MCQ/question

2. Technical Interview
The first interview was primarily focused on Data Structures and CS fundamentals. I was asked two Data Structures problems, followed by questions covering core CS subjects. The discussion particularly included:

C programming and fundamental concepts

DBMS

Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs) principles

The round involved both problem-solving and conceptual questions, so having a strong understanding of fundamental concepts was important.

3. Project + Resume-Based Interview
The second round focused mainly on my resume, projects, technical experience, and co-curricular activities. The interviewer went through my resume in detail and asked questions about the projects and technologies mentioned in it. I was also asked to explain my co-curricular activities, roles, responsibilities, and involvement in various college activities. I was expected to clearly explain my contributions and experiences mentioned on my resume.

4. HR/Behavioral Interview
The final round focused on HR and behavioral questions. The discussion covered general behavioral situations, experiences, and questions aimed at understanding my approach to different situations.

During the two-month internship, we had regular demos and review meetings with our mentors and managers. These sessions were an important part of the evaluation process. We were expected to present our work, explain the approach we had taken, discuss the challenges we faced, and demonstrate our progress. Based on my overall performance during the two-month internship, I received a PPO for Full-Time Employment (FTE) at Zscaler.

full_text:
I joined Mondelēz International through the on-campus summer internship process and later converted it into a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) following the mid-term and final project reviews. If you are preparing for Mondelēz, here is the honest truth about what the team actually looks for and how the process works.

The Biggest Myth: Branch Preference

There is a common misconception on campus that Mondelēz only looks for IPE students. That is completely untrue. Every eligible branch has an equal shot. What actually differentiates candidates isn’t your department name on paper—it’s ownership and your practical, problem-solving mindset.

Shortlisting Criteria

Strict 8.0+ CGPA: Keep your grades up. They adhere strictly to the cutoff for initial shortlisting.

Round 1: The Group Discussion (Data & Case-Based)

The GD isn’t a generic debate on current affairs. They hand you a real, operational case study packed with numbers.

The Reality: Analyzing the numbers matters, but your assertiveness and communication carry far more weight. Honestly, the panel isn’t just looking for textbook correct math; they want to see who can command the room, speak with calm confidence, and drive the discussion without getting flustered. Make your presence felt early and hold your ground.

Round 2: Personal Interview (~30 to 35 Minutes)

Coursework over Academic Projects: The interviewers focused much more on core engineering and supply chain coursework rather than standard academic projects.

Resume Strategy: If you have coding or software projects, tone them down. Unless you applied programming directly to solve an industrial or automation problem, Mondelēz is interested in manufacturing, logistics, and process efficiency. Reframe any technical work around automation and business impact.

Case Studies & Mindset: Expect scenarios centered around inventory management, bottlenecks, and supply chain trade-offs. If you understand Lean Six Sigma and can frame your answers using structured root-cause thinking, you will immediately stand out.

Prior Internships Matter: They will grill you thoroughly on past hands-on training or internship experience. You must know your numbers, your exact contribution, and why you took every single decision.

Converting the Internship into a PPO

The internship itself is all about execution. Treat your project like you own the facility: identify gaps, apply continuous improvement tools, stay proactive on the shop floor, and communicate your deliverables clearly to the mentors. Complete ownership of your project from day one is what seals the PPO.

key_questions: Group Discussion (GD) – 15–20 Minutes

full_text:
1. Group Discussion (GD) – 15–20 Minutes

The GD round lasted around 15–20 minutes. We were given a supply-related case study and approximately 2 minutes to read and understand the case before the discussion started.

The case required us to analyse the situation, identify the key problem, and discuss possible solutions from a practical business and supply-chain perspective.

The panel mainly observed communication, logical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, listening skills, and how we handled different opinions. The focus was not on speaking continuously but on making relevant points and contributing meaningfully to the discussion.

2. Personal Interview – 40–45 Minutes

The personal interview lasted around 40–45 minutes, with the main focus on the resume.

They went through the resume in detail and asked questions from internships, projects, and core subjects. For core subjects, it is better to prepare at least 2–3 subjects in depth. The questions were not limited to definitions; they focused more on practical applications, real-life scenarios, and how the concepts are used in industry.

Internships and projects should be prepared very thoroughly. Be clear about what you did, why you did it, your individual contribution, challenges faced, and what you learned. They can ask follow-up questions to check whether you genuinely understand the work mentioned on your resume.

Basic supply-chain concepts should also be prepared, especially for an operations/supply-chain-oriented role. The interviewer may connect your technical knowledge and internship experience with practical industrial situations.

Along with technical and resume-based questions, they also asked HR questions to understand my motivation, experiences, teamwork, and overall personality.

Overall Takeaway

The most important thing is to prepare your resume thoroughly. If you have mentioned an internship, project, or technical subject, be ready for detailed questions and practical applications. For core subjects, prepare 2–3 subjects deeply rather than trying to memorise definitions from many subjects. Also, have a good understanding of basic supply-chain concepts and common HR questions

full_text:
My interview process at Tredence comprised of 3 rounds of discussions – 2 technical and 1 HR round.

Round 1 – Technical Round

The 1st round was of about an hour and the interviewers focused on core programming concepts, intermediate and advanced level SQL, and basic Python/PySpark. The SQL questions revolved mainly around self-join and consecutive number problems and a few other query-based sums. The interviewer also asked me about my basic understanding of programming concepts and my approach to solving any given problem.

Round 2 – Technical Round

The 2nd technical round was more elaborate and lasted for about 1 hour 30 minutes. The discussion revolved mainly around my resume – the interviewer asked me detailed questions about all the projects mentioned there. I had to explain the architecture of the projects, cloud platforms used, optimization techniques applied, and the rationale behind my decision for any specific project. Additionally, I was also asked 2 medium level DSA problems and had to explain my approach while solving them.

Round 3 – HR / Behavioral Round

The last round was comparatively shorter (about 25 minutes) and started with a casual introduction and a few questions about my experiences. This was followed by 2 situation-based questions to gauge my communication and management skills. Finally, I was asked a guesstimate question to test my logical and analytical skills.

In general, I feel that the interview process was a good one – it tested my technical acumen and problem-solving approach while also evaluating my understanding of the projects done.

full_text:
I recently went through the placement selection process at UKG, and overall, it was a valuable learning experience for me.

The process was a little challenging in the beginning because I was not sure what areas the interview would focus on. I prepared by revising my core technical subjects, practicing coding questions, reviewing my resume, and making sure I was comfortable explaining my projects and the technologies I had worked with.

During the interview, I was asked questions about my projects, programming concepts, problem-solving approach, and technical skills mentioned on my resume. There were also questions that tested my understanding of the basics and how I would approach a problem in a real-world situation. This helped me understand that interviewers are interested not only in the final answer but also in how you think and explain your approach.

One thing I learned from this experience is that preparation should not be limited to memorizing interview questions. It is much more important to understand your concepts and projects so that you can explain them confidently in your own words.

My advice to other students would be to start preparing early, focus on the basics, practice coding regularly, and thoroughly understand everything mentioned on your resume. During the interview, stay calm and don't be afraid to admit when you don't know something.

Overall, the UKG placement experience helped me improve my technical knowledge, problem-solving skills, and confidence, while also teaching me how to handle interviews in a better way.

The second interview was more comprehensive, covering resume/project-based questions, CS fundamentals, System Design, AI concepts, React, and general software development. There was also some HR-style interaction, including questions about background, experience, and behavioral aspects.

full_text:
The interview at Nestle is something that I think will always stay with me because it was my very first interview. Initially, I was really nervous, but once the interview started and I got into the flow, that nervousness kind of went away.

Talking about the group discussion, I don't think it's really about whether your thought process is 100% accurate or whether you have the perfect answer. It's more about how actively you participate, whether you're able to understand the topic, put your thoughts across clearly, and, at the same time, listen to and understand what other people are saying.

So, I think clarity is really important. You should be clear about what you're saying and confident enough to communicate it.

Then coming to the interview, it was around 20 minutes. The first half was mainly technical questions related to my core branch, and after that, there was an HR round.

And one thing I really learned from the interview is that you should just be yourself. Be honest about your likes, dislikes, strengths, and weaknesses. Don't try to pretend to be someone you're not, because eventually, the interviewer will figure it out, and it can actually make things more difficult.

I feel an interview is not just about proving how capable you are. It's also about showing the interviewer who you are and whether you're a good fit for the particular role they're looking for.

So, instead of trying to give the "perfect" answer, I think it's better to be genuine, stay calm, and communicate your thoughts clearly.
