full_text:
I recently appeared for the EY Data Analyst Intern interview process. The selection process consisted of three rounds: Online Assessment (OA), Technical Interview, and HR Interview.

Here is a brief overview of my experience and the topics asked in each round.

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The OA mainly focused on aptitude and communication-based questions.

Topics covered:

Aptitude questions
Communication-based questions
One DSA coding question

The DSA question was around the easy to medium level. Overall, the assessment focused more on problem-solving ability, aptitude, and communication.

Round 2: Technical Interview

The technical interview mainly focused on the projects mentioned in my resume and fundamental technical concepts.

Topics covered:

Resume-based project discussion
SQL fundamentals and queries
Python fundamentals
Generative AI (GenAI)
Questions related to my technical knowledge and project implementation

The interviewer mainly asked about the projects I had worked on and the concepts I had mentioned in my resume. I would recommend preparing your projects thoroughly and being able to explain your approach and implementation clearly.

Round 3: HR Interview

The HR interview focused mainly on general and career-related questions.

Topics covered:

Where do you see yourself in the next 5 years?
What are your future plans?
General HR and behavioral questions
Career goals and aspirations

The questions were mostly about my future plans, career goals, and how I see myself developing professionally.

My Advice to Future Candidates

Based on my experience, I would recommend focusing on your communication skills along with your technical preparation.

The technical questions were mainly based on fundamentals, projects, SQL, Python, and GenAI. You should be able to explain what you have built, why you used a particular approach, and how you solved problems.

Most importantly, work on your communication skills. Try to explain your thoughts clearly and confidently. Even when you do not know the complete answer, present your understanding and approach as clearly as possible.

Prepare your resume projects well, revise technical fundamentals, practice aptitude and DSA, and focus on improving your communication.

All the best to everyone preparing for EY interviews!

author: NARAYAN SUNIL KAKADE
title: EY  global interview experience
full_text:
The interview started with a brief introduction. I introduced myself by talking about my educational background, technical skills, and the projects I had worked on. After that, the interviewer focused mainly on my projects and asked me to explain them in detail.

I explained each project one by one, starting with the problem statement—what problem the project was trying to solve and why it was important. Then I explained the solution I implemented, including the key features, technologies used, and my specific contribution to the project. I also explained the overall system architecture and workflow, including how the different components interacted with each other and how data flowed through the system.

The interviewer then went deeper into the technical aspects of my projects and asked follow-up questions to understand whether I actually understood the implementation rather than just knowing the technologies used. I was asked about the design decisions I made, why I selected particular technologies, and how I handled different challenges and edge cases.

After the project discussion, the interviewer moved toward AI and Generative AI concepts. Some of the questions included topics such as Knowledge Graphs, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), vector databases, embeddings, and reranking. For example, I was asked how reranking works in a RAG pipeline and how it improves the relevance of retrieved documents. I explained the retrieval process, where an initial retriever fetches a set of potentially relevant chunks and a reranker then scores those retrieved documents against the query to reorder them based on relevance before passing the most relevant context to the LLM.

Overall, the interview was quite project-oriented and focused on understanding the depth of my technical knowledge. The interviewer frequently asked follow-up questions based on my answers, so having a clear understanding of the architecture, implementation details, and reasoning behind each technical decision was important.

Round 1 – Online Assessment

The first round was an online assessment consisting of two questions. One was a medium-level DSA problem based on the Sliding Window technique, while the second was a Node.js-based coding question. For the Node.js question, a project repository was provided with some missing logic, which had to be implemented correctly. The assessment tested both problem-solving skills and practical understanding of backend development.

Round 2 – Technical Interview

The second round was a technical interview of around 30 minutes. The discussion was primarily based on my resume and the projects I had worked on. I was asked about my individual contributions, the technologies and frameworks I used, and the overall working and architecture of my projects.

The interviewer also asked several questions related to the project architecture, technology choices, backend/frontend interaction, and technical stack. Being able to explain the projects clearly and justify the decisions made during development was important.

Round 3 – AI Assessment

The third round was a technical AI-focused assessment lasting around 1.5 hours. It began with a discussion about my projects and previous internship experience. The interviewer asked about my contributions, technologies used, and how the concepts I had worked with could be applied to real-world problems.

The major part of the round involved working with an event management application repository. I was given new features to implement using an AI coding assistant. I had the freedom to choose the AI assistant I wanted to work with and was asked to explain why I preferred a particular model/tool.

The interviewer also asked about when to use an AI agent versus a planning-based approach, and how I would structure prompts for different development tasks. A significant part of the assessment focused on how I interacted with and leveraged the AI assistant — including how I prompted it, reviewed its suggestions, validated the generated code, and navigated through the implementation rather than blindly accepting its output.

Round 4 – HR Interview

The final HR round lasted around 15 minutes and was fairly conversational. It started with a brief introduction about myself, including where I am from, my previous internship, and my overall experiences. The interviewer then asked about my family background and my experience throughout the UKG interview process.

Overall Experience

Overall, the UKG interview process covered a good mix of DSA, practical development, project understanding, system architecture, AI-assisted development, and behavioral aspects. The AI assessment in particular focused not just on getting the task completed, but on how effectively and thoughtfully I could use AI as a development tool while understanding, reviewing, and validating its output.

UKG Interview Experience

Round 1 – Technical Interview

The first round of my UKG interview was a technical round of around 30 minutes. It started with a discussion about my resume and the projects I had worked on, where I was asked about my contributions, technologies used, and the overall working of my projects. This discussion lasted around 5–10 minutes.

After that, I was given a medium-level DSA problem based on arrays. The interviewer focused on my approach and problem-solving process rather than just the final solution.

The interview then moved towards Generative AI concepts. I was asked about RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), LLMs, the difference between traditional AI and Generative AI, and why RAG is useful. I was also asked questions related to how these concepts can be applied in real-world applications.

Towards the end, the discussion shifted to system design and design patterns. I was asked to explain the Singleton Design Pattern, its benefits, and situations where it can be used. I was then asked to implement the Singleton pattern for a book-ticket booking system.

Overall, the round covered a good mix of projects, DSA, Generative AI, and system-design concepts.

Round 2 : Technical Round

The technical round lasted around 1.5 hours and started with a discussion about my projects and previous internship experience. The interviewer asked about my contributions, technologies used, and real-world applications of the concepts I had worked with.

I was also asked about the practical use cases of singly and doubly linked list.

The major part of the round involved a music-streaming application repository. I was asked to implement some new features with the help of an AI assistant. I was given the freedom to choose an AI assistant and was asked why I preferred a particular one, such as Claude Sonnet, GPT, or other available tools.

The interviewer also asked when to use an AI agent versus a planning approach while writing prompts.

I explained the problem statement to the interviewer and used the AI assistant to understand and implement the required changes. By refining my prompts and approach, I was able to pass all 13 test cases using only 2–3 prompts.

After completing the task, I explained the backend implementation and the changes I had made.

The interviewer also asked about the purpose of the MD file in the repository, followed by a few additional Gen AI-related questions.

Overall, the round tested my technical fundamentals, practical coding skills, problem-solving ability.

HR Round

The HR round lasted around 15 minutes and started with a brief introduction about myself, where I belong, my previous internship, and my AI-related projects. She then asked about my family background and my overall experience throughout the UKG interview process. Towards the end, she gave me an opportunity to ask any questions I had regarding the company or role. The round was quite conversational and ended on a positive note.

full_text:
My Nestlé Placement Experience

The Nestlé placement drive was an intense but rewarding experience that thoroughly tested both technical fundamentals and personality. The process was divided into three distinct phases, each filtering candidates based on different skill sets.

Round 1: The Written Test

The drive kicked off with a comprehensive written test divided into two main sections: Logical Reasoning and Core Electrical Engineering.

The Details: The logical reasoning section required quick thinking with standard puzzles, pattern recognition, and quantitative aptitude. The core electrical section tested fundamental circuit theory, machines, and basic power systems.

The Challenge (Honesty): The biggest hurdle was time management. Shifting gears from fast-paced logical deduction to solving calculation-heavy core electrical problems under a ticking clock was stressful.

Actionable Advice (Helpful): Do not spend too much time on a single logical reasoning question. For the core section, having your fundamental formulas at your fingertips is an absolute must to save time.

Round 2: Group Discussion (GD)

I was placed in Group 4 for the GD, which featured a diverse mix of Electrical, Instrumentation, and Mechanical engineering students.

The Details: Our topic was exactly in my wheelhouse: Introduction of Automation in a working Factory for inventory management and production optimization.

The Challenge (Honesty): With such a mixed group, the conversation easily could have derailed into branch-specific jargon. It was challenging to make my points stand out without talking over the Mechanical students who were focusing heavily on physical factory flow.

Actionable Advice (Helpful): In a mixed-branch GD, try to be the bridge. I focused on how sensors and control systems integrate with mechanical hardware to streamline inventory, which helped structure the group's overall narrative. Focus on collaboration, not domination.

Round 3: Final Interview (Technical + HR)

The final hurdle was a rapid-fire, 15-minute interview that combined technical grilling with psychological evaluation.

Technical Assessment:

They tested my core instrumentation knowledge heavily, focusing on sensor characteristics and control loops.

When the discussion shifted to my summer internship at Tata Motors, they asked specific questions about the practical challenges I faced while developing PLC logic and designing safety interlocks on the factory floor.

They also probed my robotics knowledge. I had to explain my perception architecture, detailing how I integrated custom ONNX models for classification and maturity detection rather than relying on standard markers.

HR Assessment:

The HR questions were designed to assess my personality and cultural fit. They asked standard but crucial questions like, "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?" and "Why do you want to join Nestlé over other core companies?"

They also threw in situational questions to see how I would handle sudden production line failures and team conflicts.

Actionable Advice (Helpful): Know every single detail of your resume. When answering HR questions, be authentic and tie your personal career goals to the company's actual operations.

full_text:
I recently appeared for the EY campus hiring process and was fortunate enough to get selected. The overall process consisted of an Online Assessment ( happened in reading room ) , Technical Interview, and HR Interview. Both interviews were conducted offline at the TPO office.

1. Online Assessment

The online assessment consisted of multiple sections covering aptitude, communication, Excel, technical/AI concepts, and one coding question. Each section was time-bound, so managing time effectively while maintaining a balance between speed and accuracy was important.

2. Technical Interview – Around 45 Minutes to 1 Hour

The technical interview started with the interviewer asking me to choose one of three areas: AI, Problem Solving, or Database. Since the job description was heavily focused on LLMs and Generative AI, I chose AI.

He started with some basic questions:

What is an LLM?

What is the difference between an LLM and RAG? Why do we use RAG ?

After that, most of the interview revolved around my projects.

Project 1 – AI-Based Interview Platform

I was asked to explain my AI-based interview platform in detail, including:

Which LLM/model I used

Overall architecture of the project / the entire flow

While explaining my project, I mentioned terms such as temperature and hallucination, and the interviewer immediately asked me to explain both.

This is something I would strongly recommend keeping in mind: whatever technical terms you mention, be prepared for follow-up questions on them. Don't use terminology just because it sounds impressive. Make sure you actually understand what you're talking about.

Project 2 – Real-Time Chat Application

The interviewer then moved to my real-time chat application.

He asked questions such as:

What is Redis?

Why did you use Redis in your project?

What is the real-world use case of this application?

This highlighted another important point: know the problem your project is solving.

You should also be able to clearly explain why you built the project, what problem it addresses.

Internship Verification

I had mentioned a remote internship on my resume, so the interviewer actually searched for the company on his laptop and cross-checked it.

So, make sure that everything on your resume is genuine and something you can confidently explain if asked.

SQL / DBMS

The interviewer then moved to SQL.

He asked me output-based questions on joins. Interestingly, he did not ask me to write SQL queries; instead, I was given queries/tables and asked to determine the expected output.

He also asked me questions on star schema, snowflake schema and even gave me a notebook to draw their structures.

After that, we discussed normalisation, including its different types, followed by denormalisation. He asked why denormalisation is sometimes preferred and in what situations it can be useful.

Case Study

Towards the end, he gave me a practical case study:

Suppose Myntra wants to accurately predict the delivery date of an order. How would you approach the problem?

I proposed using a Linear Regression model, explaining how historical order and delivery data could be used to predict delivery time. He seemed satisfied with my approach.

Final Question

At the end of the technical interview, he asked me to speak for about a minute on: Why are you a good fit for EY?

I believe this was mainly to assess my confidence, communication, and ability to present my profile clearly.

3. HR Interview – Around 15 Minutes

The HR round was comparatively short and conversational.

The questions mainly revolved around:

Tell me about yourself

My academic background

Interests and hobbies

Career goals

Why EY?

Behavioral and situational questions

Overall Experience

Overall, the entire process was smooth, and the interviewers were professional and supportive.

Based on my experience, I would recommend focusing on these areas while preparing:

Know your projects inside out

Revise important CS fundamentals

Practice basic problem-solving and SQL

Understand the technical terms you mention on your resume

Be prepared to explain the real-world use case of your projects

Practice communicating your approach clearly

Don't panic if you don't immediately know an answer

In the end 3 students got selected out of 29 shortlisted for interview.

One of the most important things I learned is that you don't necessarily need to know everything. If you're unsure about something, stay calm, think through the problem, and explain your reasoning honestly. And interviewers do give you hint so don't get so panick.

The key is to be genuine, clear, and confident throughout the interview.

author: HEMANT JAIN
title: Juspay Campus Recruitment Experience — 6-Month Internship + PPO

rounds.summary: I was eventually selected for the 6-month internship + PPO role. Here is the complete process, round by round.
I initially didn't receive anything. At that point, I was pretty much convinced that I hadn't made it.

full_text:
The Juspay recruitment process was one of the most intense campus recruitment processes I went through. It took around 20 days and six rounds, starting with an online assessment and ending with a managerial/architect-level interview.

I was eventually selected for the 6-month internship + PPO role.

Here is the complete process, round by round.

Round 1 — Online Assessment (OA)

Day 0 — 27th

The process started with an online assessment.

There were three DSA questions. The broad pattern throughout the recruitment process had a strong emphasis on trees and graphs, which is also relevant to the kind of systems built in fintech and financial infrastructure.

I was able to:

Fully solve the first question

Solve around 10/20 test cases for the second question

Not completely solve the third question

So, effectively, I had around 1.5 questions.

There were approximately 500–600 candidates in this round, and around 40 candidates were selected for the next stage.

Interestingly, I received the result only around one hours after the OA, which was much faster than I expected.

Round 2 — Pen-and-Paper / CS Fundamentals Round

Around 40 candidates reached this round.

This was a pen-and-paper examination and, honestly, this round felt quite different from a conventional DSA test.

A large portion of the questions were based on CS fundamentals.

The topics included things such as:

Operating systems

Data structures internals

Database Internals

Basic probability

NLM-related questions

There were some probability questions that could be approached intuitively too.

The NLM section was something many candidates were less prepared for, so it was some luck game too.

Around 19–20 candidates moved forward from this round.

Round 3 — Hackathon A

The next round was Hackathon A.

The problem was based on the Tree of Space / Locking Tree problem. It is a standard problem they ask everytime, so i prepared it beforehand.

The core requirement was to implement operations that allow nodes in a tree to be locked and unlocked while maintaining constraints around their ancestors and descendants.

The primary operations were:

lock(node)

unlock(node)

upgrade(node)

The interesting part was not simply implementing these functions.

The interviewer/test system was evaluating whether the implementation correctly maintained the locking invariants across the tree.

For example, a node generally cannot be locked if:

It is already locked

One of its ancestors is locked

One of its descendants is locked

The upgrade operation introduces additional conditions, such as requiring appropriate locked descendants and changing the locking state of the subtree.

This makes the problem significantly more interesting than a simple tree traversal.

Out of roughly 19 candidates, around 16 were able to get their code running and pass the required test cases.

The cutoff here was relatively straightforward: If your implementation worked correctly against the test cases, you moved forward.

I cleared the round and moved to Hackathon B.

Round 4 — Hackathon B

Hackathon B happened around three days later.

This was a much deeper technical round and lasted approximately 5–6 hours.

Most of the interaction happened through Slack and a video call.

The interviewer was an SDE at Juspay with around one year of experience.

He initially gave me the problem statement and then left me to work on it.

The first part was essentially:

Explain your existing solution.

I had to explain:

What I had implemented

Why I chose that approach

Its time complexity

Its space complexity

What could be optimized

Why certain complexities could or could not be improved

What trade-offs would occur if I optimized one part of the solution

This was an important part of the interview because it tested whether I actually understood the solution rather than simply producing working code.

Concurrency and Multithreading

Then came the difficult part.

I was asked to extend the locking mechanism to support concurrent/multithreaded execution without using mutexes or semaphores.

Initially, I approached the problem using mutexes because I was trying to reason about the concurrency problem from the most obvious synchronization primitive.

The interviewer pushed me away from that approach.

I then explored another approach involving Windows synchronization-related functions, but that wasn't the intended direction either.

Eventually, after several iterations and guidance from the interviewer, I reached the correct direction.

The key idea was to use atomic operations to coordinate access to shared state rather than relying on traditional mutex/semaphore primitives.

The important conceptual shift was:

Instead of thinking only about "locking a node," think about how multiple threads can observe and modify the shared locking state simultaneously.

This round tested much more than coding.

It tested:

Concurrency

Race conditions

Atomicity

Synchronization

Data structures

Complexity

Ability to reason through an unfamiliar problem

Ability to take hints and iterate

After this round, 9 candidates were selected for the in-person interview.

Round 5 — In-Person Technical Interview

The results came around the 3rd, and our interviews were scheduled for the 7th.

We flew to Bangalore on the 6th.

My interview at the Juspay office lasted around three hours.

It was a broad technical + product + behavioral discussion.

Introduction and Experiences

It started with my introduction and my previous experiences.

I had been actively involved with my college's Institution's Innovation Council (IIC), so the interviewer asked me about things such as:

Organizing hackathons

Planning competitions

Working with teams

Evaluating products

How I approach building things

This gradually transitioned into discussions about technology and product development.

Technical Discussion

We discussed:

Programming languages

Why different languages exist

Their respective strengths

How products are built

How I make technical decisions

How I think about products

Then we moved into my projects.

I was asked to explain:

The architecture

Technology stack

Why I selected particular technologies

How I implemented different features

What problems I encountered

How I would improve the system

The interviewer then went deeper into architecture and scalability.

For both of my major projects, we discussed:

How I would scale the system

Current bottlenecks

Potential failure points

Architectural limitations

How the architecture could evolve

What trade-offs different solutions would introduce

This was not just:

"What technology did you use?"

It was more:

"Why did you use it, and what happens when the system becomes 100× larger?"

DSA

After the project discussion, we moved to DSA.

The first question was relatively straightforward — a Two Sum-style problem.

The second was a mathematical problem involving a harmonic progression, which required more mathematical reasoning.

Both went reasonably well.

System Design

After DSA came system design.

I was asked to design a system for verification of documents in a bank.

This became a higher-level system-design discussion.

We discussed things such as:

How the system would accept documents

Processing and verification

Different components

Scalability

Reliability

Data flow

Potential failure scenarios

Quickest Resources : Piyush Garg Sytem Design 2 videos
Other Resources I followed(I covered it before interview process started) : Arpit Bhayani, InterviewBit(Articles), HelloInterview(GOAT for any problem explanation)

So the interview essentially moved through multiple levels:

Product → Architecture → HLD → LLD (Smaller Component)

Round 6 — Managerial / Architect Interview

This was the round I honestly didn't expect to get.

After the in-person interviews, results started coming out gradually.

One candidate received an email on Monday.

Two candidates received their results directly from Bangalore on Tuesday.

Some candidates were called for another managerial round.

I initially didn't receive anything.

At that point, I was pretty much convinced that I hadn't made it.

Then, on Friday evening, I received the email.

My interview was scheduled for 15 August.

The interviewer was a very senior architect.

This round was quite different from the previous technical rounds.

It was much more about how I think.

There were questions around:

Probability

Physics

Lifestyle

Current activities

My college experiences

Club experiences

General problem-solving

System design

There was also another small HLD question involving a car-key-related system.

But the most important lesson I took away from this round was about communicating my thinking.

First-Principles Thinking

One thing I would strongly recommend to anyone preparing for a similar interview is:

Don't try to sound intelligent. Show how you think.

If you naturally approach problems from first principles, communicate that.

Don't use unnecessary jargon.

Instead, explain:

What the fundamental problem is

What assumptions you're making

Why something works

What happens underneath the abstraction

What changes if one assumption changes

What trade-offs are introduced

The interviewer seemed much more interested in the reasoning process than in whether I could throw around advanced terminology.

The Result

The interview was on 15 August.

I received the final result roughly one day later.

I had been selected for the Juspay 6-month internship + PPO role.

From the initial OA to the final selection, the entire process took approximately:

20 days → 6 rounds → 500–600 candidates → final selection

It was one of the most exhausting recruitment processes I had experienced.

For Anyone preparing for Interviews:
Memorize Striver, Do HLD and LLD (It started with our seniors but it will increase only in coming times)

If you need any help DM anytime: +91 9878132532

Signing off🤰

I recently appeared for the EPAM interview, and the overall selection process focused primarily on CS fundamentals, my resume, projects, and DSA.

1. GD / Pen-and-Paper Round

The process also included a GD/pen-and-paper round. Some students discussed the questions from this round during their interviews. The questions were not limited to DSA; they also tested logical thinking, problem-solving ability, and basic technical concepts.

2. Technical Round

The technical interview lasted approximately one hour. The interviewer went through my resume in considerable detail, so being familiar with every skill, technology, project mentioned on the resume.

Most of the questions focused on core CS fundamentals and were related to the concepts and technologies I had listed on my resume. The interviewer also asked detailed questions about my projects, including the technologies I used and how I implemented different parts of them.

There was some discussion involving DSA and logical reasoning, but DSA was not the primary focus. Rather than solving a large number of difficult coding problems, the interviewer was more interested in understanding my approach, logic, and grasp of fundamental concepts. I was also asked a puzzle-based logical question.

One key takeaway from the technical round was that interviewers can directly pick questions from your resume. Therefore, it is very important to have a thorough understanding of everything you mention on it.

3. Managerial Round

The managerial round focused mainly on my projects, previous work experience, and the responsibilities I had handled. The interviewer discussed my past experiences in detail and asked how I approached different situations and challenges.

There were also questions related to my working style, decision-making, teamwork, and how I would handle practical situations in a professional environment.

Overall Experience

Overall, my EPAM interview was more focused on evaluating my understanding of CS fundamentals and the projects and experiences mentioned on my resume rather than testing me with a large number of difficult DSA problems.

The most important preparation areas, in my experience, were strong CS fundamentals, complete knowledge of your resume, a clear understanding of your projects, and the ability to explain your approach and reasoning.

full_text:
Tredence Data Engineer Interview Experience | Campus Placement

I recently got selected for the Data Engineer role at Tredence through campus placement. I’m sharing my complete interview experience and the selection process so that students preparing for Tredence can get an idea of what actually happens in each round.

Overall Selection Process

There were around 400 students who appeared for the Online Assessment. Tredence allowed students from almost all branches (except, I believe, Civil).

The selection process consisted of:

1. Online Assessment (OA)

2. Communication Round

3. Technical Interview – Round 1

4. Technical Interview – Round 2

5. HR Interview

Out of around 400 students, only 21 students cleared the OA. All 21 students who appeared for the communication round qualified for the next stage. After Technical Round 1, 14 students were eliminated and 7 students proceeded to Round 2. All 7 students then appeared for the HR round, after which 5 students were finally selected.

---

Round 1: Online Assessment

The OA consisted of different sections:

- Aptitude questions

- English questions

- 1 Guesstimate question

- 2 Coding questions

The coding questions were of approximately medium difficulty.

The two coding questions were based on:

- Arrays

- Strings

---

Round 2: Communication Round

The communication round was approximately 45 minutes.

The round mainly tested communication, listening, speaking and basic English skills.

The activities included:

- Reading a given statement aloud

- Listening to a statement/audio and speaking what you heard

- Some basic grammar questions

- Speaking on a given topic for around one minute

After completing this round, I was selected for the technical interview rounds.

---

Round 3: Technical Interview – Round 1

The interviewer started by asking questions from my resume.

My resume contained several technical skills, including:

- Computer Science fundamentals

- DBMS

- SQL

- Machine Learning

- LLMs

- Agentic AI

- Other technical concepts

- Three projects

The interviewer asked questions from almost everything I had mentioned in my resume. So, I would strongly recommend that you only mention technologies and concepts on your resume that you can confidently explain.

The interviewer also asked several cross-questions based on my answers and projects.

Apart from resume-based questions, I was also asked to:

- Write a SQL query

- Solve a DSA problem

- Explain my approach

While solving the DSA problem, the interviewer was also observing how I wrote the code and the quality/structure of my code, rather than only looking at the final answer.

After this round, I successfully cleared Technical Round 1 and proceeded to Round 2.

---

Round 4: Technical Interview – Round 2

The second technical interview was again largely based on my resume and projects.

The interviewer went into much more depth regarding my projects and asked several cross-questions.

Some areas/questions included:

- Explain your project's architecture

- Draw the architecture of your project

- Explain the complete tech stack

- Explain one particular functionality in detail

- Explain how different components of your project interact

- Questions based on the technologies used in the project

- Basic SQL questions

- Some managerial/behavioral-type questions

The interviewer particularly focused on whether I actually understood the projects mentioned on my resume rather than just having built them by following something.

So, if you have projects on your resume, make sure you understand every important component, technology, functionality and design decision used in them.

After completing the second technical round, I was called for the HR round.

---

Round 5: HR Interview

The interviewer asked basic HR and behavioral questions, along with some questions related to my resume.

Some areas covered were:

- Introduction/background

- Projects

- Explain your project to a non-technical person

- Project input and output

- Extracurricular activities

- Situation-based questions

- How would you handle a conflict?

- Other basic behavioral/HR questions

The interviewer also checked whether I could explain my technical work in a simple way to someone from a non-technical background.

---

Final Result

After completing all the rounds, the final result was announced.

Out of approximately 400 students who appeared for the OA, 5 students were finally selected, and I was one of them for the Data Engineer role at Tredence.

My biggest takeaway from the process

The most important thing I learned is that your resume matters a lot.

The interviewers repeatedly went back to the things I had mentioned on my resume and asked cross-questions. Projects were discussed in considerable depth, including architecture, tech stack, functionality and what happens under the hood.

So my advice to anyone preparing for a similar placement interview would be:

Don't put something on your resume just because it looks impressive. If you mention it, be prepared to explain it and answer cross-questions about it.

Also prepare DSA, SQL, CS fundamentals, projects and communication, because the selection process tested all of these areas at different stages.

All the best to everyone preparing for placements! 🚀

author: SAKSHAM DODA
title: Increff - Campus Placement / Interview experience

rounds.summary: Round 2 – Online Assessment (OA) The second assessment was a 90-minute Online Assessment.

full_text:
I got selected for the Increff campus recruitment process. Sharing my complete placement experience below to help future candidates understand the selection process and prepare accordingly.

Eligibility Criteria

Eligible CGPA: 7.0+

Branches Allowed: All Circuital branches

Students who met the eligibility criteria were allowed to register for the opportunity and participate in the selection process.

Round 1 – Behavioral Assessment + 12-Minute MCQ Test

The first stage consisted of two assessments.

Behavioral Assessment

Candidates first had to complete a behavioral assessment designed to evaluate different aspects of their personality, working style and behavioral tendencies.

12-Minute MCQ Assessment

After the behavioral assessment, candidates had to attempt a short and highly time-constrained MCQ test.

The test consisted of:

50 MCQs
12 minutes
Questions based mainly on:
Logical reasoning
Basic mathematics
Quantitative aptitude
General problem-solving

The main challenge of this round was managing time effectively, as there were only around 14 seconds available per question on average.

After the behavioral assessment and the 12-minute MCQ test, candidates were shortlisted for the next round.

Out of approximately 270 students, 170 students were shortlisted for the next Online Assessment.

Round 2 – Online Assessment (OA)

The second assessment was a 90-minute Online Assessment.

The test consisted of approximately 100 questions covering multiple areas, including:

Computer Science fundamentals
DSA
Logical reasoning
Mathematics
Quantitative aptitude

This round tested both technical knowledge and the ability to solve questions quickly under a strict time limit.

After this round, 30 students were shortlisted for the next stage of the selection process.

Round 3 – LLD / OOPS Problem-Solving Round

The first major technical stage involved a Low-Level Design (LLD) problem based on OOPS concepts.

Candidates were given a problem statement that required us to design a solution using classes and objects and implement around 10 different functions based on the given requirements.

The overall session was scheduled for approximately 3 hours, but the process was not simply a three-hour coding task.

Initial Evaluation / First Hour

During the initial part of the session, the interviewer discussed our approach to the problem.

We were asked to explain:

How we understood the problem statement
Our approach to solving the problem
How we planned to design the classes
How the different objects and functions would interact
Our introduction
Projects mentioned in our resume
Technologies we had worked with

The interviewer evaluated our understanding of the problem, our approach and our technical background.

Based on this initial discussion, the interviewer decided whether the candidate would continue with the complete problem-solving task.

If the interviewer was satisfied with the candidate’s approach and understanding, the candidate was allowed to continue working on the problem for the remaining time.

Therefore, this round was not simply about completing a coding task. Problem understanding, approach, communication and technical discussion during the initial evaluation were also important parts of the assessment.

LLD Implementation

Candidates who proceeded with the task had the remaining time to work on the LLD problem.

The task required us to use OOPS principles, classes and objects, and implement approximately 10 functions according to the requirements provided in the problem statement.

The round focused heavily on:

Object-Oriented Programming
Classes and objects
Low-Level Design
Designing a solution based on requirements
Function implementation
Code structure
Problem-solving
Understanding requirements
Explaining design decisions

The interviewer was interested not only in whether the functions were completed but also in how the candidate designed and approached the problem.

Technical Review

After the implementation period, the interviewer reviewed the work done during the session.

We had to explain:

What we implemented
How the solution worked
Why we chose a particular approach
How the classes and objects interacted
How the different functions were designed
The reasoning behind our design decisions
Any challenges faced while solving the problem

This made the round a combination of LLD implementation, OOPS knowledge, problem-solving and technical discussion rather than a conventional coding test.

After this stage, 5 students were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 4 – AI-Assisted Coding Round

The next round was an AI-assisted coding/development round.

This was one of the most interesting parts of the selection process.

Candidates were given an extended version of the problem statement from the previous LLD round.

The round lasted approximately 2 hours.

We were required to use AI tools to develop a fully functional website based on the given requirements.

The problem involved a hostel booking system, and we had to implement the features specified in the problem statement.

The objective was not simply to generate code using AI. We had to understand the requirements, decide how to build the application, select an appropriate technology stack and use AI effectively to develop the solution.

The round tested:

Problem understanding
Web development
OOPS and programming concepts
Technology-stack knowledge
AI-assisted development
Debugging
Testing
Requirement understanding
Ability to verify and modify AI-generated code

Candidates were expected to produce a functional implementation within the given two-hour time limit.

Round 5 – AI Coding Review / Technical Interview

After completing the two-hour AI-assisted coding task, we had another technical interview.

The interview primarily focused on the solution we had developed during the AI coding round.

Some of the areas discussed included:

Approach taken to solve the problem
Technology stack used
Why we selected that particular tech stack
How AI was used during development
What exactly AI contributed to the project
Which parts of the code were generated by AI
Understanding of the AI-generated code
How AI was used to debug or improve the solution
How the application worked
Database-related concepts
Basic Computer Science fundamentals

The interviewer also asked detailed questions about the implementation.

We had to demonstrate that we actually understood the code generated with the help of AI rather than simply relying on the generated output.

The discussion also included CS fundamentals and basic database concepts.

This round therefore tested both technical knowledge and the ability to work effectively with AI as a development tool.

Final Result

The selection process started with approximately 270 students.

The progression was:

270 students → 170 students → 30 students → 5 students → 3 students(selected)

The final selection was based on performance across the different assessment, problem-solving, LLD, AI-assisted development and interview rounds.

I was fortunate to be selected through the Increff campus recruitment process.

Overall Experience & Preparation

Overall, the Increff selection process was quite different from a traditional placement process because it placed significant emphasis on OOPS, Low-Level Design, practical development and AI-assisted coding, along with fundamental CS knowledge and aptitude.

For preparation, I would recommend focusing on:

OOPS concepts
Classes and objects
LLD basics
DSA fundamentals
CS fundamentals
DBMS and basic SQL
Logical reasoning
Quantitative aptitude
Web development fundamentals
Understanding at least one technology stack properly
Building and explaining projects
Debugging and testing
Effective use of AI coding tools

One of the most important things I would recommend is to understand whatever code you write, especially when using AI.

During the interviews, it was not enough to say that AI generated the solution. We were asked what AI had done, how the generated code worked, what technology was being used and why we had taken a particular approach.

The AI-assisted coding round particularly showed that modern technical interviews can evaluate candidates on more than just their ability to write code from scratch. Being able to understand requirements, design a solution, use AI effectively, verify its output, debug the implementation and explain the final solution are becoming important parts of the development process.

Overall, the Increff placement process provided a strong combination of aptitude, CS fundamentals, OOPS, LLD, practical development, database concepts, problem-solving and AI-assisted software development.

It was a valuable experience and gave me a good understanding of how technical interviews can combine traditional software engineering fundamentals with modern AI-assisted development.

rounds.summary: Online Assessment The first stage was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting of MCQs and coding questions.
Interview Round 2 The second interview was more technically detailed.

full_text:
I appeared for BlackRock's Software Engineer campus recruitment process. The process consisted of an Online Assessment followed by two technical interview rounds, after which I was shortlisted.

Online Assessment

The first stage was an Online Assessment (OA) consisting of MCQs and coding questions.

The MCQs covered technical/computer science concepts, while the coding section tested my problem-solving and DSA skills. The OA was the first screening round, after which shortlisted candidates were called for interviews.

Interview Round 1

After clearing the OA, I was called for the first interview round.

The interview started with a brief discussion about my internship experience, interests, and hobbies. This part was fairly short and was mainly introductory.

The interviewer then moved on to DSA. I was asked two coding questions, both based on trees. I had to explain my approach and work through the solutions.

After the DSA questions, we discussed my projects, with the interviewer asking about what I had worked on and my contributions.

That was essentially the first round — a combination of a brief introduction, internship discussion, two tree-based DSA problems, and projects.

Interview Round 2

The second interview was more technically detailed.

A significant portion of the discussion was centered around Unix and Python. I was asked several questions to test my understanding of these areas, along with questions about my internship experience and projects.

The interviewers went into my projects in considerably more detail than in the first round. I was asked about the implementation, the technologies I had used, and different aspects of the projects.

There were also questions on core CS fundamentals, so preparation wasn't limited to DSA. The discussion covered multiple areas of computer science and was fairly resume-oriented.

Result

After the second interview, I was shortlisted for the Software Engineer role at BlackRock.

My Takeaways

For anyone preparing for a similar campus recruitment process, my experience suggests that preparation should go beyond just DSA. The interview process tested different dimensions:

Online Assessment: MCQs + coding
Round 1: Internship + interests/hobbies + 2 tree-based DSA questions + projects
Round 2: Unix + Python + internship + detailed project discussion + CS fundamentals
Resume: Be prepared to explain everything you have mentioned, particularly your projects and internship.

One thing I found particularly important was being comfortable discussing my own projects and internship in depth. The interviews weren't solely about solving coding problems; they also tested whether I genuinely understood the technical work I had put on my resume.

full_text:
I got selected for the UKG Internship + PPO for SDE role. Sharing my complete placement experience below to help future candidates understand the selection process and prepare accordingly.

Eligibility Criteria

Eligible CGPA: 7.5

Branches Allowed: BCSC, IT and EC

Role: Internship + BPO

Eligible students who registered for the opportunity were shortlisted for the Online Assessment (OA).

Round 1 – Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was conducted on the HackerRank platform and consisted of 2 coding questions.

Question 1 – DSA

The first question was a basic DSA problem based on arrays. It primarily tested problem-solving ability and understanding of fundamental data structures and algorithms.

Question 2 – Tech Stack / Project-Based Coding

The second question was project-oriented, where candidates could choose a suitable technology stack to implement the solution.

The problem was based on a To-Do List application. Candidates had to implement different functionalities and make the solution pass the given test cases.

Some of the functionalities included:

- Adding an item

- Listing items

- Updating an item

- Deleting an item

- Handling the required operations through appropriate functions

The main focus of this question was on understanding the problem, choosing an appropriate tech stack, implementing the required functions and ensuring that the solution passed the test cases.

Round 2 – Virtual Technical Interview

After the OA, 32 students were initially shortlisted. An additional list of 6 students was also released.

The next round was a virtual interview, with approximately a 30-minute slot for each student. The interviews were conducted over multiple days, with around 10 students scheduled per day.

The interview mainly focused on:

- Introduction

- Basic Computer Science fundamentals

- OOPS

- DBMS

- Resume-based questions

- Internship experience, if applicable

- Projects and technologies mentioned in the resume

The interviewer also asked follow-up questions based on the candidate's answers and resume.

For me, the major focus areas in this round were OOPS and DBMS, along with questions related to my resume and internship experience.

After this round, 19 students were shortlisted for the next stage.

Round 3 – Live Problem-Solving / AI-Assisted Technical Round

The third round was a live one-to-one technical/problem-solving round. This was one of the most interesting parts of the entire selection process.

The candidate was asked to explain their preferred technology stack, after which the interviewer provided a larger/scalable problem statement and multiple problems that had to be solved.

The important part was that AI assistance was allowed during this round. Candidates were provided access to AI and were expected to use it effectively while working on the problem.

The round was not simply about writing code from scratch. It involved understanding the given problem, using AI appropriately, debugging, testing, reasoning about the solution and discussing the implementation with the interviewer.

The difficulty and type of problem varied from student to student. There was considerable diversity in the questions. Depending on the candidate, the problem could involve:

- DSA-based problems

- System Design

- OOPS, such as designing and implementing classes

- Technology-stack-based development

- Full-stack/web development projects

- Debugging and testing an existing or partially implemented solution

For example, one candidate could receive a DSA problem, while another could receive an OOPS-based class-design problem or a complete web-development project based on their chosen tech stack.

Therefore, the round tested more than just coding ability. It focused on problem-solving, understanding requirements, debugging, testing, system thinking, technology knowledge and the ability to work effectively with AI.

The interviewer remained present throughout the session, so candidates also had to explain their approach and discuss their decisions while solving the problem.

The round generally lasted around 1 to 1.5 hours, depending on the problem and discussion.

After this round, 7 students were shortlisted for the HR round.

Round 4 – HR Interview

The final round was an HR interview.

Compared to the technical rounds, this round was relatively straightforward and focused mainly on understanding the candidate's personality, career goals and motivation.

Some of the questions included:

- Tell me about yourself.

- Why do you want to join UKG?

- Where do you see yourself in 5 years?

- Questions about your interests and career goals.

- Basic questions related to teamwork and experiences.

The HR round consisted mainly of basic HR and behavioral questions.

Final Result

A total of 7 students reached the HR round.

Out of these, 5 students were finally selected for the UKG Internship + BPO role.

I was fortunate to be one of the students selected.

Overall Experience & Preparation

Overall, the UKG selection process was focused on a combination of fundamental CS knowledge, problem-solving, practical development skills, projects, communication and the ability to work with AI.

For preparation, I would recommend focusing on:

- DSA, especially basic problem-solving and arrays

- OOPS

- DBMS and SQL

- Basic Computer Science fundamentals

- Your projects and technology stack

- Web development fundamentals, if applying with a web-development background

- System Design basics

- Debugging and testing

- Understanding how to use AI tools effectively during development

- Basic HR and behavioral questions

One of the most important things I would recommend is to know your resume and projects thoroughly. Be prepared to explain your technology choices, your individual contribution, implementation details and the challenges you faced.

The third round particularly showed that interviews are increasingly moving beyond simply checking whether a candidate can write code. Being able to understand a problem, break it down, use available tools such as AI effectively, verify the generated solution, debug it and explain your reasoning is equally important.

Overall, the process provided a good mix of DSA, CS fundamentals, project knowledge, practical development, system thinking and AI-assisted problem-solving, making it a very different experience from a purely traditional coding interview.

rounds.summary: Online Assessment (OA) The OA consisted of 95 MCQs along with coding questions.

full_text:
I got selected for the IAM (Identity and Access Management) role at BlackRock. Sharing my complete placement experience below.

Eligibility Criteria

Eligible Batch: 2027
Course: B.Tech
Minimum CGPA: 7.5
Gender: Any
Active Backlogs: No active backlogs allowed
Backlog History: Allowed

Branches Allowed:All

All eligible students who filled the form were shortlisted for the Online Assessment (OA).

Online Assessment (OA)

The OA consisted of 95 MCQs along with coding questions.

MCQ Topics: Design Patterns, Advanced Design Patterns, Aptitude, SQL, Advanced SQL.

There were 2 coding sets, with 2 questions in each set:

Set 1: 1 question in Java, 1 question in any programming language.
Set 2: 1 question in JavaScript, 1 question in any programming language.

The first coding question was based on a JavaScript Document Approval System. It involved yield, await, asynchronous processing, classes, async generators, sorting, priority-based processing and FIFO. Documents had to be processed according to priority + FIFO.

The second coding question was comparatively simple and was mainly based on if-else/conditional logic.

OA MCQ Topics: Design Patterns, Advanced Design Patterns, Aptitude, SQL, Advanced SQL, Java,OOPs

Shortlisting After OA

After the OA, 30 students were shortlisted.

There were 4 different roles – IAM, SE/SWE, Aladdin and one other role. Students were assigned the roles they had opted for. Students who selected Open to All were assigned the IAM role.

I had selected Open to All, so I was assigned the IAM role.

The interviews were conducted virtually through Webex and started around 2 days after the OA.

Round 1 – Technical + HR

My first interview was taken by a female interviewer from the Singapore office. It started at around 9:00 AM and lasted approximately 20-25 minutes for me. Some students had interviews of around 30–35 minutes as well.

Questions Asked

Introduce yourself, explain all projects, explain internship experience, IAM (Identity and Access Management), RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), IAM security mechanisms, Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP), Zero Trust Architecture, handling feedback, teamwork vs individual work, challenges faced in projects.

The interviewer went deeper into IAM and security concepts through follow-up and counter-questions.

Round 2 – Technical + Projects + HR

After Round 1 was completed for all students, around 15 students were selected for Round 2.

The second interview was taken by a male interviewer. My interview lasted around 20-25 minutes.

Questions Asked

Introduce yourself, explain projects, project-based counter questions, Java multithreading, concurrency, thread management, determining the optimal number of threads, Java single-threaded vs multithreaded, SQL query optimization, REST APIs, AI IDEs, NLP tokenization, tokens in NLP, prompt grounding, team project architecture, individual contribution, teammates' roles, teamwork experience, time management.

There were no major questions from traditional CS fundamentals apart from the SQL/query optimization discussion.

For the SWE/SE role, some students were also asked 1–2 DSA questions, generally ranging from simple to medium difficulty.

Final Result

The result was announced on the same day.

A total of 7 students were finally selected:

3 – SWE

3 – IAM

1 – Aladdin

I was selected for the IAM role.

Overall Experience & Preparation

Overall, my interview experience was good. The process focused more on practical understanding, projects, role-specific concepts and problem-solving rather than only theoretical CS fundamentals.

For preparation, I would recommend focusing on IAM, RBAC, Authentication and Authorization, Principle of Least Privilege, Zero Trust Architecture, security mechanisms, Java, Java Multithreading, SQL, Advanced SQL, Query Optimization, REST APIs, Design Patterns, Advanced Design Patterns, JavaScript, DSA, Aptitude, AI/NLP basics, NLP Tokenization, Prompt Grounding, and your projects/internships.

My biggest suggestion would be to know your resume and projects very well. The interviewers asked several counter-questions based on my projects, so it is important to understand your actual contribution, implementation details and technologies used rather than just memorizing the project description.

full_text:
Cisco Software Engineer Interview Experience (On-Campus 2025)

About Me

Paras Garg

📞 +91 9041594574
💼 LinkedIn

Overall Hiring Process

I interviewed for the Software Engineer role through campus placements in 2025 and was eventually selected. The process was spread over multiple stages and involved both coding and in-depth technical discussions.

Round 1: Online Assessment (1.5 Hours)

The OA consisted of:

40 MCQs
2 DSA/Coding Questions

MCQ Topics

Mental Ability
Mathematics
DBMS
Operating Systems
Computer Networks
Object-Oriented Programming
Machine Learning fundamentals

Coding Problems

1. Minimum Time Path with Tasks

The problem described an unweighted and undirected tree representing a distributed server system. Given a starting node, a set of mandatory task nodes, and a destination node, the objective was to determine the minimum time required to visit all required task nodes in any order before finally reaching the destination. The challenge involved carefully planning the traversal to avoid unnecessary movements while ensuring every mandatory node was visited.

2. Tree Coin Collection with Proximity Rules

The second problem was also based on trees but introduced an interesting twist. Coins were placed on certain vertices, and whenever the collector stood at a vertex, all coins within a distance of two edges were automatically collected. The task was to compute the minimum number of edge traversals needed to collect every coin in the tree. Solving it efficiently required understanding how the proximity rule could reduce redundant traversal.

Both questions were medium-level tree/graph problems requiring optimized thinking rather than straightforward implementation.

Code With Cisco Hackathon

After the OA, around 75 students across India were shortlisted for the onsite Code With Cisco Hackathon. ( i was not one of them.)

Teams of three were formed randomly, and participants were given approximately 10–12 hours to build a complete solution (AI tools allowed) and present it to the judges. Cisco sponsored travel and accommodation for shortlisted candidates.

Although I was not among the hackathon participants, I later learned that the hackathon is independent of the final hiring process. It is important to note that being shortlisted for the Code With Cisco Hackathon did not guarantee selection. Those candidates also had to undergo the same interview stages as the rest of the shortlisted applicants before receiving an offer.
Different Cisco Business Units (Software Engineering, SRE, IT, Consulting, Data Analytics, etc.) continue evaluating candidates separately based on their requirements and resumes.

Resume Shortlisting

Near the end of July, I received an email through my college TPO stating that I had been shortlisted for Software Engineer interviews along with three other students from my college. I was shortlitsed under IT Business Unit (BU).

Cisco asked candidates to prepare a resume using their own template, where identifying information such as name, college, CGPA, and gender was hidden to reduce evaluation bias.

A few days before the interviews, I also received a phone call from HR asking which programming languages I was most comfortable using.

Another unique aspect was that Cisco created a dedicated Webex group containing all candidates for that Business Unit along with HR representatives, making communication and scheduling very smooth. The interviews are run in parallel for all the candidates shortlisted from different colleges at once.

Technical Round 1 (1 Hour)

Approximately 75 candidates participated.

The interview started with introductions, where I briefly spoke about myself, my academic background, previous internship experiences, and the technologies I had worked with. The interviewer then moved on to discussing my internship projects and asked several follow-up questions, including how certain features were implemented and how security concerns could be handled in those systems. Next came a detailed discussion of the projects listed on my resume. The interviewer was interested not only in what I had built but also in the motivation behind the projects, architectural decisions, challenges faced during development, possible optimizations, and alternative approaches. This reinforced the importance of thoroughly understanding every line written on the resume.

After project discussions, I was asked questions from:

DBMS
Operating Systems
Computer Networks
OOP
Machine Learning

The coding and problem-solving section consisted of three parts:

Debugging a Given Solution
I was presented with an existing implementation for a problem and asked to identify flaws in its logic. Instead of rewriting the entire solution, the focus was on understanding the algorithm, spotting incorrect assumptions, and explaining how it could be fixed.
Three Sum Problem
The interviewer asked me to explain multiple approaches for solving the classic Three Sum problem. I discussed the brute-force solution, followed by optimized techniques, comparing their time complexities and explaining the underlying intuition. I was expected to provide pseudocode and reasoning rather than a fully coded implementation.
Custom Greedy Chocolate Distribution Problem
Finally, I was given a custom greedy problem involving chocolate distribution. I first explained a straightforward brute-force approach and then derived an optimized greedy solution. For this question, I was required to write code and explain the logic as I progressed.

The interviewer concluded with a few general questions and allowed me to ask questions as well.

Technical Round 2 (45 Minutes)

Roughly 45 candidates advanced.

After introductions, the interviewer spent nearly ten minutes discussing my SmartNav project in detail. I explained the overall architecture, motivation behind the project, AI components involved, backend design, implementation choices, and practical use cases. This was followed by several follow-up questions that tested my understanding of the system rather than just its functionality.

The remaining time consisted of rapid-fire questions from:

DBMS
Operating Systems
Computer Networks
OOP
Machine Learning

There were also a few conceptual DSA questions such as:

Which data structure would you use in a given scenario?
Time complexity analysis
Trade-offs between different approaches

The interviewer ended by sharing insights about working at Cisco.

ETR / HR Round (15 Minutes)

Around 21 candidates reached this stage.

The discussion was conversational and included:

Feedback on the interview experience
How the previous interview rounds went
Future plans (including higher studies)
Preferred work locations
Internship stipend
Full-time compensation structure
Questions for HR

The interaction was relaxed and primarily intended to understand career goals and answer candidate queries.

Final Result

The results were announced the following day at around 4 PM.

Out of approximately 75 candidates who entered the interview process, around 10–12 students were selected for the Software Engineer role.

Fortunately, I was one of them.

Additional Hiring Batches

The hiring process did not end with my batch.

During September, Cisco continued sending interview shortlists in multiple waves. Sometimes only one or two students received interview calls, while other times a batch of around ten candidates was shortlisted together.

For most of these later batches, the interview structure remained similar:

Technical Round 1
Technical Round 2
Executive Round
HR Round

The Executive Round primarily focused on resume deep-dives, project discussions, system design decisions, and CS fundamentals. It was essentially an intensive resume-grilling round where interviewers explored implementation details and technical choices.

AI Problem-Solving Round (Final Batch)

For one of the final hiring batches, Cisco introduced a new AI Problem-Solving Round.

Candidates received a problem statement approximately two days before the interview and were given 24 hours to build and submit their solution.

During the first interview round, the discussion revolved around:

Their submitted solution
Design choices
Implementation details
Trade-offs and reasoning

Subsequent rounds followed the familiar pattern of technical interviews and HR discussions.

Preparation Tips

Based on both my experience and discussions with other shortlisted candidates:

Your resume is extremely important. Every project and claim mentioned on it should be something you can confidently explain in depth.
Be comfortable with DBMS, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and OOP, as these topics are asked extensively.
Strong fundamentals in Data Structures and Algorithms are sufficient; highly advanced competitive programming is generally not required.
Complete the Striver SDE Sheet thoroughly and supplement it with additional practice on:
Practice explaining both brute-force and optimized solutions, including time and space complexity.
Expect interviewers to ask why you chose a particular data structure or algorithm instead of alternatives.
During project discussions, be ready to justify architecture decisions, scalability, edge cases, and security considerations.

Overall, I found Cisco's interview process to be fair and knowledge-driven. The interviewers emphasized clear thinking, solid fundamentals, and genuine understanding of projects rather than memorized answers.

full_text:
There were three rounds in total: two technical rounds followed by an HR round.

i. In the first technical round, my overall technical knowledge was assessed. The interview covered core computer science subjects as well as web development concepts related to my projects. I was asked about different HTTP error codes, their meanings, and real-world scenarios where I had encountered them. There was also a detailed discussion about my projects, including the challenges I faced and how I resolved them.

The round also included two DSA questions: Boundary Traversal of a matrix and Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA). Both questions were asked verbally, and I had to write the solutions on paper and demonstrate their correctness through dry runs. Towards the end, the interviewer invited questions from my side, and I took the opportunity to ask about the team’s tech stack and how they were integrating AI into their products and workflows.(40 45 minutes)

ii. The second technical round was primarily focused on system design and scalability. It started with a discussion on how I would integrate another website or application into an existing system. As the conversation progressed, the focus shifted toward handling a growing number of users. I proposed 3–4 different approaches and discussed the advantages, disadvantages, and trade-offs associated with each. This led to an in-depth discussion where the interviewer explored the reasoning behind my design decisions, scalability considerations, and overall problem-solving approach. Towards the end of the round, I was also asked a puzzle: how to measure exactly 4 litres of water using 3-litre and 5-litre bottles.(45 50 minutes)

iii. The final round was an HR discussion that lasted around 30–35 minutes. The interviewer began by asking general questions about my background, education, experiences, and career aspirations. The conversation then moved to several situational and behavioral scenarios designed to assess my communication skills, decision-making, problem-solving approach, and overall fit for the organization. Throughout the discussion, the interviewer appeared to be actively evaluating my responses, frequently making notes on the back of my resume after each answer. The round was conversational in nature and focused on understanding both my personality and professional mindset.(30–35 minutes)

full_text:
Selected as Graduate Engineer Trainee – Suzuki Motor Gujarat Pvt. Ltd.

I am pleased to share that I have been selected by Suzuki Motor Gujarat Pvt. Ltd. (SMG) through the recent Campus Recruitment Drive for the position of Graduate Engineer Trainee. Coming from a Civil Engineering background, this opportunity reinforced the importance of fundamentals, honesty, and practical understanding.

Eligibility and Selection Process (as experienced):

Graduation: Minimum 65% / 7.0 CGPA, completed within the stipulated time with no pending backlogs

Class X and XII: Minimum 60% marks

Gap criteria: No gap between 10th, 12th, and graduation (one-year gap after 12th permitted only for entrance exam preparation)

Age limit: 18–23 years as on 1st August 2026

Selection stages included registration of eligible candidates, online assessment (domain test and aptitude test), interview, pre-employment medical examination, issuance of Letter of Intent, and background verification.

My Key Learnings and Thoughts:

Be honest and authentic during the interview. Do not create a false profile; clearly communicate who you are and what you actually know.

Confidence plays a major role. Even if you do not know everything, explaining your understanding clearly makes a strong impression.

Focus on acquiring in-depth practical knowledge rather than only theoretical concepts, as organizations look for real-world application and problem-solving ability.

Maintain a loyal and professional attitude. Companies value discipline, commitment, and a long-term mindset.

Strengthen your core fundamentals, especially construction basics, materials, quality control, safety practices, drawings, and coordination roles.

Communication and clarity are essential. Answer calmly, stay structured, and think before responding.

Final Note:
This experience reaffirmed that consistent effort, honesty, and practical learning truly matter. I am grateful to my mentors, faculty members, and peers for their continuous support. I look forward to learning, growing, and contributing at Suzuki Motor Gujarat Pvt. Ltd.

Hey everyone! Guess what? I landed a job at Honeywell! I'm Jasmine Kaur, a final-year ECE student, and this whole process was such a ride—and luckily, I was one of the two people selected from our class!

The interview was actually a wonderful experience, and it felt super focused. She started off easy with the classic "Tell me about yourself", and then it was straight into the deep end. We talked about my projects, how they link to real-life applications, and then we spent ages just on my BEL internship focusing on avionics and sensors. I had to be able to clearly explain what I did, how the sensors worked, and why it all mattered. It was all about showing that I could actually apply the core knowledge. It was my first proper core interview, and honestly, even though it was challenging, it was such a great feeling to talk about the stuff I'd actually done. Super happy that it all worked out! GD - 27 students were shortlisted for GD. 3 groups were made. But at the time of GD, appointed groups were not followed i.e anyone irrespective of the group he/she is appointed, can go first. So I was in the first group and 8 students were in my group. Topic given was "Which is the better career option- private job or govt job". Time for noting down points was 30 seconds and time for discussion was 10 min. Everyone got there chance to speak and at the end we were just repeating points and were left with nothing to speak, company delegates prompted to go more in depth into the topic and not just give superficial points. Then discussion moved to internship and it was discussed more thouroghly. I stuck on the part where they asked did I follow up on whether the organisation where I did my project were doing something with that or not.

6 were selected, 2 from chemical.

full_text:
JSW Steels visited our campus for Mechanical Engineering placements this year. The entire process consisted of multiple shortlisting and evaluation rounds, each testing different skills ranging from aptitude to technical knowledge to HR competencies.

Round 1: Initial Shortlisting

The process began with a detailed application form. JSW did not ask us to upload our resumes. Instead, we had to manually fill in all academic details, achievements, internships, and project information. Based on this data, an automated resume was generated by the system itself and used for shortlisting. Some students were rejected at this stage, though the criteria were not explicitly disclosed.

Round 2: First Online Test (Aptitude + Technical)

The next step was an online assessment that included both technical and aptitude-based questions. The technical section covered fundamental mechanical engineering concepts, while the aptitude section focused on numerical ability and logical thinking.
This round was moderately difficult, and some eliminations took place based on performance.

Round 3: Second Online Test (Higher-Level Aptitude + Reasoning)

This was the major elimination round. The test involved higher-level aptitude, reasoning, and analytical questions. Compared to the previous test, the difficulty level was noticeably higher, and accuracy as well as speed mattered. A significant number of candidates were screened out after this stage.

Round 4: Personal Interview (Offline – 35 to 40 Minutes)

The final round was an offline personal interview, which was a mix of both HR and technical discussion. My interview leaned more towards the HR side, making it conversational and engaging.

HR Discussion

The interview began with:

Self-introduction

Family background

Reason for choosing Mechanical Engineering

Why JSW Steel?

Why this sector and not any other?

Willingness to relocate

JSW’s first office and some basic company-related questions

How I would adapt to working in a faraway location

The interviewers were very friendly, and the HR questions mainly checked clarity of thought, confidence, and willingness to work in challenging locations.

Technical Discussion

The technical portion included:

Questions from my major project

1–2 questions related to my internship

Basic questions on steel manufacturing

Awareness of various departments within JSW Steel

No question was extremely difficult. Even if I did not know something, I simply mentioned that I would read about it, and they appreciated the honesty.

Conclusion

Overall, it was a smooth and positive experience. The interviewers focused more on understanding the candidate rather than conducting a strict interrogation. In my opinion, being genuine, clear, and confident matters more than trying to give perfect answers.

For future aspirants, I would suggest:

Be honest and confident

Have clarity about your projects and internships

Read basic information about JSW, steel manufacturing, and its work culture

Be prepared for questions on relocation and adaptability

Getting placed at JSW Steels was a proud moment and I hope my experience helps future students prepare better.

BEST OF LUCK!
