full_text:
Denso International India Pvt. Ltd. (R & D Engineer)

I am extremely happy to share that I have been placed in Denso International Pvt. Ltd., and here is my complete interview experience. The entire process consisted of three rounds conducted over two days.

Round 1: Written Test (Offline MCQ Test)

A total of 150+ candidates from Mechanical, CSE, and ECE appeared for this round. Denso provided branch-specific question papers.

For CSE students, the paper difficulty was easy to medium, covering:

Data Structures & Algorithms

Operating Systems

OOPs

DBMS

Machine Learning

Python

Computer Architecture

General Aptitude

No. of Questions: 90
Time Allocated: 90 minutes
Marking Scheme: No negative marking

I attempted around 80 questions because most were from core fundamentals and required clarity, not depth.

Round 2: Group Discussion (GD)

From 150 candidates, only 18 were shortlisted for the GD round—and I was among them.

A 30-minute GD was conducted for all 18 at once. The candidates were divided into two groups (9–9).

GD Topic: “Is Artificial Intelligence beneficial for all of us or not?”

I was in the Group B and our group was assigned to speak "against" the topic.

GD Flow:

Opening Statement – Group A (5 mins)

Opening Statement – Group B (5 mins)

Open Debate – Both Groups (10 mins)

Conclusion – Group A (5 mins)

Conclusion – Group B (5 mins)

It was a long, intense, and well-structured discussion. After evaluation, only 8 candidates were selected for the final interview round—and I was fortunate to be one of them.

Round 3: Technical + HR Interview (Final Round)

The final round was conducted the next day by a panel of three interviewers from Denso. It lasted approximately 30–35 minutes, covering both technical and HR aspects.

Questions/Topics Covered:

Self-Introduction

Internship work and responsibilities

Project discussions

SDLC – steps and applying SDLC to a real-life scenario

Writing a small code snippet (MCP integration from my internship)

Concepts of AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning

IoT basics

Situational & behavioral questions:

Teamwork

Project management

Social adaptability

Decision-making under pressure

The interviewers tested both technical clarity and personality traits essential for a corporate environment.

Final Selection:

Out of the 8 candidates from the final round, only 2 students were selected —
✔️ 1 from Mechanical
✔️ 1 from CSE (myself)

Being selected among the final two was truly a proud and memorable moment.

My Suggestions to Juniors:

1️⃣ Written Test

No negative marking → attempt all questions.

Focus on strengthening core subjects (DSA, OS, DBMS, OOPs).

2️⃣ Group Discussion

Take initiative, but don’t dominate.

Respect others’ viewpoints.

Build the discussion logically toward a balanced conclusion.

Don’t argue, but collaborate.

3️⃣ Interview Round

Know everything you’ve written in your resume.

Be prepared to discuss projects code-wise and concept-wise.

Even if you don’t know the exact answer, explain your approach confidently.

Stay calm, honest, and composed.

full_text:
This review is specifically focused on Chemical Engineering students.

There were three stages in selection process:

First Stage: An Online Assessment (OA) of 70 minutes, which was divided into two sections: Aptitude and Core Chemical Engineering. Out of 39 chemical engineering students eligible for test, 34 students were shortlisted for second stage.
Second Stage: Group Discussion (GD) on the topic “Pros & Cons of AI and Its Impact on our future”. There were 5-6 batches for group discussion considering students from all the branches. For Chemical, It was conducted in 2 batches of 14 and 20 students per batch . The topic was identical across all the batches regardless of the timing, order and branch. The discussion became very chaotic. I was able to spoke only once but try to speak something relevant 2-3 times to increase your chances of selection. Almost everyone shared their points. Creating unnecessary chaos will not get you selected. Out of 34 students, 16 students were selected for third stage.

Third Stage: The third stage was a combined Technical and HR interview of approximately 10-15 minutes in duration. In my case, no HR questions were asked. Apart from introduction where I explained them about my academic background, my internship projects and minor project in detail. They asked me about the applications of polyurethane (from my intern), what type of operating conditions did you considered and how you optimized them for separating glycerol - methyl oleate mixture (from my minor project), why they (glycerol - methyl oleate mixture) separates to make two different phases (from minor project). Then they aksed me for my favourite subject. I selected fluid mechanics but also mentioned having a good understanding of heat and mass transfer. They asked me very simple questions on fluid mechanics. No questions were asked from other subjects.

Interview Ends

General Recommendations:

Prioritize Physical Internships: Chemical companies generally prefer candidates who have done on-site internships preferably in chemical plants, regardless of the quality of online work. This preference is often due to the assumption that candidates with industry exposure possess a better understanding of the operational environment, leading to fewer adaptability issues and lower attrition risk compared to those whose experience is solely remote.

Use your introduction to thoroughly explain your internship and project work in detail. L&T Interview Experience (GET – Civil Engineering)

My L&T GET interview was completely technical and followed a structured flow. The interviewer first started with questions from my project, where I explained the objectives, methodology, and major outcomes.

After discussing the project, the interviewer moved into core subjects — mainly RCC, Design of Steel Structures, and Concrete Technology. The technical questions were very concept-oriented. The main topics covered were:

Reinforcement: types of reinforcement, cover, spacing, and placement requirements

Limit State Method: types of limit states, assumptions, stress–strain relationships, partial safety factors, and the basic philosophy behind LSM

Design Procedure of Compression Members: load capacity, slenderness limits, interaction curves, and steps involved in designing short/long columns

Bolt and Weld Connections: types of bolts, failure modes, design strength, weld types, throat thickness, and design steps

Detailing Requirements: bar curtailment, anchorage length, lap length, spacing rules, and ductile detailing basics

Once the technical portion was covered, the interviewer shifted focus to my internship at NHAI. I was asked about the QA/QC activities I performed — including concrete cube testing, bitumen and soil tests, field density tests, RMC plant exposure, RE block unit visit, and my overall responsibilities at the site. I also shared how staying alone at a remote location taught me independence, discipline, and adaptability.

There were no HR questions. The entire interview focused on assessing my understanding of design fundamentals, code-based procedures, and my practical exposure. It was a smooth and positive experience, and it helped me gain confidence about my preparation for core technical roles.

Getting selected at GlobalLogic was an excellent learning experience. The recruitment process tested both my technical fundamentals and my problem-solving approach, so having strong basics paid off. Interviewers were friendly and focused more on how I approached problems rather than only on the final answer that made the rounds feel collaborative instead of intimidating.

Consistent coding practice and steady revision of core CS subjects (data structures, algorithms, OOP, and system design basics) played a major role in my preparation. During interviews I made sure to communicate my thought process clearly, ask clarifying questions when needed, and stay calm under pressure.

A few practical takeaways:

Practice explaining your approach step-by-step interviewers value your reasoning.
Work through coding problems out loud, not just on paper or in your head.
Strengthen fundamentals: arrays, linked lists, trees, graphs, hashing, sorting, and complexity analysis.
Keep a few real-world project examples ready to explain design choices and trade-offs.
Stay confident and take pauses to think ..silence is okay if it leads to a correct design or solution.

Overall, it was a smooth and encouraging journey. With focused practice and continuous improvement, anyone can achieve similar results.

full_text:
I recently interviewed for the position of Digital Verification Engineer in the semiconductor domain, and it turned out to be a very enriching experience.

The interview started with a brief introduction about myself. One of the early questions was why I wanted to build a career in the semiconductor industry and specifically in digital verification. I shared how my interest in this field began during my undergraduate degree, particularly in the Digital Electronics course taught by Dr. Gopal Sharma. His teaching style — especially the way he used visual reasoning, logical breakdowns, and systematic problem-solving — sparked my curiosity. I was fascinated by how digital systems are engineered, validated, and optimized at the bit level.

As I explored more, I realized that Digital Verification is the backbone of chip development, ensuring functionality and correctness before tape-out. The idea that verification helps identify logical corner cases and strengthens a design before it becomes a physical chip strongly resonated with me. It aligns perfectly with how I naturally approach problems—by breaking them down, analyzing root causes, and building solutions step by step. That clarity made me confident that this is where I want to contribute and grow.

Technical Discussion

From there, the interview progressed toward the technical aspects of my profile. I was asked questions based on the projects mentioned in my resume — not just what I built, but also:

the reasoning behind my approach

challenges I faced

debugging techniques I applied

and what I learned during the process

The discussion then moved into core concepts and fundamentals related to digital logic, verification concepts, and debugging methodologies. The interviewer focused not only on knowledge, but on how I think through a problem.

A Puzzle to Test Reasoning

Toward the end, I was given a logical IQ puzzle:

Four people must cross a bridge at night using one torch. Only two can cross at a time. Their individual crossing speeds are 10 min, 5 min, 2 min, and 1 min. What is the minimum total time required for all of them to cross?

It was interesting because the puzzle wasn’t about speed—it was about strategy, constraints, and optimizing steps under rules, which closely reflects real-world verification thinking.

Reflection

Overall, the interview was a blend of self-reflection, technical depth, and problem-solving. It gave me valuable insight into what the role demands and reaffirmed my interest in pursuing verification engineering.

rounds.summary: •Binary Tree question – Create a new tree where each node stores the sum of consecutive right-child nodes. Round 2 (LeetCode):

full_text:
There were 3 rounds, all eliminatory. First two were technical, and the last one was resume-based + HR.

Round 1 (Online Code Editor):

I greeted the interviewer and gave my introduction (which I had practiced many times a night before).

I was asked 2 DSA questions:

•Majority Element (LC) – I explained 3 approaches, but only one of my codes worked fully.

•Binary Tree question – Create a new tree where each node stores the sum of consecutive right-child nodes.

Round 2 (LeetCode):

•Trips and Users (SQL Hard) – My code didn’t give the correct output, but I explained each step, and the interviewer seemed satisfied.

•Valid Parenthesis (LC Easy)– Submitted and accepted.

•Longest Valid Parenthesis (LC Hard) – I reused the approach of the previous question, but it wasn’t optimised. The interviewer asked me to optimise it.

Then he asked:

•What subjects are taught in ICE

•Why I want a tech role despite being in ICE

•If I had any questions for him

Round 3 (HR + Resume Discussion)

Started with an introduction.

She shared my resume and picked points from it — especially the part where I mentioned my music club event management.

Questions included:

•How I would manage an event in the office

•How I’d convince maximum employees to attend if they had an upcoming project submission.

•What I’d do if I realised I couldn’t meet a project deadline.

Then she asked basic SQL theory and some queries.

She asked me to explain my 1 best project so I explained my Power BI project.

She asked what I think a Data Engineer does, and later also explained her view.

Result : Selected
Key Takeaways:

•Don’t rush — it’s okay to ask the interviewer some time to think.

•Interviews are just conversations; your communication skills do matter a lot.

•It's fine to ask “Am I going in the right direction?” if you’re stuck in a coding question.

•Don’t lie on your resume and even if you're lying , have strong points to justify yourself.

•The interview depends a lot on the interviewer; I wasn’t asked CS fundamentals, but I had prepared them.

full_text:
When Honeywell visited our campus, my interview process turned out to be one of the most comfortable and engaging experiences I’ve had. The conversation began with my resume—specifically my internship experience and the projects I had worked on. The panel genuinely seemed interested in understanding why I chose those projects and what challenges I faced during implementation.

After a few technical follow-ups, the discussion naturally shifted to core subjects. They asked about my favourite subject, and once I mentioned it, the panel encouraged me to dive deeper. The best part was that nothing felt like a rapid-fire test—they allowed me to think, explain my reasoning, and even corrected me politely whenever needed.

What I really appreciated was how the interview felt more like a discussion rather than a formal Q&A. They asked conceptual questions, some basics from algorithms and data structures, and connected them to practical scenarios. A few problem-solving questions were also included, but the panel was very cooperative throughout, guiding me when I got stuck.

Even the HR round was extremely pleasant. Instead of formal interrogation-style questions, it was more about understanding my motivations, interests, and how I approach teamwork and learning. The HR panelist was friendly and made the conversation very smooth.

Overall, the Honeywell interview process was one of the best I’ve experienced—it was interactive, encouraging, and helped me present my skills confidently. I’m grateful that it ended with an offer, and the entire experience boosted my confidence for future interviews as well.

Nikhil Singh

I got internship at Siemens and my internship experience at Siemens was great. It provided an invaluable opportunity to apply my academic knowledge in a real-world, industry setting. I gained exposure to professional software development processes and improved my problem-solving skills significantly.

Selection Procedure

The selection process was thorough and focused heavily on foundational computer science concepts and programming skills. It typically involved the following stages (Online Test -> Technical Interview(s) ):

Online Assessment/Screening:

Technical Interview(s): Focused on core CS concepts and coding.
Key Interview Topics & Questions

The questions primarily revolved around the foundational pillars of Computer Science relevant to a software role, specifically focusing on the core technologies mentioned in the job description:

1. Programming (C++)
2. Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA)
3. Puzzles/Apltitude
Preparation Strategies

My preparation was highly targeted and paid off well:

Resume Mastery: I prepared thoroughly on every project, technology, and keyword mentioned in my resume. This allowed me to confidently answer follow-up questions and steer the conversation toward my strengths.

Job Description (JD) Alignment: I studied the job description carefully to anticipate the required technical skills (C++, DSA) and focused my preparation primarily on those areas.

Practice Coding: Solved numerous DSA problems on standard platforms, focusing on implementing solutions efficiently in C++.

Conceptual Clarity: I ensured a clear understanding of the core Computer Fundamentals (OS, DBMS, CN), as they are critical for any software role.

Recommendation for Peers

Be Honest and Confident: Only include skills on your resume that you are comfortable discussing in depth.

Focus on Fundamentals: Strong foundations in DSA and C++/OOP are non-negotiable for a role like this.

Think Out Loud: When solving a problem or puzzle, articulate your thought process to the interviewer. This shows your problem-solving approach, even if you don't arrive at the final, optimal solution immediately.

full_text:
The Accenture placement process consisted of five rounds, covering cognitive and behavioral skills, technical fundamentals, coding, communication, and a final interview.

Round 1: Behavioral & Cognitive Assessment

The first round was a combination of behavioral and cognitive assessment.

The behavioral section included questions based on workplace situations and personality traits. The cognitive section consisted of logical reasoning and puzzles, where we had to analyze the given situation and select the appropriate answer.

Preparation: Practice aptitude, logical reasoning, puzzles, and common behavioral questions.

Round 2: Technical Assessment

The second round was a technical assessment consisting mainly of MCQs based on Computer Science fundamentals.

The topics included:

Computer Networks

Basic Linux/command-line concepts

MS Excel

Programming fundamentals

Other basic CS concepts

This round mainly tested our understanding of fundamental technical concepts rather than advanced programming.

Preparation: Revise core CS subjects and practice MCQs covering networking, operating systems, databases, programming fundamentals, Excel, and basic commands.

Round 3: Coding Assessment

The third round was a coding assessment consisting of three different sections:

DSA: One basic Data Structures and Algorithms problem.

SQL: One SQL query based on database concepts.

Frontend: One question involving HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

For the coding question, the available languages were Java and Python; C++ was not available in my assessment.

The DSA problem was of basic difficulty, so understanding fundamental concepts and being comfortable with problem-solving was sufficient.

Preparation: Practice basic DSA problems, SQL queries, and fundamental HTML, CSS, and JavaScript concepts.

Round 4: Communication Assessment

The fourth round focused on English communication and listening skills.

It consisted of multiple activities, including:

Correcting grammatically incorrect sentences.

Speaking on a given topic for around one minute.

Listening to sentences and repeating them accurately.

Other exercises designed to evaluate communication and comprehension.

The main focus was on clarity, pronunciation, grammar, listening ability, and confidence while speaking.

Preparation: Practice speaking English on random topics for 1–2 minutes, improve basic grammar, and practice listening and repeating sentences.

Round 5: Virtual Interview

The final round was a virtual interview, which lasted approximately 15–20 minutes.

The interview mainly consisted of:

General HR questions.

Questions about my resume.

Discussion about projects.

Questions about my technical background and interests.

The questions were mostly straightforward, so having a good understanding of everything mentioned on your resume is important.

For HR preparation, resources such as InterviewBit and commonly asked HR interview questions can be useful.

full_text:
My Accenture hiring experience had multiple rounds, and overall I would say the process was manageable if your basics were clear and you had knowledge across different areas.

The first round was an Ability + Aptitude assessment. It had a mix of mathematical aptitude, logical reasoning, and puzzle-based questions. Nothing felt extremely difficult, but time management was important because some questions and puzzles could take a little longer to solve.

After that, there was an MCQ round with around 40 questions. One important thing about this round was that the questions were spread across a lot of different topics rather than being focused on just one subject.

There were questions from CS fundamentals, databases, programming fundamentals, operating systems, DevOps, and even some questions related to AI and deep learning. So having knowledge across different fields definitely helps. You don't need to know every topic in extreme depth, but having a good understanding of the basics across different areas is useful.

The next round was the coding assessment. It wasn't only focused on DSA, which made it a little different from a typical coding round.

There were three types of questions:

One Data Structures/Programming problem, which I had to solve using Python.

One SQL problem, where we had to write a query according to the given requirements.

One frontend question, where we were provided with three files — index.html, styles.css, and script.js. We had to understand the existing code and make some basic changes according to the requirements.

I would recommend being comfortable with basic Python problem-solving, SQL queries, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript rather than preparing only DSA.

After the coding round, there was a communication assessment.

This round was fairly simple but had multiple sections. There were email-writing questions and grammar-based questions where a sentence had an error and we had to correct it.

There was also a repeat-the-sentence section where a sentence was played and we had to repeat it correctly.

Another section involved being given a topic with around 15 seconds to prepare, after which we had to speak about that topic for approximately 60 seconds. The topics were generally simple, so the main thing was being able to quickly organize your thoughts and communicate clearly.

After that came the interview round.

My interview was relatively simple and conversational. They asked me a few questions about my projects, but a large part of the interview focused on behavioral and situational questions around teamwork, leadership, and conflict resolution.

Some questions I remember were:

If one of your team members is not contributing properly, how would you handle the situation?

What role did you play in your last project?

What were the main technical difficulties you faced?

Was there a situation where you had to make a technical trade-off? Why did you make that decision?

What is the difference between an array, a set, a hash map, and a hash table?

For the project questions, I think it is much better to genuinely understand what you built instead of memorizing an explanation. Be prepared to talk about your contribution, the challenges you faced, the technical decisions you made, and any trade-offs you had to consider.

One unusual thing happened in my case after these rounds.

Most of the other candidates received their results before me, while my result did not clearly mention whether I was selected or rejected. Later, I was informed that there had been an error with my communication assessment.

Because of that, I was asked to take the communication assessment again. I completed it, and after that my process continued normally. Eventually, I was selected.

So one thing I would point out about Accenture is that the results can sometimes come at different times for different candidates. If other people receive their results before you and yours is still pending, it does not necessarily mean that you have been rejected.

Overall, my preparation advice would be to focus on aptitude, programming fundamentals, CS fundamentals, databases, operating systems, DevOps, basic AI/ML concepts, Python, SQL, frontend basics, communication skills, and your own projects.

The biggest takeaway from my experience is that Accenture's process tests you across a wide variety of areas. You don't have to be an expert in everything, but having good breadth of knowledge and being able to explain your projects and experiences clearly can help a lot.

title: Accenture AEH Internship Selection Experience
key_questions: Communication Assessment
full_text:
I had a great experience with the Accenture selection process for the Advanced Application Engineering (AEH) Internship. Accenture visited our campus in December 2025, and I applied for the opportunity. The selection process was conducted in multiple stages and tested cognitive ability, technical knowledge, coding skills, communication, and interview performance.

1. Assessment Rounds

The first stage consisted of three assessments conducted on the same day, and these were elimination rounds.

Cognitive Assessment:

The cognitive assessment consisted of three game-based sections designed to test logical thinking, problem-solving, attention, and reasoning abilities. The games included Bubble Math, Key & Door, and a Path Finder-type game. The format was quite different from a traditional aptitude test and required quick thinking and accuracy.

Technical MCQ Assessment:

The technical round consisted of around 45 MCQs covering different areas of computer science and software development. The questions included pseudocode, computer fundamentals, web technologies, web development, and other technical concepts. A good understanding of CS fundamentals was important for this round.

Coding Assessment:

The coding assessment was divided into three sections:

Backend: Python, Java, or C#

Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

SQL: Database and SQL-related problems

This round tested both programming fundamentals and practical development knowledge.

One interesting aspect of the process was that the rounds were elimination-based, and candidates could know whether they had qualified for the next stage after completing the respective assessments.

I successfully cleared all three assessments and was shortlisted for the communication round.

2. Communication Assessment

The communication assessment was conducted a few days later. It focused on overall English communication skills and consisted of different sections covering Listening, Speaking, Reading, and Writing (LSRW) skills.

There was also an email-writing section, where communication and writing ability were evaluated. I successfully cleared this round as well.

3. Interview Round

Around a week after the communication assessment, I received the opportunity to appear for the interview.

The interview was primarily an HR-oriented round, along with a few technical questions from computer science fundamentals. The interviewer asked normal HR questions along with questions related to my technical background, projects, and CS concepts.

After successfully completing the interview, I was selected for the Accenture Advanced Application Engineering (AEH) Internship.

4. Internship and PPO

I completed the internship and subsequently received a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) from Accenture for the Advanced Technology Engineer role, with a CTC of ₹13.6 LPA.

Thank you and All the best👍

-V Sai Kiran Reddy

full_text:
I’m happy to share that I got selected at Accenture for the role of Advanced Engineering Analyst (AEH). I wanted to share my experience to help juniors understand the process better and prepare in the right direction.

The hiring process consisted of multiple rounds:

Assessment 1: Behavioral & Cognitive (40 minutes)
This round mainly focused on personality-based and situational questions. Along with that, there were logical puzzles, number series, pattern recognition, and numerical reasoning questions. The key here is to stay calm and focus on accuracy rather than speed.

Assessment 2: Technical (45 minutes)
This section covered basic technical concepts like MS Office, common IT applications, and pseudocode (loops, conditions, flow). You should also be clear with networking basics (OSI, TCP/IP), cloud concepts (SaaS, PaaS, IaaS), and fundamental CS topics like arrays, functions, and OOPs.

Assessment 3: Coding (60 minutes)
There were 3 coding questions, and you could choose your preferred language or stack (Java, Python, C++, C#, SQL, or web stack). The questions ranged from easy to medium level, with one being more logic-based. Topics were mostly arrays, strings, loops, conditions, and basic SQL queries.

Assessment 4: Communication (~30 minutes)
This round evaluated spoken English, pronunciation, fluency, and listening skills. It also included grammar, vocabulary, and professional email writing.

Final Round: Interview
The interview was a mix of technical and HR questions. They asked questions based on my resume, discussed my projects in detail, and also included situational questions related to teamwork, adaptability, and strengths/weaknesses.

If you’re preparing for Accenture, make sure your basics are clear and practice regularly.

full_text:
The Amazon interview process started with the Online Assessment. After clearing it, I was shortlisted for Round 1 and had only two days to prepare. I mainly focused on Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles, my resume, projects, and behavioral questions using the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach. I also prepared guesstimate questions, supply chain basics, KPI tracking, and root cause analysis, but none of these were asked in my interview.My biggest advice is to quantify your STAR answers. Clearly explain the Situation, define your Task, describe the Actions you took, and finish with a measurable Result. Mention the size of your team, your specific responsibility, and the impact you created. For projects, clearly explain your role and include numbers wherever possible.

Some of the questions I was asked were:

Tell me about yourself.

Why Amazon?

Why Operations?

You are a Mechanical Engineering student, so why do you want to move into Operations?

Most of your internships and projects are in Design Engineering. How will those experiences help you in an Operations role?

Explain your projects and your specific contribution.

Multiple behavioral and situational questions based on Amazon's Leadership Principles.

What is your biggest achievement in the Cricket Club?

If your goal was to build a career at Amazon in Operations, why did you choose Mechanical Engineering instead of pursuing an MBA?

My Aircraft Landing System project was discussed in both interviews. While explaining it, I asked the interviewers if I could draw a simple sketch of the project. Drawing the project made it much easier for them to understand the design and my explanation, and it also created a positive impression. So, if you have a technical project, don't hesitate to use a simple diagram or flowchart while explaining it.After Round 1, I was shortlisted for Round 2 and had only one day to prepare. Since I had experiences from different clubs and leadership roles, I had enough situations to answer the behavioral questions confidently.Most importantly, be confident during the interview. Even if you don't know the perfect answer, stay calm, think for a few seconds, and answer confidently. The interviewer is not only evaluating your knowledge but also your communication, problem-solving approach, and confidence.Lastly, practice mock interviews (ChatGPT helped me a lot), ask 2–3 thoughtful questions at the end of the interview, and don't hesitate to ask for feedback.After successfully clearing both interview rounds, I was finally placed at Amazon.

All the best to everyone preparing for Amazon interviews! Stay confident, prepare your STAR stories well, understand Amazon's Leadership Principles, and practice explaining your projects clearly. Believe in yourself, keep improving, and give your best. I hope you achieve your dream of getting placed at Amazon. Good luck!

full_text:
When my name appeared in Amazon’s interview shortlist, I honestly didn’t know what to expect.

Like many students, I had been applying continuously to different companies, giving OAs, interviewing at startups, and facing rejections along the way.

So when I got shortlisted for Amazon, I was obviously excited, but I also tried not to keep my expectations too high.

A lot of things in the previous semesters had already taught me that no matter how much preparation you do, the final result is never guaranteed.

Still, this was an opportunity I wanted to give my best shot.

The First Interview (HM Round)

The first round was the Hiring Manager (HM) round.

Going into the interview, I expected most of the discussion to revolve around my projects, previous internship experience, freelancing work, and technical background.

To be honest, I was not expecting DSA right from the beginning.

But that is exactly what happened.

The interviewer started with a DSA problem that I would classify somewhere between Medium and Hard level.

For a moment, I was surprised because I had mentally prepared for project discussions first.

Thankfully, all the DSA preparation I had done over the past months helped me stay calm.

I discussed my approach, explained my thought process, and eventually solved the problem.

After that, the conversation shifted towards my projects and previous experiences.

There were questions about the decisions I had made while building projects, challenges I faced, and why I chose certain approaches over others.

The discussion felt more like a technical conversation rather than a strict question-answer session.

The entire round lasted around 1 hour and 15 minutes.

When the interview ended, I genuinely had no idea how it went.

I thought I had done reasonably well, but after enough interviews, I had learned not to make assumptions.

The Second Interview (SDE Round)

A few days later, I received the schedule for the second round.

This time, I was more mentally prepared for DSA.

The interviewer again focused heavily on problem-solving.

I was asked two DSA questions, both of which I would again place somewhere in the Medium-Hard category.

The challenge wasn’t just solving them.

The challenge was explaining the thought process clearly, discussing edge cases, handling follow-up questions, and writing clean code while being observed.

Fortunately, I was able to solve both problems and explain my reasoning properly.

The discussion also included questions around optimization and alternative approaches.

This round lasted approximately 1 hour and 25 minutes.

By the end of it, I felt satisfied because I had given my best effort.

At that point, the result was completely out of my hands.

The Waiting Period

For me, waiting after interviews is usually the hardest part.

Once an interview ends, there is nothing more you can do.

No additional preparation.

No additional coding.

No additional explanations.

You simply wait.

And after experiencing enough rejections in previous semesters, I had become comfortable with uncertainty.

I wasn’t assuming I would get selected.

I wasn’t assuming I would get rejected.

I was simply waiting for whatever came next.

The Email

The interesting part is that I didn’t first hear the result through the placement list.

Instead, I received a surprise email.

I remember looking at it and realizing that I had been selected for the 6-month Software Development Engineer Internship at Amazon.

Final Thoughts

If there is one thing I would tell anyone preparing for interviews, it is this:

->>>>>>> Focus on what you can control.

Build projects.

Learn continuously.

Practice DSA.

Improve communication.

Apply consistently.

The outcome is never guaranteed.

But preparation is never wasted.

Good luck to everyone preparing for interviews.

For daily updates, feel free to connect with me on X:

https://x.com/KushagraAg0717

full_text:
I participated in the Cognizant ACE Team recruitment process, which consisted of three rounds. The overall process was technically oriented and evaluated candidates on problem-solving ability, programming fundamentals, technical knowledge, practical development skills, and project understanding. There was no separate HR interview.

Round 1 – Online Assessment (~1hr)

The first round was an online assessment designed to evaluate aptitude, logical reasoning, verbal ability, programming fundamentals, and basic technical knowledge.

The assessment was time-bound, making effective time management an important aspect of the round. The questions tested both conceptual understanding and the ability to analyse problems within a limited time.

For preparation, it is useful to revise basic programming concepts, aptitude, logical reasoning, and fundamental computer science subjects.

Round 2 – Technical Online Assessment (~3hr)

The second round was a more technically focused online assessment consisting of 24 questions:

20 Multiple Choice Questions

1 DSA coding problem

1 React.js coding problem

1 RAG coding problem

1 Prompt Engineering question

20 MCQs - Gen Ai fundamentals, Cloud fundamentals and AI/ML concepts.

DSA -

The DSA section involved a programming problem that required developing an efficient solution while considering the given constraints and test cases. Preparation for this section should include arrays, strings, hashing, two pointers, sliding window, sorting, binary search, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, recursion, and complexity analysis.

React.js -

The React.js question was a practical implementation task based on a dataset of people. The task involved providing options to sort the data based on name or age using radio buttons and displaying the resulting information appropriately.

The question required familiarity with functional components, useState, event handling, array sorting, conditional logic, and rendering data in React.

RAG -

The RAG section tested practical understanding of Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

The interviewer also discussed ETL concepts and application performance, including identifying potential performance bottlenecks and understanding where delays can occur within a system.

Projects

A substantial part of the interview revolved around the projects mentioned on the resume. Questions focused on the architecture, technologies, implementation details, APIs, databases, challenges, and individual contributions to the projects.

This highlighted the importance of having a thorough understanding of every project and technology mentioned on the resume.

Overall Experience

Overall, the Cognizant ACE Team recruitment process was a comprehensive and technically demanding experience. The three rounds evaluated different aspects of a candidate's technical capabilities, ranging from aptitude and fundamental concepts to practical coding and technical discussions.

The process was particularly valuable because it combined core computer science fundamentals with modern software-development and Generative AI concepts. Candidates preparing for a similar recruitment process should focus on DSA, OOP, DBMS/SQL, OS, Computer Networks, React.js, backend development, APIs, and AI/ML fundamentals, while also developing a strong understanding of their projects.

Most importantly, candidates should be prepared to explain the implementation and technical decisions behind every project listed on their resume, as project-based questions can form an important part of the technical interview.

full_text:
Cognizant hiring process

Round 1 – Aptitude and communication round
The first round consisted of questions based on aptitude (MCQs) and communication skills. The apti consisted of the standard stuff like reading charts, quant questions (profit loss, percentages etc.), logical reasoning etc. In the communication part you had to listen to an audio and answer questions based on that audio. The overall difficulty was easy.

Round 2 – Technical assessment
This was the most challenging step of the process; we had to solve 5 questions, each requiring a different skillset.
Q1 → DSA problem – An easy-medium LeetCode problem. I got a problem similar to Subsets on LeetCode, which was to be solved using recursion.
Q2 → React – A React codebase was given along with a readme and a few tests; we had to navigate the codebase to trace out why the test cases actually failed.
Q3 → Prompt engineering – This was fairly simple. We had to write a prompt such that the constraints in the question are satisfied. Going over basic prompt engineering principles like zero-shot, few-shot, CoT etc. is sufficient.
Q4 → RAG implementation – A part of the RAG pipeline had to be built; it could be anything like implementing chunking, embedding etc.
Q5 → 20 MCQs based on general AI concepts.

Round 3 – Interview
The interview was a mixture of technical + HR questions, with the weightage being approximately 75:25 respectively (at least in my case). The interview started with the implementation of a few SQL queries and showing an example of function overloading. After that, a large part of the discussion revolved around AI (LLM) concepts. Most of the questions were focused on RAG and explaining the components of the RAG pipeline (what it does and why it exists). Questions around cloud were also asked. The conversation then shifted to my resume and questions about my projects in depth. The main thing here is not to explain the architecture of the project, but why the architecture of the project is the way it is. I was constantly cross-questioned regarding why I made particular design choices or why I used a particular library. After this, behavioral questions were asked and the HR phase of the interview began. Certain situational questions were given which could be answered using the STAR method.

Overall, one should avoid giving half-baked answers.

To conclude, the whole process was a great learning experience and allowed me to test my mettle.

full_text:
Flipkart Placement Experience

A stage-wise account and preparation tips for juniors

I’m sharing my experience of the Flipkart placement process to help juniors understand what to expect and how they can prepare. My process had three stages: an online assessment, a technical interview, and an HR interview. The questions can vary from person to person, especially depending on the resume and the answers given during the interview, so treat this as a guide rather than a fixed question list.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The online assessment mainly covered technical questions related to Excel and supply chain, along with basic aptitude and English questions. There was also a supply chain case study.

How to prepare

Revise basic Excel concepts and commonly used functions.

Go through supply chain fundamentals and practise case-study-based questions.

Practise basic aptitude and English questions.

2. Technical Interview

The first interview began with my introduction. The interviewer then asked questions about my internship, particularly the results I achieved and the numbers or data I had derived from my work. There were a few follow-up questions based on my answers.

After that, the interviewer asked situation-based questions, including:

“If your senior manager disagrees with your project, how would you convince them?” I answered by explaining a similar situation that I had experienced during my previous internship.

“What would you do or change during your first 30 days as an intern in the warehouse?”

“How would you implement AI in warehouse systems to improve efficiency?”

My recommendations for this round

Prepare your answers using the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, and Result.

Be ready to explain every important project and internship on your resume, especially the outcomes, results, and numbers. You should be comfortable discussing them without having to search for details.

Prepare around 30–40 situational questions and practise answering them with real examples from your own experience.

Read about Flipkart’s core values and prepare stories from your experience that demonstrate those values.

For technical preparation, revise basic Excel, Lean Six Sigma, and supply chain theory.

3. HR Interview

The second interview was a basic HR round. After my introduction, the interviewer picked up a few points from my resume. I mentioned that I had started my own e-commerce brand and managed its end-to-end operations, so most of the discussion focused on that experience.

My experience was that the questions were closely linked to the candidate’s resume and the follow-up answers. Different candidates may therefore have different interview experiences.

Overall Interview Experience

Both interviews lasted approximately 20–25 minutes each.

In my experience, neither interview was extremely technical; the discussion focused more on my experience, the results I had achieved, and how I approached practical situations.

Your resume matters a lot, because interviewers may build much of the conversation around the projects, internships, and experiences you mention.

Final Advice for Juniors

Prepare your resume thoroughly and make sure you can explain the impact of your work with clear examples and numbers. Practise structured answers using the STAR method, revise the basics of Excel and supply chain, and prepare for situational questions. Most importantly, use genuine examples from your own experiences rather than memorising generic answers. The process may differ for each candidate, but being clear about your own work will help you handle follow-up questions with confidence.

full_text:
The Flipkart NEEV program targets high-potential talent for supply chain and operational roles. The selection process generally consists of an online assessment test followed by technical and behavioral interview rounds.

Round 1: Online Assessment (Aptitude & Technical)

Format: Multiple-choice assessment along with a case study testing quantitative aptitude, data interpretation, logical reasoning, and basic domain knowledge.

Tip: Time management is crucial. Practicing standard quantitative and analytical reasoning questions will help clear this round.

Round 2: Technical & Operational Interview

Format: One-on-one interview with a senior operational lead or supply chain manager.

Key Focus Areas:

In-depth walk-through of projects, internships, and technical skills listed on your resume.

Core concepts of supply chain management, logistics, and process optimization (e.g., Lean, Six Sigma, inventory planning).

Case-based scenario questions assessing your analytical thinking and ability to handle operational bottlenecks.

Tip: Use data and structured frameworks (like root-cause analysis or the ECRS framework) when answering scenario-based questions.

Round 3: Managerial & HR Interview

Format: Final evaluation round focusing on leadership qualities, situational awareness, and cultural fit.

Key Questions Asked:

"Describe a situation where you managed a team under tight deadlines or high pressure."

"Why Flipkart, and what draws you to supply chain operations?"

"Why Flipkart after Textile Technology"?

Key Takeaways for Preparation

Know Your Resume: Be ready to explain every detail, metric, and responsibility mentioned in your CV.

- How would you handle last-minute deliveries at Kartarpur hub?

Supply Chain + Logistics + Warehousing + Last-mile delivery + Excel + Kaizen + Pareto + Six Sigma + HR/Situational questions.

The Barco interview process consisted of an online assessment followed by technical, managerial, and HR rounds. Overall, the process focused on DSA, core CS fundamentals, problem-solving, and communication skills.

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an online coding assessment that tested DSA and problem-solving skills. I don't remember the exact questions at this point, but the difficulty level was mostly easy to medium.

Preparation tip: Practice basic arrays, strings, sorting, searching, hashing, and common DSA patterns.

Round 2: Technical Interview

This round focused mainly on core computer science fundamentals, along with a DSA problem.

Topics discussed:

Computer Architecture and memory organization

Pointers and pointer-related concepts

Memory allocation and management

Other fundamental CS concepts

One DSA problem, which I vaguely remember involved the sliding window technique, with a heap-based approach being relevant to the solution.

The exact DSA question is not clear in my memory, so I would recommend preparing the underlying concepts rather than relying on a specific question.

Preparation tip: Revise pointers, stack vs. heap memory, dynamic memory allocation, memory layout, and common DSA patterns.

Round 3: Managerial Round

This round included basic managerial and behavioral questions, along with a few conceptual questions.

Some questions I remember:

What are your strengths and weaknesses? Explain around five strengths and weaknesses.

What happens when you type google.com into a browser?

The second question tested the understanding of how the internet works, including DNS resolution, IP addresses, TCP/TLS connections, HTTP/HTTPS, and how a browser loads a webpage.

There was also a light-hearted question to assess how I think and respond in an unexpected situation.

Preparation tip: Prepare your strengths and weaknesses with examples, practice explaining your projects, and revise basic networking concepts and the complete flow of a website request.

Round 4: HR Round

The final round consisted of basic HR questions related to your background, motivation, and career goals.

Prepare for questions such as:

Tell me about yourself.

Why do you want to join Barco?

Explain your projects and internship experience.

What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Where do you see yourself in the next few years?

Do you have any questions for us?

Final Advice

Focus on DSA (especially easy-to-medium problems), core CS subjects such as OS, computer architecture, memory management, and networking, and clear communication. Be comfortable explaining your approach and reasoning instead of just giving the final answer.

This experience is based on my recollection, so some exact questions and details may be missing.

full_text:
Round 1 — Technical

The first round was completely technical and focused heavily on my resume, projects, and core development concepts.

I was asked questions around frontend and backend development, including:
How APIs work
How frontend communicates with the backend
Different ways to reduce API/application latency
What happens when we enter https://www.google.com in a browser
There was a deep dive into my projects, where I was asked to explain the architecture, technologies used, and the reasoning behind each implementation.
The interviewer also justified almost every word written on my resume, so I had to be able to explain every technology, metric, and claim mentioned.
I was asked about conflicts/challenges I faced while working on projects and how I approached and solved them.
The discussion was more about understanding my concepts and whether I had actually worked on the projects rather than just memorizing definitions.
Round 2 — HR + Technical

The second round was a combination of HR and some technical questions.

Some questions included:

How do you handle conflicting opinions within a team?
How would you deal with messy or unstructured data?
If you were given a laptop and some data, what is the first thing you would build?
I was also asked to explain one project I had built, particularly the problem it was solving and how my solution addressed it.
Final Tips

The biggest takeaway from my interview experience was:

Go thoroughly through your resume.

If you have written something on your resume, be prepared to explain what it means, why you used it, how you implemented it, and what challenges you faced.

Also, communication is key. You don't always need extremely long answers. Try to be:

Clear
Crisp
Structured
Confident

Even when you know the concept, make sure you can communicate your thought process clearly.

full_text:
SunPharma visited our college twice-first on 10/10/2025 and then on 18/11/2025-for the GET role on an Intern + FTE basis, offering a CTC of 10 LPA (8 LPA fixed). I was selected during their first visit. In that round, 6 students (5 males, 1 female) from ICE and 5 students from IPE were selected. During the second visit, 2 students (both females) were selected exclusively from ICE.

Internship Experience (05/01/2026 - 30/06/2026)

Even though SunPharma offered intern+FTE role on college placement portal, it changed to 6 month intern+PPO. During internship all the travel (By air) and first 15 days accomodation was company provided. Our internship began on 05-Jan-2026 at CTA (Central training academy) Vadodara where we stayed for 1 week and then everyone was sent to their respective alloted plants where we were assigned our individual internship projects.
At CTA Vadodara we got to know that, for 2022-26 batch, SunPharma selected over 40 GET interns from different NITs and the PPO conversion rate was about 50%. During our stay at CTA Vadodara, we visited Halol and Panoli plants and one R&D centre in Vadodara only.
At our alloted plants, we were assigned individual internship projects along with a mentor (manager).
PPO assesment was as follows:
Mid-review: Review on the project taken by manager and plant HR as an organiser (Last week of February)
End-review: Review on the project and over internship work and plant understanding

Round 1: Review on the project taken by manager, plant Head and plant HR (Admin HR) as an organiser (Last week of May).
Round 2: Those who will clear R1 will ascend to R2 in which final review would be taken by Cluster head and Recruitment/ Talent acquisition Head HR from coorporate office from Mumbai (2nd week of June).

Hiring Flow:

Their hiring process was straightforward:

CGPA Criteria (min. 6) → Online Assessment (30 min, from hostel) → Interview (2-day process)

Online Assesment:

The OA lasted 30 minutes and consisted of objective-type questions. The topics covered included:

Biomedical Instrumentation

Industrial Measurement Systems

Sensors and Transducers

Analog Electronics

Digital Electronics

For most core-sector companies, a substantial portion of the OA is focused on both analog and digital electronics.

Interview Process:

From ICE, 18 students were shortlisted after the OA for the interview round. The panel typically consisted of 2, and sometimes 3, interviewers. In my case, there were three members- a General HR, a Technical HR, and the Talent Acquisition Head.

The interviews for all shortlisted students were conducted over two days. Sessions were taken in order, and my interview was scheduled toward the end. It lasted around 35-40 minutes, and I chose to give my interview in English.

The interview was a mix of HR and technical questions, asked in a dynamic and unpredictable sequence. The panelists were attentive and kept shifting between technical and behavioral topics to maintain the flow.

When I entered the room, the interviewers greeted me politely, introduced themselves, and briefly reviewed my resume. The General HR began with a few general questions about my background and family. Soon after, theTechnical HR stepped in and asked a series of questions based on core ICE concepts and my technical projects.The Talent Acquisition Head intervened occasionally-not as frequently as the other two-but whenever he did, his questions were unexpectedly deep and thought-provoking (not numerical or analytical, but designed to test critical thinking and perspective).

Interview Experience and Questions:

My interview began with the General HR, who opened with the question, “Tell me something that isn’t mentioned in your resume.” I responded by sharing my family background, since such details are not typically included in a resume.
Because my father serves in the Indian Air Force, the Technical HR followed up with questions related to defense technologies-drones, aerospace applications, radars in defense platforms, and various sensors used in fighter aircraft for measuring speed, pressure, and flow. I answered these by applying my core knowledge of Instrumentation, Sensors & Transducers, and Control Systems. Although my answers were not perfect, they demonstrated my understanding and willingness to attempt every question.
The Technical HR then reviewed my resume but filtered out topics that had already been discussed with other candidates throughout the day, such as my internship at RCF Kapurthala and my piezoelectric energy-harvesting project. Since I was the last candidate to be interviewed, these subjects were already familiar to the panel.
Fortunately, I had included several unique projects in my resume, and the interview shifted toward those. I was asked to explain each project in detail-its objective, real-life applicability, limitations, and the underlying technical aspects. My projects spanned biomedical instrumentation, electric vehicles, drones (ISL online course), and robotics.
Midway through this technical discussion, the General HR asked a question about drone warfare: “What differences did you observe between the drone strategies used by India and Pakistan during Operation Sindoor?” Even the Talent Acquisition Head joined in, asking me to differentiate them in technical terms.
The Technical HR then moved to core instrumentation topics-PLC, DCS, and SCADA with particular focus on PLC hardware. I was asked about types of PLCs, programming languages, communication protocols (Modbus, Profibus- only the names), sinking/sourcing I/Os, and some basic electronics (logic gates and diodes). Additional questions covered temperature sensors, flow meters, and basic control system concepts.
Unexpectedly, the Talent Acquisition Head shifted the interview toward AI, automation, and robotics. Pointing at a digital podium, he asked me to identify the ports on it, adding, “Google Lens can identify these from an image-why shouldn’t I hire AI instead of you?” The General HR built on this and asked, “List three skills a person can develop to stay ahead of AI in the job market.” I answered these questions by including a mix of general facts and technical terms and we had a productive discussion.
The Technical HR then asked, “How is ICE a good fit for you, and how are you a good fit for Sun Pharma?” He also questioned me on the three pillars of ICE. The General HR followed up with “Why did you choose Sun Pharma?” I answered using my domain knowledge along with key facts, performance metrics, and growth indicators (including CAGR) that were discussed during the pre-placement talk.
Toward the end, the Talent Acquisition Head posed a situational question: “If after completing a six-month internship at Sun Pharma, a top robotics company like Yaskawa offers you a much better CTC, which company would you choose?” I paused, sensing they might be evaluating honesty, especially as the General HR encouraged me to “be honest,” smiling. I replied truthfully: “Yes, I would accept the offer from the other company.”
In a light-hearted moment near the end, they even asked if I had a girlfriend. The overall interview remained calm, conversational, and smooth throughout, with frequent overlaps between technical and HR questions.

That was my overall experience. I hope it helps someone who is preparing for the same!. I tried to be as detailed as possible. For more information you contact me on given email/ linkedIn.

full_text:
My HCLTech selection process was divided into three major stages: the AI Interview on BerryBot, the Hackathon Round, and the HR Round.

1. AI Interview – BerryBot

Before the hackathon, we had an AI-based interview on the BerryBot platform.

The interview was mainly based on my resume, projects, technical skills, and previous experiences. The AI asked questions related to the technologies and projects mentioned in my resume and also asked follow-up questions based on my responses.

So, my suggestion for this round is to prepare your resume properly. You should be able to explain every project, technology, internship, and skill that you have mentioned.

After the BerryBot interview, shortlisted candidates were selected for the next stage, which was the HCLTech Hackathon.

2. HCLTech Hackathon Experience

The hackathon started at around 10:00 AM. At the beginning, we were given a problem statement and approximately one hour for design thinking and solution planning.

During this one hour, our team discussed the complete approach, architecture, workflow, technologies, and models that we planned to use. We prepared a PPT explaining our proposed solution.

The evaluators were continuously interacting with the teams during the hackathon. They would come to our table, check our progress, ask what we were working on, understand our approach, and also ask whether we required any help.

After approximately one hour, we presented our design and PPT to the evaluators. They asked several questions regarding our solution. A major focus was on the technical choices.

For example, they asked questions such as:

- Why are you using this particular technology?

- Why did you select this model?

- Why this model instead of another model?

- What would be the difference if you used another approach?

- Why is your proposed tech stack suitable for this problem?

They sometimes intentionally cross-questioned us to check whether we actually understood the technologies we were proposing or were simply mentioning them.

After our design was approved, we were asked to start implementing the solution.

During the implementation phase, another evaluator came and asked me several Machine Learning and AI fundamentals, including topics such as:

- Bias and Variance

- BM25

- Embeddings

- Chunking

- RAG

- Basic Machine Learning concepts

These questions were also part of the evaluation and marks were given based on our answers.

Later, another evaluator came for a progress review. He asked us to explain:

- What we had implemented

- How the solution was working

- What technologies we had used

- How different components were connected

He also asked me a SQL question during the interaction.

The hackathon continued with multiple reviews like this, where evaluators checked both our technical knowledge and our implementation progress.

At around 4:00 PM, we were called for the final demonstration on the third floor of the library.

During the final presentation, we demonstrated the complete working solution. We showed different test cases, explained the overall workflow, demonstrated the features we had implemented, and answered questions related to our solution.

The evaluators also asked a few questions regarding our code and implementation.

After the final demonstration, they told us that our evaluation was complete and we could leave.

3. HR Round

Approximately one hour after the hackathon, I received a call for the HR Round.

The HR round was comparatively simple and conversational. They asked basic questions such as:

- Tell me about yourself.

- What is your name?

- Where are you from?

- Questions related to my background.

- General HR and personality-related questions.

My suggestion is to prepare at least one good question to ask the HR at the end of the interview. It creates a good impression and shows that you are genuinely interested in the organization and the role.

My Suggestions for Future Candidates

The most important thing during the hackathon and interview is to communicate confidently and clearly.

Even if you do not know everything, do not become silent or nervous. Be open and explain whatever you understand. If you know something, present it properly and confidently.

During a hackathon, technical knowledge is important, but your ability to present your solution, explain your decisions, communicate with evaluators, and handle cross-questions is equally important.

You should be able to market your skills properly. The evaluators can only understand your capabilities if you explain what you have done and why you have done it.

So, during the hackathon:

- Be active and communicate with the evaluators.

- Clearly explain your contribution.

- Know the reason behind every technology and model you use.

- Be prepared for cross-questioning.

- Revise basic ML, AI, SQL, RAG, and project-related concepts.

- Prepare your resume thoroughly for the AI interview.

- Present your final solution with proper test cases.

- Stay confident even if you do not know the answer to every question.

- Prepare one meaningful question for the HR round.

Overall, the HCLTech process was not only about building a solution. They were evaluating our technical fundamentals, problem-solving approach, communication skills, teamwork, implementation ability, and confidence throughout the process.

full_text:
HCLTech Placement Experience

I recently got placed at HCLTech, and I wanted to share my overall interview experience to help others preparing for the recruitment process.

The selection process consisted of three rounds.

Round 1: AI Bot Interview (Technical + Communication)

The first round was an AI-based interview conducted by a bot.

It started with a basic self-introduction, followed by questions about my projects, including the technologies I used and my contributions.

I was also asked to solve:

1 DSA coding question
1 SQL query

Overall, this round mainly evaluated our communication skills, coding knowledge, and ability to explain our projects clearly.

Round 2: Hackathon + Technical Interview

The second round was a hackathon where we were given two case studies, and each team had to select one.

Our team chose RetailPulse AI.

Throughout the hackathon, mentors and evaluators visited our team at regular intervals, almost every hour, to monitor our progress.

They asked questions such as:

How did you approach the problem?
How did you implement this functionality?
Can you explain your code?
Why did you choose this particular approach?

Even though we were allowed to use AI tools for development, we were expected to understand the code, explain the implementation, and justify our technical decisions.

After the development phase, we had a group evaluation, where our project was tested for its functionality and overall implementation. We were also given two additional use cases to evaluate how well our solution could handle new requirements.

Following this, we had an individual technical interview.

In my interview, I was mainly asked questions from:

SQL
Object-Oriented Programming (OOPs)
Operating Systems (OS)

The questions focused on fundamental concepts and understanding rather than just memorized definitions.

Round 3: HR Interview

The final round was an HR interview, which was a non-elimination round.

It was mainly a general interaction to understand our communication skills, personality, and overall fit for the company.

My Key Takeaways

One thing I learned from this process is that communication matters just as much as technical knowledge.

Especially during the hackathon, it wasn’t only about building a working project. It was equally important to understand what we were developing, explain our approach confidently, and demonstrate teamwork.

Using AI tools was fine, but being able to explain the AI-generated code and the logic behind it was extremely important.

My advice: Focus on your DSA and SQL basics, revise core CS subjects like OOPs and OS, be thorough with your projects, and most importantly, work on explaining your thought process clearly.

All the best to everyone preparing for placements!

full_text:
Online Assessment

The Online Assessment was conducted on the HirePro platform in the CC Lab and consisted of 4 DSA questions.

The difficulty progression was basically:

Easy → Medium → Hard → Why am I even here?

Question 1 — Easy: A basic array problem with some greedy logic and a little brain usage. Thankfully, my brain was functioning. I solved it in around 5 minutes.

Question 2 — Medium: This one involved prefix sums, array manipulation and greedy thinking. The real problem wasn't coding — it was figuring out what the hell the question wanted. After a lot of struggle, I managed to pass 8/12 test cases.

Question 3 — Hard: Then came the DP nightmare. I tried approaching it with 3 DP states, but at that point my brain was not training. Somehow, I still managed to pass 6/12 test cases.

There was still a fourth question left, but after getting mentally destroyed by the first three, I decided I had seen enough. I switched off my PC and called it a day.

Shortlisting

Considering how my OA went, I was pretty sure my chances were gone.

Then the next evening shortlisted

And the interview was scheduled for the very next day at 4 PM. After waiting at TPO office till eternity I will got my chance around 8PM .

Interview

After that OA, I entered the interview room with just one thought:

“After that OA, nothing can surprise me anymore.”

The interviewer gave me a medium-level DSA problem and around 45 minutes to solve it.

And somehow, with God's grace, I came up with the solution in around 5 minutes.

The interviewer was surprised. So was I.

After that, things became pretty chill. The interviewer went through my resume in detail and asked questions about my projects, technical background and basic CS fundamentals. I was able to answer around 90% of the questions confidently.

I walked out feeling pretty good.

At this point, my brain had already decided:

“Maybe SP L2... ₹16 LPA... not bad.”

Result

Then came the result.

Infosys Specialist Programmer L1 — ₹11 LPA

After the emotional roller coaster of the OA, I was honestly just relieved and happy to finally get placed.

Keep studying and have fun !

I appeared for this placement mainly to get some experience with the interview and placement process, without having particularly high expectations for the role. However, I got selected.

full_text:
INTRODUCTION

Infosys conducts recruitment through multiple channels, including HackWithInfy, On-Campus Hiring, and Off-Campus Hiring.

I participated in the HackWithInfy recruitment process and was selected for the Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE) profile.

The selection process consisted of 3 rounds:

Round 1 – Online Coding Assessment

Round 2 – In-Person Coding Assessment

Round 3 – Technical Interview

ROUND 1: HACKWITHINFY ONLINE CODING ASSESSMENT

The first round was the HackWithInfy Online Coding Assessment.

There were 3 coding questions, and the total time allotted was 3 hours.

The questions were based on Data Structures and Algorithms and tested problem-solving and algorithmic thinking.

I was able to solve all 3 questions successfully within the given time.

After successfully completing the first round, I was shortlisted for the next stage of the recruitment process.

ROUND 2: IN-PERSON CODING ASSESSMENT

The second round was an in-person coding assessment conducted at the college.

There were 4 coding questions in this round.

My performance was:

Question 1: Solved completely.

Question 2: 6 out of 12 test cases passed.

Question 3: 2 out of 12 test cases passed.

Question 4: I was not able to solve it completely.

I was shortlisted for the Technical Interview for the DSE profile.

This round was conducted in person, so the interviewer was able to observe my problem-solving approach and how I approached the coding problems.

ROUND 3: TECHNICAL INTERVIEW

The technical interview was conducted in person.

I was the first candidate to enter the interview room, so I was a little nervous initially. However, the interview proceeded in a friendly and conversational manner.

1. Tell Me About Yourself

The interviewer started by asking:

"Tell me about yourself."

I introduced myself, talked about my academic background, technical skills, interests, and projects.

2. Project Discussion

After the introduction, the interviewer asked me to explain my project.

I explained the project, including:

Project idea

Workflow

Technologies used

My contribution

Implementation

Backend/frontend interaction

After that, the interviewer asked me several follow-up questions related to my project to check my understanding of the implementation and technologies I had used.

3. Fibonacci Series – Coding Question

The interviewer then asked me to write code for the Fibonacci series.

I implemented the solution using Dynamic Programming (DP).

After writing the code, he asked me to:

Explain the code

Explain the logic

Explain how Dynamic Programming was being used

Discuss the approach

I explained the solution and its logic to the interviewer.

4. Python Questions

Since Python was my preferred programming language, the interviewer asked me several questions related to Python.

The questions were mainly focused on my understanding of Python fundamentals and programming concepts.

This was a good reminder that whatever programming language you mention as your preferred language, you should be prepared to answer questions about its fundamentals.

5. Cloud Computing

The interviewer noticed that I had mentioned a Cloud Computing certification on my resume.

He therefore asked me some questions related to Cloud Computing and my understanding of the concepts covered by the certification.

6. About Infosys

Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer asked me:

"Tell me about Infosys."

I answered by discussing my understanding of the company and its work.

7. My Question to the Interviewer

Finally, the interviewer told me:

"Your interview is done. Do you have any questions?"

I asked him:

"What technology should I learn?"

He suggested that I should pursue more certifications related to Cloud Computing.

The interview then concluded.

FINAL RESULT 🎉

After completing the HackWithInfy recruitment process, I was selected for the:

Infosys DSE – Digital Specialist Engineer
Key Takeaways

Prepare DSA properly for both coding rounds.

Be ready to explain every project mentioned on your resume.

Prepare your preferred programming language thoroughly.

Certifications mentioned on your resume can become a topic of discussion.

Revise the fundamentals of every technical skill mentioned in your resume.

Don't panic if you cannot solve every coding question completely. Focus on your approach and keep trying.

In the interview, communicate your thought process clearly.

Overall, my Infosys HackWithInfy journey consisted of two coding rounds followed by an in-person technical interview, and I was fortunate to be selected for the DSE profile.

full_text:
My Placement Experience On Campus , HackwithInfy

I want to share my complete placement experience, starting from the Online Assessments to the final selection.

First Online Assessment — 21 March 2024

My first Online Assessment was conducted from room.

There were 4 coding questions, ranging from medium to hard/advanced level.

I was able to solve 3 questions completely, and all 3 were fully accepted. The 4th question was partially accepted.

Second Online Assessment — Late March 2024

My second Online Assessment was conducted from the college library using the college system.

There were again 4 questions:

The first question was easy and basic.
The second question was medium-level and based on Greedy.
The third question was medium-level and involved Greedy with a simple pattern.
The fourth question was a hard 3D Grid-based DP problem.

I was able to get the 1st and 4th questions fully accepted, while the 2nd and 3rd were partially accepted.

Shortlisting

After around 20–25 days, the shortlisting list was released, and I was shortlisted for the L3 role.

After around 10 days, I had both technical interviews on the same day.

Technical Interview — 28 April 2024

First Technical Round

Generally, the first technical round focused on DSA. Depending on the interviewer and the difficulty of the questions, candidates could get 2–3 DSA questions along with questions from CS fundamentals such as DBMS, CN, Software Engineering, etc.

However, the experience completely depends on the interviewer.

In my case, the interviewer asked me to open my LeetCode profile and checked whether I had solved the question before.

He then gave me a question that was tagged as Medium, but I found it much harder than a typical Medium problem. It was not from any standard DSA sheet.

I first came up with an algorithm and explained my approach to him. Then he asked me to implement it.

After implementing the solution, I got TLE.

He gave me some additional time to optimize it. I came up with an optimization idea and explained it, but my solution was still failing on some test cases.

Then he asked me to find the error myself.

I went through my solution, found the issue, and fixed it.

After that, he told me to wait for the result of the second round.

Overall, I would say my performance in the first round was average from my side. I was able to approach the problem, I wasa able to comes up with optimization and debugging but that was not accepted for all leetcode tescases.

Second Technical Round

The second round started with a short introduction, and then the interviewer directly moved to my project.

We had a detailed discussion about my project for around 8–10 minutes.

He asked questions like:

Why did you build this project?

What problem were you trying to solve?

What challenges did you face?

What is the data flow?

What is the overall pipeline?

How do the different components work together?

After that, he asked me a standard DSA question:

Find the sum of two nodes in a BST equal to a given target.

I explained my approach, and then he asked me how I could optimize the time complexity.

He also asked me about the time and space complexity of some standard algorithms.

There was no implementation in this round because the interview was conducted online.

After DSA, he asked me about how I built a website using AI/prompting. He also asked some questions related to Gen AI and how I had used AI in my projects.

Then he moved to System Design.

He asked me to design a voting machine.

I first explained the HLD and then he asked me to explain the LLD. I suggested two possible LLD approaches and explained them.

Finally, he asked me about the SOLID principles, which I explained.

There was no implementation required in the second round.

Overall, I would consider my performance in the second round excellent from my side. I was comfortable discussing my project, DSA, AI, system design, LLD, and software engineering concepts.

Final Result — 24 June 2024

After around one month, the final result was released.

I was selected for the L1 role.

Overall Experience

My overall journey was:

2 Online Assessments → Shortlisting → 2 Technical Interviews → Final Selection

The biggest thing I learned from this experience is that the interview can vary a lot depending on the interviewer.

In my case, the first round focused more on problem-solving, optimization, and debugging, while the second round covered a much broader range of topics including DSA, CS fundamentals, projects, AI, prompting, HLD, LLD, and SOLID principles.

From my side, the first round was average, while the second round went very well.

Overall, it was a great learning experience and taught me that preparation should not be limited to DSA alone.
