full_text:
My Infosys on-campus selection process consisted of two main rounds: a coding/online assessment followed by a technical interview.

Round 1: Coding Assessment

The first round consisted of 4 coding questions arranged in increasing order of difficulty. In my experience, the questions were based on standard and commonly practiced DSA concepts. They were not necessarily based on unusual or unfamiliar topics, but someone who has not practiced enough problems might find them difficult, especially when trying to understand the problem statement and identify the underlying pattern.

I would recommend having a good amount of practice on platforms like LeetCode before the assessment. Rather than focusing only on solving a large number of questions, it is useful to understand common DSA patterns and recognize when to apply them.

Round 2: Technical Interview

After clearing the coding round, there was one technical interview. The interview started with two coding questions, out of which I was asked to solve one. Compared to the coding assessment, these questions were relatively easier, although the problem statement was somewhat lengthy or bit tricky.

After the coding part, the interviewer asked questions about the projects mentioned on my resume, including the technology stack I used and the basic architecture of my projects. Since I had worked with React, I was also asked some basic React concepts such as props, hooks, and their usage.

I was then given a small React-based coding task to write. The interview mainly focused on whether I understood the technologies and projects I had mentioned rather than just knowing definitions.

Preparation Tips

My main advice to future candidates would be:

Practice DSA problems consistently, particularly on platforms such as LeetCode.

Focus on understanding common problem-solving patterns rather than memorizing solutions.

Be thorough with every project mentioned on your resume. Be prepared to explain the tech stack, architecture, your individual contribution, and important implementation decisions.

If you mention a framework such as React, make sure you understand its fundamentals, including components, props, state, hooks, and basic implementation.

During coding rounds, read the complete problem statement carefully and manage your time according to the difficulty of the questions.

When practicing, try to read and understand the problem statement yourself before watching a solution or having someone explain it. If you are following a DSA playlist, it can be tempting to immediately listen to the explanation. However, practicing reading the question independently helps you develop the habit of quickly identifying what the problem is asking, even when the statement is lengthy or worded differently from what you are used to.

Try to solve problems under a time limit occasionally. This helps you become comfortable with understanding the question, forming an approach, and coding within limited time.

Overall, the process gave me a good opportunity to demonstrate both my problem-solving skills and my understanding of the projects and technologies I had worked with.

full_text:
How It Started

Intel visited our campus as part of the campus recruitment process for an AI-related role. I was contacted by the HR team at Intel, and my resume was considered for the opportunity.

Round 1 — Resume Shortlisting

The first stage was the resume shortlisting round. My resume was shortlisted based on my academic background, projects, technical skills, and previous work experience relevant to the role.

After the resume was selected, I received a call from the HR team to schedule the interview. The interview was then conducted virtually through a scheduled meeting.

Interview Day Experience

The interview started with a basic self-introduction. The interviewer also wanted to understand my career journey and asked questions such as:

Why did you decide to leave your job and pursue an M.Tech?

Why did you choose this particular branch/specialization?

Tell me about yourself and your previous experience.

After the introduction, the interview moved into technical discussions based on my resume and experience.

1. Resume & Experience-Based Questions

The interviewer went through my resume in detail and asked about the kinds of technical issues I had encountered in my previous work and projects.

I was asked to explain specific problems I had faced, how I approached debugging them, and how I eventually resolved them.

There were also system-design-oriented questions around:

Microservices architecture

System scalability

Latency

Number of requests/hits a system can handle

Overall system architecture

Handling performance-related issues

2. Programming & DSA

The interviewer asked about the programming languages I had worked with and my experience with DSA.

I was asked what I had done in DSA and which concepts I was comfortable with. This was followed by a DSA problem to evaluate my problem-solving approach and coding fundamentals.

3. Project Deep Dive

A significant part of the interview focused on my projects and the technologies I had used.

The interviewer asked questions such as:

What technologies did you use?

Which packages and libraries did you use?

Why did you choose those technologies?

How does the project work internally?

What challenges did you face?

How did you identify and resolve issues?

Which Jira platform/tools did you use for project management?

The discussion was not limited to the high-level architecture. The interviewer also went into implementation and development practices to understand how familiar I was with the technologies mentioned on my resume.

4. MERN & Backend-Related Questions

Since I had mentioned MERN and related technologies, I was asked questions around the development stack and some supporting technologies.

The discussion included:

React Hooks

Lazy loading

Validation schemas

Regex

WebSockets/sockets and their basic working

Apache Kafka and its role in distributed systems

Caching and why it is used

Grafana and its use for monitoring/observability

Backend and microservices architecture

The interviewer also asked how some of these technologies could be used together in a real-world application and how they help with communication, performance, scalability, and monitoring.

5. AI/ML & Technical Skills

Since the role was AI-related, I was also asked questions around Machine Learning and Deep Learning.

The discussion included:

Transformers

LLMs

Tokenization

How transformers work at a high level

Fundamentals of AI/ML systems

The interviewer was interested in understanding both my theoretical knowledge and how well I could explain these concepts practically.

6. Core Computer Science Questions

Towards the end, the interviewer also asked some fundamental Computer Science questions, including:

What is a process?

What is a thread?

Process vs. thread

What is multithreading?

What is multitasking?

How do processes and threads work during concurrent execution?

Overall Experience

Overall, the interview covered a broad range of topics, starting from my career journey and resume, followed by project discussions, DSA, system design, AI/ML, MERN, backend technologies, and core Computer Science fundamentals.

One of my biggest takeaways from the interview was that anything mentioned on your resume can become a discussion point. It is therefore important to understand your projects and technologies beyond just their definitions — including why you used them, how they work internally, the problems they solve, and how they fit into the overall architecture.

Tips

Mention only the technologies and skills you are genuinely confident in, because anything on your resume can become a follow-up question.

Focus on understanding concepts rather than memorising definitions, especially the “why” and “how.”

Prepare thoroughly according to your resume and the job role, and answer questions confidently and clearly.

For SDE/AI/Software roles, have a strong grasp of DSA, especially easy and medium-level problems.

Don’t ignore core CS fundamentals like System Design & Architecture, DBMS, OS, Computer Networks, and OOP.

How It Started

full_text:
I'm excited to share that I interned as a Hardware Engineer at Microsoft this summer and received a Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) at the end of it. Here's how it went.

The interview process (2 rounds)

Round 1: Technical
This round tested fundamentals more than anything else:

C programming and C coding questions
Computer Organization & Architecture (COA)
Embedded systems basics
Communication protocols
Data structures: linked lists and arrays
Memory allocation
A deep dive into the projects on my resume

My biggest takeaway: know your resume inside out. Every project I listed was fair game, and being able to explain why I made certain choices mattered more than reciting definitions.

Round 2: Behavioural
This round focused on how I work with people:

Being a team player
Helping teammates
Situational questions about how I'd handle real workplace scenarios

I answered with honest examples from my own experience instead of rehearsed lines.

The internship

I worked on hardware/firmware validation, which gave me hands-on exposure to how real systems get tested before they ship:

Validating CXL sensor test cases
Working on CPER (Common Platform Error Record) decoding
Managing and organizing test cases in Azure DevOps
Applying embedded systems fundamentals in a real validation workflow

What stood out most was seeing how much rigor goes into making hardware reliable at scale. A single test case can catch an issue that would otherwise surface in production.

What I learned

Strong fundamentals (C, COA, embedded) matter more than fancy buzzwords.
Ask questions early. The people around you want you to learn.
Own your work, document it well, and be a good teammate.
Curiosity gets noticed.
Staying attentive: I paid close attention in meetings and discussions, so I understood the context behind my tasks and didn't need things repeated.
Always eager to learn: I treated every unfamiliar concept as a chance to learn. I asked questions, read up on my own, and came back with better understanding.
Being helpful: I offered help when teammates needed an extra hand, even on things outside my direct scope.
Staying in touch with my team: I gave regular updates, flagged blockers early, and kept communication open instead of working in isolation.
Asking for feedback: I asked for feedback regularly, not just at the end. It helped me correct course early and improve week over week.

The PPO

By the end of the internship, I received the PPO. I'm grateful and proud, but I also know it came from the support of my mentor and teammates, who were generous with their time and guidance.

What I learned

Strong fundamentals (C, COA, embedded) get you in the door.
Attitude, communication, and willingness to learn help you stand out once you're in.
Feedback is a gift. Ask for it early and often.
Being a good teammate matters as much as being a good engineer.

Tips if you're preparing

Revise C deeply: pointers, memory allocation, linked lists.
Know every line of your resume.
Prepare real stories for behavioural questions.
Think out loud. Interviewers care about your approach.
In your internship, be curious, be helpful, and keep communicating.

My Microsoft Internship & PPO Experience 💙✨

Internship Selection Process:

Generally, the process consists of one Online Assessment (OA) followed by two interview rounds.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The OA usually consists of 2 DSA questions, generally ranging from easy to medium difficulty.

So, having a strong foundation in DSA is extremely important. Practice consistently and focus on understanding patterns rather than just memorizing solutions.

2. Interviews

There are usually two interview rounds, but the exact structure can depend on the interviewer. Both rounds can be technical, or one can be technical while the other may include more HR/behavioral discussion.

For preparation, I would strongly recommend:

- Be thorough with CS fundamentals.

- DSA is a must, interview questions are generally around the easy-to-medium level.

- Know your projects inside out. Be prepared to explain what your project does, why you built it, the technologies you used, the challenges you faced, and how you solved those challenges.

The Internship & PPO Journey:

My biggest advice for getting a PPO would be, Stay cooperative with your manager and mentor and team.

Be open to feedback, communicate properly, and don't hesitate to ask questions. Learn as much as you can. You don't have to know everything from day one. Be curious and genuinely eager to learn. Be confident, but stay humble. Believe in your abilities while being open to learning from everyone around you.

Give your best.

Take ownership of your work, put in sincere effort, and try to continuously improve.

And most importantly. enjoy your internship! ✨

Focus on learning, contributing, building good relationships with your team and friends, and making the most of the experience.

If you do your work sincerely, keep learning, and give your best, you put yourself in a strong position for a PPO. ❤️✨

full_text:
Internship Rounds
Round 1: Online Assessment

This was a 90-minute online coding test focused on evaluating algorithmic thinking and implementation ability.

• The first question was based on tree traversal and required identifying and applying the correct traversal method to arrive at the expected result.
• The second was a string problem that involved using a greedy approach around swapping to achieve the required answer.

Topics asked: tree traversal, greedy approach, strings.
Key advice: Keep your fundamentals strong and maintain a CGPA of 8+ to stay on the safer side for shortlist criteria.

Round 2: Technical Interview 1

This was a one-on-one technical interview where the interviewer began with a short introduction and asked me to introduce myself before moving to problem-solving.

• The first question was a medium-level linked list problem. We discussed two approaches and I coded one of them.
• The second was a medium-level array and bit manipulation problem, similar to LeetCode. I completed both coding questions within 40–45 minutes.
• After the coding segment, I was asked theory questions from Computer Networks, including TCP vs UDP, the network layer, and whether two processes can run on the same port and how that is handled.
• This was followed by Operating Systems questions related to threads and the kernel.

Topics asked: linked lists, arrays, bit manipulation, TCP vs UDP, network layer, port sharing, threads, kernel.
Key advice: Stay calm, keep explaining your thoughts throughout, and avoid going silent so the interviewer can clearly understand your reasoning and code.

Round 3: Technical Interview 2

This round began similarly, with a short introduction from the interviewer followed by a brief self-introduction before transitioning into resume-focused discussion.

• The interviewer asked about a project listed in my resume, and I explained the design decisions, how I applied SOLID principles, and how I efficiently used JavaScript promises during implementation.
• The discussion then moved to OOP theory, where I was asked questions on core concepts and their application in real project scenarios.

Topics asked: project explanation, SOLID principles, JavaScript promises, OOP concepts.
Key advice: Have two strong projects instead of many weak ones, prepare them thoroughly, and maintain clear fundamentals around OOP principles.

Internship Experience and PPO Evaluation

During the internship, I worked with the Azure Firewall team on a project related to IDPS, contributing to feature enhancements and deliverables under the guidance of my mentor and manager.

The internship feedback framework had three evaluation tiers:

• If an intern does not meet the assigned task expectations: No Hire
• If an intern meets task expectations and delivers reliably: Hire
• If an intern meets expectations and additionally takes ownership by proposing and executing extra actionable work with the mentor and manager: Strong Hire

The feedback category determined the PPO pathway:

• No Hire: rejected
• Hire: required to clear two PPO interviews
• Strong Hire: required to clear only one PPO interview

I received a Strong Hire feedback rating.

Key advice: Focus on completing assigned tasks well, communicate proactively, take initiative beyond minimum expectations, and demonstrate ownership to move toward a Strong Hire outcome.

PPO Interview

This was a single PPO interview since I had received a Strong Hire rating. The interviewer was familiar with my internship work and began by asking questions related to the IDPS project I had worked on.

• The DSA problem given was an ad-hoc question. I initially wrote the most time-optimized solution, but the interviewer asked to focus on memory optimization instead. We discussed multiple approaches, moved from a BST-based idea toward a bit manipulation approach, and I coded the most memory-efficient version.
• In total, I coded two solutions(most time optimised and most memory optimised), and we verified them against sample and edge test cases successfully.
• Between the coding discussions, I was asked questions related to Computer Architecture, including how memory allocation works, differences in 32-bit and 64-bit architectures, and related practical reasoning.
• The interview lasted around 60–65 minutes.

Topics asked: ad-hoc problem solving, memory-optimized coding, bit manipulation, BST reasoning, computer architecture, memory allocation, 32-bit vs 64-bit execution.
Key advice: Be flexible with constraints, openly discuss alternative approaches, adapt your solution direction based on interviewer expectations, and maintain clarity on low-level memory and architecture fundamentals.

Final Result

The PPO interview concluded successfully, and I was selected :)

full_text:
Company: Optum
Selection Process: Online Assessment (OA), HR Interview, and Technical Interview

My placement experience with Optum was a three-stage process that evaluated practical problem-solving skills, communication, personality, and technical knowledge. Here is a detailed overview of each round, along with some preparation tips for students aspiring to join Optum.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The first stage was an AI-assisted online assessment designed to evaluate our ability to work on an existing project. We were provided with a VS Code-like development environment containing a project directory and an integrated AI assistant.

The assessment involved approximately 4–5 tasks related to frontend and backend development. We had to modify the existing code and implement the required functionalities using the provided environment. The total score was 600 marks.

My suggestions for this round:

Aim to score as high as possible, ideally securing the full 600 marks.

Make effective use of the internal AI assistant, as it can guide you through understanding the codebase, implementing features, and resolving errors.

Read each task carefully and verify that the implemented functionality works as expected.

Stay calm and manage your time effectively rather than getting stuck on a single task.

The assessment was manageable with the right approach. The key was to understand the requirements and use the available AI assistance effectively.

2. HR Interview

After the online assessment, the next stage was the HR interview. This round focused primarily on understanding the candidate beyond their resume, including their personality, interests, motivations, and approach to different situations.

Some of the areas discussed during my interview were:

Personal Introduction and Time Management

Tell me about yourself beyond what is mentioned in your resume.

What do you do in your daily life?

How do you manage your time when handling multiple responsibilities?

I spoke about my curiosity and willingness to explore new things, along with my involvement in basketball, academics, and responsibilities as a placement representative and class representative.

Understanding Optum and Motivation

What do you know about Optum?

Why do you want to join Optum?

What interests you about the company and the role?

These questions highlighted the importance of researching the company and understanding its work before the interview.

Projects and Problem-Solving

Explain a project you have worked on and the problem it solves.

Was it an individual or a team project?

How did you manage your team and handle disagreements or difficulties?

What did you do when you got stuck while developing your project?

There were also situational questions designed to assess decision-making, accountability, and the ability to handle unexpected challenges.

My suggestions for this round:

Prepare a clear and natural introduction that goes beyond your resume.

Research Optum, its healthcare technology ecosystem, and the GDP role.

Understand every project mentioned on your resume, including your specific contribution and the challenges you faced.

Prepare real examples demonstrating leadership, teamwork, curiosity, and time management.

Answer situational questions logically, explaining how you would approach the problem and communicate with the people involved.

3. Technical Interview

The final interview stage focused on technical fundamentals, projects, and situational problem-solving. The questions I encountered were not excessively difficult, but they required a clear understanding of the concepts and the ability to explain them confidently.

Computer Science Fundamentals

Some of the topics discussed included:

Differences between C and C++, and their respective use cases.

Differences between data structures such as vector and list.

Error handling and how to manage errors in the absence of conventional try and except blocks.

Core computer science concepts and programming fundamentals.

Based on discussions with other candidates, the questions could also vary according to an individual's background and technical interests. Some candidates encountered questions related to AI/ML, machine learning, transformers, and the research paper Attention Is All You Need.

Therefore, I would recommend preparing your core CS fundamentals thoroughly while also revising the subjects and technologies relevant to your resume.

Project Discussion

Projects were an important part of the technical interview. The interviewer asked about my major and minor projects, their objectives, the technologies used, and my individual contributions.

Be prepared to explain:

The problem statement and motivation behind the project.

The architecture, technology stack, and implementation.

Your specific role and the features you developed.

Technical challenges encountered and how you resolved them.

Possible improvements or alternative approaches.

Avoid limiting your explanation to the project's features. Understanding why you chose a particular technology and how the different components work together is equally important.

Situational Questions

The technical round also included situational questions to evaluate professional judgment and responsibility.

For example, I was asked how I would respond if a problem occurred in code I had worked on while I was on vacation, and my manager contacted me when I did not have access to my laptop.

Such questions assess how you prioritize issues, communicate with your manager, take ownership, and identify practical solutions. The goal is not simply to give a technically correct answer but to demonstrate sound professional judgment.

My suggestions for this round:

Revise OOP, DBMS, operating systems, computer networks, and programming fundamentals.

Practise explaining your projects in depth.

Review the technologies and concepts mentioned on your resume.

If you have an AI/ML background, revise the fundamentals of machine learning, neural networks, and transformers.

For situational questions, focus on clear communication, accountability, collaboration, and a practical resolution.

Selection Statistics

The approximate candidate progression during the process was as follows:

Stage Candidates
Shortlisted after OA 40
Progressed after HR Around 30
Final selections 11

Around 10–11 candidates were eliminated after the HR round, leaving approximately 30 candidates for the technical interview. Ultimately, 11 candidates were selected.

These figures reflect my experience of the process and may vary across recruitment drives.

Final Advice

My biggest takeaway from the entire process is that you do not need to know everything; you need to understand what you know and communicate it clearly.

For the online assessment, use the internal AI assistant effectively and focus on completing the tasks correctly. For the HR round, be genuine, confident, and well-informed about Optum. For the technical round, strengthen your fundamentals and prepare to discuss every project on your resume in detail.

Most importantly, do not underestimate situational questions. They provide an opportunity to demonstrate how you think, take responsibility, and approach real-world challenges.

All the best to everyone preparing for Optum. Stay consistent with your preparation, trust your fundamentals, and give your best!

full_text:
My Optum hiring process had three stages: an online assessment, an HR round, and a technical interview. I'm sharing my overall experience so that juniors know what to expect and can prepare in the right direction.

1. Online Assessment

The assessment was practical and project-based rather than a typical MCQ or DSA test. It involved working with an existing project that had multiple files across the frontend and backend, and there was an AI assistant available during the test. It gave me a good sense of how real-world projects are structured.

Tip: Be comfortable reading and understanding an unfamiliar codebase. Knowing how the different parts of a full-stack project connect will help you much more than memorizing syntax.

2. HR Round

The HR round took place a few days after the assessment. It was a general conversation about my background, my motivation, and my personal experiences.

Tip: Be genuine and prepare real examples from your own life. Know why you want to join the company and be clear about your goals.

3. Technical Interview

The technical interview was held the next day and was mostly project-focused. I introduced myself and walked the interviewer through my projects. The interviewer was friendly and made me feel comfortable, which helped me stay confident. The discussion also touched on modern topics like LLMs and AI agents.

Interviews can vary a lot from person to person. Some of my friends were asked more coding and DSA-based questions, so it's best to be ready for both.

How to Prepare

Know your projects inside out: the architecture, your tech choices, the challenges you faced, and what you would improve.
Practice working with multi-file projects (frontend, backend, APIs, databases).
Learn the basics of LLMs and AI agents.
Keep your DSA, SQL, and basic coding in Python or C ready, but focus mainly on your projects.
Prepare clear, honest answers about yourself and your motivation.

Overall, it was an enjoyable process and I learned a lot. Good luck to everyone preparing!

There were three rounds in the placement process:

1. Online Assessment (OA)

It was an AI-assisted test where we were given a repository and access to an AI tool called Cosmos. We were strictly advised to use that AI, as it could generate code, find errors, and even correct the code. The only limitation was that it wasn’t an agent, so it couldn’t automatically paste the code into the repository. Honestly, the process was mostly about using the AI, copying the generated code, and pasting it into the repo.

2. HR Round

This was a basic HR round and lasted around 15 minutes. I was asked about the CEO of Optum and UHG, so it would be good to prepare basic information about the company and its leadership.

3. Technical Round

The technical round mainly focused on projects and CSE fundamentals, especially DBMS and OOPs. There were also some basic DSA questions, where they either asked for the approach or a simple implementation. For example, I was asked about finding duplicate numbers in an array. They also asked about GitHub commands, Linux commands, and why I chose the technologies in my tech stack.

by-pooja kumari

The selection process consisted of 3 rounds:

🔹 1. Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an online assessment designed to evaluate problem-solving and technical skills.

The OA included coding and technical questions, with the main focus being on logical thinking, programming fundamentals, and solving problems efficiently.

The key areas to prepare for were:

Data Structures & Algorithms
Problem-solving
Programming fundamentals
Time & Space Complexity
Core Computer Science concepts

The assessment required understanding the problem carefully and coming up with an efficient approach rather than simply writing code.

After clearing the assessment, shortlisted candidates proceeded to the interview rounds.

🔹 2. HR Interview

The second round was the HR interview. It focused mainly on my background, communication, motivation, and situational questions.

Some of the questions asked were:

Tell me about yourself.
Why did you choose Software Development despite being from Electrical Engineering?
Why do you want to join Optum?
Tell me about your internship experience.
What was your major role in your team?
How do you collaborate with your team members?
How do you handle conflicts within a team?
What would you do if a team member was underperforming?
Questions related to my academic background and placement process.

Since I come from an Electrical Engineering background and was interviewing for a Software Development role, the interviewer specifically asked about my transition into software development.

The round was not just about giving prepared answers. The interviewer also wanted to understand how I communicate, approach different situations, and explain my decisions.

One important tip is to listen carefully to the question and answer according to your actual experience rather than giving memorized answers.

🔹 3. Technical Interview

The technical round was the most detailed round and focused on a combination of DSA, projects, technical fundamentals, and practical problem-solving.

Some of the questions discussed with me were:

Find a duplicate element in an array.
Explain your approach and time complexity.
A puzzle involving balls where one ball had a different weight.
Another logical puzzle.
Suppose you are given a very large file, such as a 10 GB file. How would you process it efficiently?
How would you read the relevant portions of a large file?
What type of database would you suggest for storing large amounts of data and why?
Questions related to databases and APIs.
Explain your projects in detail.
What was your major contribution to the project?
How do you work with team members?
How do you handle conflicts while working in a team?

A significant part of the technical discussion was also based on my projects. I was asked about the technologies I used, project architecture, database choices, APIs, challenges I faced, and my individual contribution.

The interviewer was interested not only in the final answer but also in how I approached the problem and explained my reasoning.

The technical round was not limited to theoretical definitions. Being able to explain concepts clearly and apply them to real-world scenarios was important.

Preparation Strategy

For preparation, I focused mainly on:

DSA and common coding problems
OOP concepts
DBMS and SQL
Computer Networks
Time & Space Complexity
Backend and API concepts
Project architecture
Resume-based questions
Logical puzzles
HR and situational questions

I would strongly recommend knowing your resume and projects thoroughly. Interviewers can easily move from a project to a technical concept, then to a coding problem or a real-world scenario.

For DSA questions, practice explaining your approach before jumping directly into the code. Understanding the time and space complexity is equally important.

Final Verdict

Overall, the Optum interview process was challenging but a great learning experience. The questions covered a wide range of areas, including DSA, logical reasoning, projects, technical fundamentals, and real-world scenarios.

After successfully completing all the rounds, I was finally selected and received an offer from Optum. 🎉❤️

The entire journey taught me that consistent preparation, strong fundamentals, knowing your projects well, and staying calm during the interview can make a big difference.

For anyone preparing for Optum, focus on DSA, core CS fundamentals, project knowledge, problem-solving, and communication. Most importantly, be confident about everything written on your resume and be ready to explain your thought process.

And finally, all the preparation paid off — I got the offer! 🎉

The Optum placement process consisted of three rounds: an Online Assessment, an HR round, and a Technical Interview.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an AI-assisted coding assessment. We were provided with a repository containing the problem statement and project setup, along with access to Cosmos AI.

We were specifically instructed to use Cosmos AI to solve the given problem, so the assessment focused not only on coding but also on how effectively we could understand the problem, interact with the AI, debug the solution, and integrate the solution into the given codebase.

2. HR Round

The second round was an HR interview. It mainly focused on behavioral and situational questions.

Some questions were based on situations such as:

How would you handle a disagreement with a teammate?

How do you handle pressure or deadlines?

How would you react if you made a mistake?

Questions about teamwork, communication, and adaptability.

Overall, this round focused more on understanding my behavior, communication skills, and approach toward different situations.

3. Technical Interview

The final round was a technical interview of around one hour.

The interview started with a basic DSA problem, where I was asked how I would find a duplicate element in an array. I was not required to write the complete code; the interviewer mainly wanted to understand my approach and thought process.

After that, the discussion covered several core CS and software engineering topics:

OOPs: Classes, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, encapsulation, and applying OOP principles to real-world problems.

Database Design: Designing a database using OOP principles and explaining the relationships between different entities.

Operating Systems: Basic OS concepts such as processes, memory management, and related fundamentals.

Linux: Basic Linux commands and their use.

AI and ML Concepts: Basics of LLMs and how they work, Basics of Deep learning and real world AI applications(other then common ones).

Prompt Engineering: How to write effective prompts and improve the quality of AI-generated responses.

Git & GitHub: Learn important github commands and their work. How you can manage merge conflicts.

full_text:
I am happy to share my placement experience for the Optum Technology Development Program role .The overall process was smooth, and the interviewers were very supportive and friendly throughout.

Online Assessment — AI-Integrated Coding Assessment

The first stage was an online coding assessment. Instead of traditional coding questions, we were given a pre-existing codebase along with a problem statement.

The assessment was divided into 4 tiers, where we had to progressively modify and complete the given project. The codebase had multiple files, with some parts incomplete and some bugs that needed to be identified and fixed.

One interesting part was that the platform had an integrated AI coding assistant. We could use the AI to understand the codebase, identify bugs and incomplete implementations, understand the requirements, and implement the required changes.

The AI could also provide the steps and commands required to run and test the project. This made it possible to solve the tasks without manually writing every part of the code from scratch.

After completing the assessment, I was shortlisted for the interview rounds.

⸻

Round 1 — HR Discussion

The first interview round was the HR round. It was a short and friendly discussion mainly focused on getting to know me, my interest in Optum, and my flexibility regarding the role.

The HR asked me:

A short introduction about myself
What do you know about Optum?
How did you get to know about Optum?
Are you comfortable working in night shifts or different shifts?
Do you have any preferred work location?

The conversation was very comfortable and felt more like a discussion than a stressful interview. The main focus was on communication, personality, interest in the company, and flexibility.

After this round, I received an email informing me that I had been selected for the technical interview.

⸻

Round 2 — Technical Interview

The second round was the main technical interview, and it lasted more than 60 minutes. The interviewer was very supportive and the discussion covered a wide range of topics.

It started with my introduction, followed by questions about my internship and projects. They asked about my favourite project, why I built it, my technology choices, implementation details, and challenges I faced.

I was also asked two puzzles, followed by questions on HTTP status codes, APIs, databases, traditional vs. vector databases, RAG, and cloud technologies like AWS, GCP, and Azure.

Towards the end, we discussed different data structures and DSA concepts, followed by one relatively simple DSA coding question.

Overall, the round focused on understanding my projects, technical fundamentals, problem-solving approach, and DSA knowledge, rather than simply testing memorised definitions.

⸻

Final Outcome — Offer Letter

After the technical interview, I received my acceptance/offer letter from Optum, and it honestly felt great.

I really appreciated how smooth and respectful the entire process was. The interviewers were supportive and made the conversations comfortable throughout.

⸻

Final Thoughts

If you’re preparing for Optum, I would suggest:

Be very confident about everything mentioned on your resume.
Understand your projects and internship deeply.
Be ready to explain why you chose a particular technology.
Keep your technical fundamentals and DSA concepts clear.
For the AI-integrated assessment, understand the codebase and use that Ai properly it will do everything for you.
Practice explaining your thought process while solving puzzles and coding problems.
Focus more on understanding concepts than memorising definitions.
Stay calm and communicate clearly during the interview.

The overall process was a great learning experience for me. The interviewers were genuinely supportive, and the discussions were more about understanding my knowledge and thought process than making the interview unnecessarily difficult.

That was my overall Optum placement experience. I hope this helps anyone preparing for the same process.

full_text:
I recently went through the interview process at Optum, and I wanted to share my honest experience for anyone who might find it useful. The whole process was simple, well-structured, and much smoother than I expected.

Round 1 — HR Discussion

The first round was actually the HR round, which surprised me because most companies start with technical interviews. This round was mainly about understanding who I am and how I communicate.

The HR asked me questions like:

A short introduction about myself

What projects I’ve worked on

Why I’m interested in Optum

My preferred location and some basic behavioural questions

A few questions to check communication and clarity

The conversation was very friendly and not stressful at all. It felt more like a casual discussion to check if I’d be a good fit for the company. After this round, I received an email stating that I was selected for a technical interview.

Round 2 — Technical Interview

The second round was the main technical interview. It lasted around 40–50 minutes, and the interviewer was supportive and straightforward.

Here’s what they asked:

1. Questions about my projects

They wanted to know:

What each project does, they were really interested in knowing why I only chose this particular tech stack

Also, they were asking DSA questions based on trees and graphs and also limitations of some graph algorithms, eg, Dijkstra. So be prepared for that.

What exactly do I implement

Any challenges I faced and how I solved them

They were mainly checking if I understood my work clearly.

2. Technical fundamentals

They asked basic questions:

OOP concepts

DBMS (joins, keys, normalisation)

Operating systems (process vs thread, basic definitions)

Some backend-related questions, like APIs and authentication

Nothing was extremely difficult. They were more interested in how I think rather than memorised definitions.

3. Practical scenario questions

Examples:

How I would debug an API issue

What I’d do if code works locally but fails in production

How I handle errors or exceptions

These questions tested my practical understanding, not advanced DSA.

Overall, the technical round felt very fair and comfortable. The interviewer gave me time to think and answer.

Final Outcome — Offer Letter

The next day after the technical interview, I received my acceptance letter from Optum, and it honestly felt great. I really appreciated how smooth and respectful the entire process was.

Final Thoughts

If you’re preparing for Optum:

Be confident about your projects.

Keep your fundamentals clear

Focus more on understanding than memorising

Stay calm, the interviewers are genuinely nice

That was my overall experience. I hope it helps someone who is preparing for the same!.

My interview process with Optum started with an HR + behavioral round, which lasted for about 15–20 minutes. This round mainly focused on my communication, attitude, and responses to situational questions. The interviewers carefully read everything written in the resume, so it’s very important not to include anything you aren’t confident about.

The behavioral questions were quite practical — they presented different situations to see how I would respond or make decisions. Hence, preparing well for such questions is crucial.

My projects played a significant role in the technical discussions. The interviewers were more interested in projects that had real-world utility rather than simple website clones. They asked questions like “What problem does your project solve?” and “Why did you build this project?” During my online interview, they even checked my project’s codebase and asked me to make modifications and implement additional functionality, so being hands-on with your own project is a must.

The DSA questions were of easy to medium difficulty, and most were standard problems that tested fundamental concepts. Apart from that, they also asked questions from core CS subjects like OOPs, DBMS, Computer Networks, and Operating Systems — so having a good grasp of these topics is essential.

Throughout the process, communication played a key role. Being clear, confident, and precise with answers left a positive impression. The interviewers value authenticity, so it’s better to stay honest and real rather than trying to fake knowledge or experience.

Overall, Optum’s interview experience was balanced — testing both technical understanding and behavioral competence. With the right preparation in projects, fundamentals, and communication, you can perform well in their process.

author: ANANYA BHATIA
title: My Software Engineering Internship Experience at Fidelity International
full_text:
My internship at Fidelity International was my first real exposure to how software engineering works beyond academics. The journey—from preparing for the selection process to working within an enterprise engineering team—taught me as much about communication and problem-solving as it did about technology.

During the selection process, having strong fundamentals was important. My preparation focused on DSA, OOP, DBMS, SQL, Operating Systems, and Computer Networks, along with being thoroughly prepared to discuss my resume and projects. One thing I learned is that simply knowing definitions is not enough—you should be able to explain concepts in simple words, connect them to practical situations, and clearly describe the decisions you made in your own projects.

During my internship, I worked on End User Computing (EUC) financial workflows and contributed to the reconciliation of fund data for mutual funds. My work gave me hands-on exposure to Java, Spring Boot, Angular, REST APIs, Oracle SQL, Liquibase, Jenkins, Kubernetes, Git and GitHub. I also used Jira and Confluence while working in an Agile environment.

Initially, understanding a large existing codebase, financial terminology, and enterprise processes was challenging. Concepts such as SIT, UAT, deployment pipelines, stand-ups, sprints, retrospectives, and different application environments were very different when experienced practically compared with simply reading about them. Asking questions, documenting what I learned, taking feedback from my mentors, and understanding the business requirement before jumping into implementation helped me gradually become more comfortable.

One of my biggest takeaways was realizing that software engineering is much more than writing code. I saw how a requirement moves through discussion, development, testing, reviews, and environments such as DEV → SIT → UAT → PROD before reaching users. Collaboration, documentation, version control, testing, ownership, and communication are all essential parts of building reliable software.

For students preparing for similar internships, my advice would be to strengthen your CS fundamentals and DSA, know every project and skill mentioned on your resume, practice explaining your thought process rather than memorizing answers, and don't hesitate to ask questions once you join. You are not expected to know everything on your first day—the ability to learn, adapt, communicate, and take feedback matters enormously.

Overall, my internship at Fidelity International gave me a much clearer understanding of professional software development and helped me grow both technically and professionally. It was an experience that changed my perspective from simply learning how to code to understanding how software is actually engineered in the real world.

full_text:
My Interview Experience – (4 Rounds: OA + 3 Technical + HR)

Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The first round was an Online Assessment consisting of:

MCQs on OS, DBMS, OOP, Networks
2 DSA coding questions

I cleared this round and moved to the interviews.

Round 2: Technical Interview – 1 hour 30 minutes

The interview started with a short introduction from my side. After that, the interviewer asked a wide range of questions covering Networking, OS, OOP, SQL, DSA, and my projects.

Networking Questions

Difference between Switch and Hub
How packets are delivered using a switch (with diagram)
How a router works
About ARP protocol
OSI model

I explained the data forwarding process, MAC tables, routing tables, and also drew the network diagram as asked.

OOPs Questions

Difference between data hiding and binding
Write abstraction code
Difference between compile-time vs run-time polymorphism
Write inheritance example code
Use of static keyword
Difference between overloading vs overriding

I gave definitions with examples and wrote small snippets.

OS Questions

Types of deadlock , how to prevent it.
Semaphore and mutex explanation
A question on multithreading

Project-Based Questions

The interviewer then moved to my projects:

Detailed discussion about API working
Questions on LLM (Large Language Models) – how they work
I explained tokenization, embeddings, training data, and inference with diagram.
(He seemed quite happy with my explanation here.)

Machine Learning Basics

Difference between Supervised vs Unsupervised learning and labeled and unlabeled data.

SQL Questions

He asked 2–3 SQL queries.

DSA Question

He gave me a medium-level DSA question:

“Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.” I explained my approach using sliding window and wrote the final solution.

Personal / Background Questions

Toward the end, he asked about my background and journey.

Round 3: Technical Interview (45 mins)

OOP questions

Write abstraction code and inheritance code.
Difference between compile-time vs run-time polymorphism.
He also asked about constructors, static keyword.

DSA

He gave me a DSA question which I solved using comparator sort.
He then asked in detail about the approach and how comparator sort works internally.

STL

Questions on STL.
Differences between Java vs C++.
Differences between dynamic vs static memory
usage of new and delete.

Puzzle Questions

He asked 7–8 puzzles back-to-back, mostly the common ones found on GFG.

Round 4: Technical Interview (35 -40 mins)

DSA

He gave me a medium-level DSA question, which I solved successfully.

Project Discussion

He asked about my project, its working, tech stack, and main features.

Puzzle Questions

He asked a puzzle, similar to the ones on GFG.

Personal Questions

He asked whether this was my first interview.
He also asked why I didn’t do any internship.

HR Round

A smooth and straightforward discussion about the role, location, relocation, communication, and overall fit. Nothing technical was asked here.

Result

After a long day of interviews, the results were announced, I was selected and it felt really great. All my hard work finally paid off. The Oracle interview process was smooth, well-organized, and the interviewers were very polite and supportive.

NOTE: If you’re preparing for Oracle:

Focus on strong basics in OS, DBMS, OOP, Networks.
Practice DSA regularly, especially medium to hard questions(Striver Sheet ).
Know your projects end-to-end , they ask in depth.
Prepare SQL queries and puzzles (GFG-level).
Whatever is on your resume will be asked, so revise everything well.

Final Words

That was my overall experience.

full_text:
Round 1: Technical Interview (DSA & Problem Solving)

This round focused heavily on DSA and logical problem-solving, with an initial focus on my resume.

Introduction and Project Deep Dive: After a brief self-introduction, the interviewer immediately focused on my resume. The most challenging project-related question was: “Explain how you managed to improve the API time.” I explained that the major improvement came from identifying non-dependent API calls and restructuring them to execute in parallel instead of sequentially, which significantly reduced the overall response time.

Core DSA Concepts:

I was asked to name my favorite topic in DSA, to which I replied, "Anything but Graph."

This led to a conceptual question: "What is the difference between a Stack and a Queue, and where are they used?" I used Tree Traversal as an application example.

Advanced DSA/Coding:

Following the mention of trees, he posed a coding challenge: "Implement Zigzag Tree Traversal using Stacks (not Queues)." This tested my understanding of using two stacks for alternating direction traversal.

Dynamic Programming Challenge: I was given the "Burst Balloons" partition DP problem.

Challenge: I was not able to solve it optimally but candidly explained a greedy approach (which I knew was wrong).

Max-Heap Application: The final coding question was a simulation problem involving rock collision (taking the top two largest elements, colliding them, and inserting the difference back).

Success: I correctly identified and explained the Max-Heap data structure as the optimal approach for maintaining and repeatedly accessing the two largest elements in O(log N) time for each collision.

Database Query: The round concluded with a simple SQL query (easy-level SELECT with a WHERE and a GROUP BY clause) which I was able to write correctly.

Challenges and How I Overcame Them

The Burst Balloons DP problem was a significant challenge.

The Struggle: I could only think of a greedy solution, which wouldn't work.

The Overcoming Action: I was vocal about my thought process. I explained why the greedy approach would fail for certain test cases and articulated the need for a dynamic programming sub-problem, demonstrating a problem-solving mindset and honesty.

Round 2: Technical & Behavioral Interview (Web Tech & Projects)

This round was conducted by a very senior engineer (>15 years of experience) and focused on my project's technology stack and core Web Development/Infrastructure concepts.

Web Technology & Fundamentals:

API Requests: Difference between GET and POST requests, and their respective use cases and security considerations.

CSS: Different types of CSS (inline, internal, external) and their priority.

Browser Mechanics: Browser DOM (Document Object Model) and the role of the User Agent.

JavaScript: Multi-threading in JavaScript (is it or isn't it, and the concept of the event loop/call stack).

TypeScript: Its significance (type safety, scalability) and how a browser processes it (transpilation to JavaScript).

Project and Tech Stack Review:

I was asked to explain my project's complete tech stack and, critically, justify my choice of using it.

Alternative Analysis: The interviewer then asked, "What are the alternatives to your chosen stack, and why did you choose not to use them?"

Non-Technical/Behavioral:

Career Goals: "Where do you see yourself 10 years down the line?" (A standard question to gauge long-term commitment and ambition.)

Another similar behavioral question (focusing on resilience or teamwork).

Actionable Advice

Master the "Why": For any technology on your resume, don't just know what it is, know "why" you chose it over alternatives. Be ready to discuss trade-offs, complexity, and scalability.

Ask a Relevant Question: I asked, "What kind of projects or technologies would a fresher like me be working on within the IGIU team if I get selected in Oracle?" This shows genuine interest in the specific unit's work.

Round 3: Technical Interview (CS Fundamentals & Optimization)

This round was led by a problem-solver who tested my ability to map real-world infrastructure/data scenarios to core CS concepts, focusing on System Internals, Data Structures, and critical thinking about complexity.

Conceptual Mapping (Tree Traversal/Data Serialization):

The Problem: The interviewer presented a scenario: "If you want to share a database table that stores a folder structure (id, type, parent_id) to a different computer while preserving the child-parent relationship and meeting a specific condition for transfer."

Solution: I correctly deduced that the complex data transfer condition boiled down to the Preorder Traversal of a tree to serialize the data efficiently while maintaining hierarchy.

DBMS/System Internals:

HashMaps Under the Hood: "How do HashMaps work under the hood?" This required an explanation of hash functions, array-of-linked-lists/trees, and collision resolution techniques.

Hash Algorithm Design: I was then asked to design and explain a simple hashing algorithm, testing my grasp of distributing keys to minimize collisions.

Process Scheduling: A conceptual question on Operating Systems was asked (e.g., context switching, different scheduling algorithms).

Advanced Coding & Optimization:

Large Number Arithmetic: "Multiply two large numbers such that the result is stored in a string (since it won't fit in any standard variable)." This tests array/string multiplication logic.

Trick Question on Linked Lists: The final question was to "optimise a linked list reversal," given both the head pointer and a middle pointer.

My Answer: I took a moment and then explained that it is not possible to optimize the full reversal beyond O(N) because every single node's pointer must be accessed and flipped, which is fundamentally an N operation.

Challenges and How I Overcame Them

The Trick Question: The Linked List optimization question was a deliberate trick to test my conceptual understanding.

The Overcoming Action: I stood my ground with strong logical reasoning. I explained the fundamental O(N) lower bound of the task, focusing on the definition of time complexity and the mandatory N operations required to touch all pointers. This showed conceptual clarity and confidence in my CS fundamentals.

In early August, our campus hosted the recruitment drive for the role of Associate Software Engineer. Excited? Yes. Nervous? Of course.
Like many students, this company had always been one of my dream workplaces. The entire experience — from the OA to the final HR round — tested my concepts, patience, consistency, and calmness.

Here’s my complete journey 👇

Round 1: Online Assessment

The OA consisted of:

2 DSA coding questions (medium–difficult)

MCQs based on OOPS, OS, DBMS, CN, Aptitude

The OA required strong concepts and fast thinking.
After this, around 70 students were shortlisted for interviews.

Round 2: Technical Interview 1 ( 60 mins around)

This round started directly with problem-solving and fundamentals.

🔹 DSA (Dynamic Programming)

The interviewer first asked a DP-based coding question.
After I solved it, he added extra constraints on top of the same problem and asked me to modify and optimize my solution accordingly.
I explained the updated approach, complexity, and reasoning.

Then he asked something like:
“Design a basic system for an Operating System — how would you structure it?”

I explained the high-level architecture, components, and how the system would manage processes, memory, and interactions.

This round was more detailed and tougher.

🔹 Project System Design

They asked:

Functional requirements , Data flows , How you handled API calls , Architectural explanation.

🔹 Hard DSA Problem

Interviewer gave a problem that even he found tough.
He said jokingly:
“Yeh question tum GPT ko bhi de do, shayad solve na kare.”

He gave me 15 minutes to think.

I explained:

Multiple approaches

Why the first solution had high complexity

How I optimized it

Then wrote pseudo-code

🔹 DBMS Questions

Short but conceptual.

🔹 General

1–2 quick questions.

Round 4: Technical Interview 3 (Short + DSA + Projects)

A crisp but technical round.

🔹 DSA

Full Bit Manipulation problem

One simple Linked List question

1–2 general follow-up questions

🔹 Projects

They asked about:

What I built

Key design decisions

Challenges & fixes

I concluded the interview by asking about their engineering practices, and I strongly encourage others to ask insightful questions at the end.

Final HR Round

A smooth and simple conversation covering:

Role

Location

Relocation

Communication

Fit

Nothing technical here.

Result

After a long day of interviews, the results were announced —
and I’m happy to share that I was selected 🎉

It was a moment of huge relief, gratitude, and happiness.

Key Takeaways

If it’s on your resume, it will be asked.

Practice DSA consistently — medium to hard questions.

Know your projects + system design basics thoroughly.

Prepare OOPS, DBMS, OS, CN, GEN-AI basics, and puzzles.

Stay calm even during long waiting periods.

Good communication leaves a strong impact.

If anyone wants to know more about the process,
feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn!

full_text:
In early August, Oracle visited our campus to recruit for the role of Associate Software Engineer. Excited? Definitely. Nervous? Absolutely. Oracle has always been one of those dream companies for many of us, and walking into the process knowing it involved multiple technical rounds was both thrilling and intimidating. The entire journey tested not just my technical knowledge, but also my patience, confidence, and ability to stay calm under pressure.

Here’s my complete experience — what happened, what I was asked, and what I learned.

Round 1: Online Assessment

The OA consisted of:

2 DSA coding questions, medium to difficult level

MCQs based on core CS fundamentals: OOPS, CN, OS, DBMS, and Aptitude

The questions were manageable but required clarity of thought and speed.
After this round, around 70 students were shortlisted for interviews.

Tip: Having a strong grip on DSA (especially medium–hard problems on LeetCode) and core subjects is essential to clear this round comfortably.

Round 2: Technical Interview 1 (50 minutes)

This round began with the interviewer going through my resume. The first task he gave me was:

“Explain and solve any hard LeetCode question you have done till now.”

Since I regularly practice on LeetCode and had a strong profile, I confidently explained a hard DP problem based on Partition DP. I walked him through the intuition, transitions, and complexity.

After this, he shifted toward my tech stack:

Express.js

Node.js

Socket.io

Since these were part of my major projects, I explained architecture, use cases, and implementation details.

We then discussed:

Why Oracle? (This turned into a detailed 15-minute conversation)

Explain any ML algorithm with an example

He also asked questions around:

My project decisions

System design at a basic level

Some conceptual checks

It was a smooth and interactive round.

Round 3: Technical Interview 2 (55 minutes)

This was the toughest round for me — not because of the questions, but because of the circumstances.

I had to wait from 2 PM to 8 PM for my turn. Many were getting rejected or selected before me. I had cold, sneezing, and gradual body pain as the day went on. By 8 PM, I was both exhausted and stressed — but also mentally prepared to give my best.

The interviewer for this round was extremely kind and supportive. This made a huge difference.

He took a deep dive into all three of my projects:

Architecture

Tech stack

APIs

What exactly I built

What was challenging

How I solved issues

Then came the technical questions:

Loop in Linked List detection

Diamond problem in OOP

Dynamic casting

SQL Trigger (situation-based)

Puzzle:
Four people on a shore, only two can cross at a time, one must return — minimum time?

Data Structure scenario:
Employees printing sheets but manager has priority → I answered Deque

Despite being tired, I remained composed and confident. This round tested my fundamentals, logic, and calmness. I walked out satisfied.

Round 4: Technical Interview 3 (15 minutes)

This round was very short.

The interviewer only asked:

To walk through my resume

If I had any questions for him

I asked a thoughtful question about Oracle’s engineering practices — and I recommend everyone to definitely ask questions at the end.

Final HR Round

This round covered:

Role explanation

Locations

Relocation

Communication-related discussion

General fit-check

It was straightforward and relaxed.

The Result

At around 9:20 PM, after a long and intense day, the final results were announced.
I was thrilled to see my name on the selection list — selected along with 18 others.

It was a moment of pure happiness, relief, and gratitude.

Key Takeaways

Know your resume thoroughly. If it’s written, it will be asked.

Practice DSA consistently — especially medium and hard-level problems, do CP like giving contests on leetcode ,codechef etc.

Be confident while explaining your projects.

Prepare for DP, OOPS, DBMS, OS ,GEN-AI and SYSTEM DESIGN basics, and puzzles on GFG .

Stay calm during long waiting periods. Mental stability is a big part of campus placements.

Ask questions to the interviewer. It makes a lasting impression.

Communication matters as much as technical knowledge

full_text:
My interview experience with Oracle was quite insightful and straightforward. The interviewers were very answer-oriented — they preferred concise and accurate responses rather than long explanations or stories. It’s important to give direct answers and, if you don’t know something, simply admit it instead of trying to make up an explanation.

One key observation was that the interviewers thoroughly go through your resume, so make sure you only include the skills and projects you genuinely know well. Be ready to discuss every line mentioned, and prepare well for common HR-style questions like “Why should we hire you?” or “What makes you better than other candidates?”

In the technical rounds, they asked medium to difficult-level DSA questions, but all were standard and conceptual — nothing out of the box. Apart from DSA, they also included puzzles to test logical thinking, so it’s worth preparing for those as well.

Another important point is that they might ask you to write code related to your own project, so be well-versed with its implementation details and logic. Also, don’t ignore System Design fundamentals — several candidates were asked questions on this topic.

Lastly, Computer Science fundamentals were covered in good depth, so brushing up on core subjects like OS, DBMS, and OOPs is highly recommended.

Overall, Oracle’s interview process is a great test of both clarity and depth of understanding, so focus on conceptual strength and honest, precise communication.

full_text:
Getting an opportunity to interview with PayPal was a great learning experience for me. The process consisted of four interview rounds after the Online Assessment, with each round focusing on a different aspect of my technical and interpersonal skills.

1. Online Assessment (OA)

The process started with an Online Assessment, which primarily tested my DSA and problem-solving abilities. The questions required a good understanding of common data structures and algorithms along with the ability to arrive at an efficient solution within the given time.

For me, the OA was a good opportunity to revise the fundamentals and get comfortable with solving problems under time constraints.

2.Round 1 - DSA

The first interview round was focused primarily on Data Structures and Algorithms.

The interviewer gave me coding problems and discussed my approach, asking me to explain my thought process rather than simply jumping to the final solution. I had to think through different approaches, discuss their time and space complexities, and optimize where possible.

This round taught me the importance of communicating your thought process clearly while solving a problem. Even when you are unsure about the solution initially, explaining how you are approaching the problem can make the discussion much more productive.

3. Round 2 - Development, Projects, DSA & Core Fundamentals

The second round was more diverse. It covered development, projects, DSA, and core CS fundamentals.

A significant part of the discussion revolved around the projects I had mentioned on my resume. I was asked about the technologies I used, the reasoning behind my technical decisions, and how different parts of my projects worked.

Along with this, there were DSA questions and discussions around core computer science fundamentals.

This round reinforced one important lesson for me: don't put anything on your resume that you cannot explain. If you mention a technology, project, or concept, you should be comfortable discussing how it works and why you used it.

4. Round 3 — HR Round

The third round was an HR/behavioural round, with a combination of DSA and behavioural questions.

The behavioural questions focused on understanding how I approach different situations, communicate with others, deal with challenges, and learn from experiences.

There were also technical discussions, so it wasn't purely a conventional HR conversation.

I realized that technical skills are only one part of the interview. Being able to communicate clearly, explain your experiences honestly, and demonstrate a willingness to learn is equally important.

5. Round 4 — Hiring Manager Round

The final round was with the Hiring Manager.

This round focused on System Design and situational-based questions. The discussion was more open-ended and required me to think about how I would approach real-world situations and design problems.

Rather than looking for a single "perfect" answer, the discussion focused on my reasoning, decision-making, and ability to think through a problem.

One thing that particularly stayed with me from this round was the emphasis on curiosity and willingness to learn. It reminded me that interviews aren't always about knowing everything beforehand; they are also about demonstrating how you think and how you approach something you don't know.

My Internship Experience & Learnings

Once you get the internship, the learning doesn't stop. In fact, that's where another important part of the journey begins.

My biggest advice would be:

Be curious.

Don't limit yourself to just completing the project assigned to you. Try to understand why things are being done, how the system works, and how your work fits into the bigger picture.

Participate beyond your assigned project.

Internships are also a great opportunity to participate in extra-curricular activities, team events, challenges, presentations, and other initiatives happening within the organization.

These experiences help you learn things that you may not encounter while working solely on your assigned tasks.

Interact and build connections.

Talk to your teammates, mentors, managers, and other interns. Ask questions, learn about their experiences, and don't hesitate to initiate conversations.

The people you meet during an internship can become an important part of your professional journey.

Keep learning.

You don't need to know everything when you join. What matters is being willing to learn, ask questions, take feedback, and improve continuously.

For me, the biggest takeaway from the entire experience was that an internship isn't just about completing a project. It's about learning from the people around you, exploring new areas, building relationships, and making the most of the opportunity you're given.

Round 3: HR Interview
full_text:
1. Introduction

I would like to share my interview experience with Samsung for an Embedded Software role. The recruitment process consisted of three stages: an Online Assessment (OA), a Technical Interview, and an HR Interview.

The interview process focused primarily on computer science fundamentals, data structures and algorithms (DSA), problem-solving ability, project knowledge, and an understanding of embedded systems. My experience taught me that having strong fundamentals is extremely important, and that candidates should be prepared to explain concepts in depth rather than just provide definitions.

I am sharing my experience in detail so that future aspirants can understand the recruitment process, prepare in a structured manner, and identify the areas that deserve the most attention.

2. Round 1: Online Assessment (OA)

The first stage was an online assessment consisting of questions from various computer science subjects. The questions covered a broad range of topics similar to those encountered during GATE preparation.

The assessment tested conceptual understanding across core CS subjects, along with problem-solving skills through a DSA question.

What was covered?

Computer science fundamentals across multiple subjects.

Conceptual questions similar in nature to GATE-CS Subjects.

One DSA coding question.

My experience and preparation advice

The OA required preparation across a broad range of CS subjects rather than concentrating on just one or two topics. Preparing for GATE or revising standard CS fundamentals can be helpful for this type of assessment.

I would recommend revising the important concepts from core subjects and practising objective questions regularly. Alongside theoretical preparation, students should solve coding problems consistently, as the assessment also included a DSA question.

It is important not to neglect any core subject while preparing only for coding rounds. A balanced preparation strategy covering both theory and problem-solving is more useful.

3. Round 2: Technical Interview

The technical interview was the most important and technically intensive stage of the process. The interviewer asked questions from core computer science subjects, discussed the project mentioned on my resume, explored concepts related to embedded systems, and asked a DSA question.

A. Operating Systems (OS)

Operating Systems was one of the most important areas discussed during the interview. The questions covered synchronization, deadlocks, and memory management in considerable depth.

The discussion involved understanding these concepts rather than merely knowing their definitions.

Topics to prepare from this experience include:

Process synchronization: Critical sections, race conditions, mutexes, semaphores, and synchronization mechanisms.

Deadlocks: The necessary conditions for deadlock, prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.

Memory management: Virtual memory, paging, segmentation, page faults, and related memory-management concepts.

These are suggested preparation topics based on the areas discussed, not an exhaustive list of the exact questions asked.

My main takeaway was that OS concepts should be studied thoroughly. Students should be comfortable explaining how a concept works, why it is required, and how it differs from related concepts. Interviewers may explore a topic further through follow-up questions, so memorising definitions alone is unlikely to be sufficient.

B. Computer Networks (CN)

Computer Networks was another subject covered in the technical round. The discussion reinforced the importance of having a sound understanding of core networking concepts.

Students preparing for similar roles should revise networking fundamentals and practise explaining the concepts clearly. In combination with OS, CN is an important subject to include in technical interview preparation.

C. Project Discussion

The interviewer also asked about the machine learning project mentioned on my resume.

My advice is to understand every project mentioned on your resume thoroughly. If you have implemented something yourself, you should be able to explain the reasoning behind your choices and discuss its limitations honestly.

D. Embedded Systems Concepts

The interviewer also asked questions related to embedded systems. At that time, I did not have prior experience in this area, so I was not familiar with all the domain-specific concepts being discussed.

I tried to approach the questions using concepts I already understood, particularly pointers. The interviewer acknowledged that my reasoning using pointers was correct, although he expected an answer framed specifically in the context of embedded systems.

This was an important learning experience for me. It demonstrated the value of understanding the fundamentals and attempting to reason through an unfamiliar problem rather than giving up immediately.

However, it also highlighted that general programming knowledge and domain-specific knowledge are not interchangeable. A candidate may understand the underlying programming concept but still need to explain how it applies to embedded software.

Preparation advice: Students targeting embedded software roles should revise C/C++ fundamentals, pointers, memory concepts, bitwise operations, and basic embedded-systems concepts. They should also understand how these concepts are applied in resource-constrained systems.

Candidates who do not have prior embedded experience should not assume that they cannot attempt such questions. They should explain their reasoning clearly, acknowledge what they do not know, and avoid presenting guesses as facts.

E. Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA)

The interviewer asked one DSA question related to detecting a cycle in a linked list.

This is a standard problem that tests a candidate's understanding of linked lists and their ability to design an efficient solution

Beyond obtaining the correct answer, it is useful to practise explaining the logic, discussing edge cases, and writing clean code.

4. Round 3: HR Interview

The final stage was an HR interview conducted over a call.

In my experience, this round was relatively formal and was less technically intensive than the preceding round. All three candidates who received the HR interview call were selected.

However, this was my experience with that particular recruitment process and should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every candidate who reaches the HR round will be selected in future recruitment cycles.

My advice is to remain professional during the HR discussion, communicate clearly, and answer questions honestly. Candidates should be prepared to discuss their background, interests, motivation for joining the company, and career goals.

5. Final Advice

My overall experience with the Samsung recruitment process was a valuable learning opportunity. The process tested a combination of theoretical knowledge, coding ability, project understanding, and the ability to reason about unfamiliar technical concepts.

If I were advising juniors, I would tell them to start preparing their core CS subjects early, practise DSA consistently, and avoid studying concepts only at a superficial level. It is equally important to understand the projects mentioned on the resume and to learn the fundamentals relevant to the role being targeted.

For students interested in embedded software, I would particularly recommend building a strong foundation in C/C++, memory management, and low-level programming concepts alongside the standard CS subjects.

Finally, do not be discouraged if you encounter a question you cannot answer immediately. Be honest about your limitations, explain your reasoning, and use the fundamentals you know to approach the problem logically. At the same time, treat unfamiliar questions as an opportunity to identify what you need to learn next.

I hope this experience helps future students prepare more effectively, approach their interviews with confidence, and understand the importance of strong fundamentals in technical recruitment.
